In just a few months, Kentucky Kindred Genealogy will celebrate its ninth anniversary. When I wrote my very first post, I never imagined how many cousins, readers, and fellow researchers I would meet along the way. Thank you for every comment, every email, and every shared memory. Today I have some news, and I promise it isn't goodbye.

Ritchey and I are moving to Rudyard, Michigan, a small community in the Upper Peninsula not far from Sault Sainte Marie. Our daughter and her family are relocating just across the St. Marys River to the Canadian city that shares the same name, and we simply couldn't bear the thought of being so many miles away from them. Family has a way of rearranging your priorities!

We recently made a scouting trip north, and let me tell you, the Upper Peninsula welcomed us with plenty of snow. It was quite a change from the rolling hills of home! Despite the cold, we found a place that felt right: 40 beautiful acres. Our offer was accepted, and we've already decided on a name. We'll call it Kentucky Kindred Farm, a way to honor the roots and the people who made us who we are.

Of course, a move this big takes time. Our Kentucky house still needs to sell, and there will be boxes to pack, papers to sort, and a whole lot of goodbyes. For that reason, I'll be pausing my daily posts until we're settled in our new home.

But please don't unsubscribe! Once we're unpacked, I plan to keep sharing the old family photos, wills, stories, and obituaries that have filled these pages for nearly nine years. Many of the families I've researched packed up and headed for new frontiers, so perhaps it's fitting that we're doing the same. As I told Ritchey on the drive home, "You can take the girl out of Kentucky, but you can't take Kentucky out of the girl." I'll see you from the farm.

I am on this quest to make my own Mexican-style food lately. Not sure why, but it could have something to do with the nice weather we have been having lately. I have made it one of my summer goals to find and perfect a recipe to make my own salsa. I came across Rick Bayless website (who is well known for his Mexican food), which has a bunch of different types of salsas to try.
I did try to make his recipe for Salsa Mexicana, which was good, but I think I need to try it again with really fresh ripe tomatoes from my garden. With the leftover cilantro I had, I made this recipe. I also found his website for Avocado-Cilantro Mayonnaise.
1/2 cup top-quality mayonnaise
1 avocado, pitted, flesh scooped from the skin
1/4 cup (loosely packed) roughly chopped cilantro
In a food processor, combine the mayonnaise, avocado and cilantro. Pulse until the mayo and avocado are thoroughly combined. Taste and season with salt, usually about 1/4 teaspoon.
Review: I am so in love with this mayo, it isn't funny. It is another one of those easy-to-make recipes since it only has 3 ingredients on the list, and you throw them all in the blender together. The taste reminded me a little bit of guacamole, and the color is just so pretty. It will be awesome on a sandwich...I have to go out and get some cold cuts now to try it out with. I also wonder if I could use plain yogurt instead of the mayo to make it a little bit healthier. This one is a keeper!

I was halfway through a road ride when I noticed a small red bicycle leaning against a folding table at a yard sale. Its chain was rusty, the saddle cracked, and one handlebar grip had gone missing. I slowed down, circled back, and stood looking at it longer than anyone shopping for a usable bicycle reasonably would.

It didn’t remind me of my first bike. That one wasn’t red. There was no sudden picture of a childhood driveway, no forgotten summer afternoon coming into focus. What I felt was less specific: a familiar tug toward something I couldn’t quite name. The little bike seemed to belong to everybody’s childhood, not just mine.

Standing there, I thought about Rob Penn’s book It’s All About the Bike. Penn describes the specialized neurons that store our motor skills, allowing our bodies to retain movements long after we stop consciously thinking about them. Then he asks a lovely question: why did riding a bicycle become our standard example of something you never forget?

His suggestion is that timing matters. Many of us learn to ride when we’re young, when the brain may hold on to those physical lessons especially securely. The wobbling, balancing, steering, and pedaling become something we can return to years later without starting from scratch.

But I wonder whether our attachment to cycling also lives alongside the movements themselves. The hippocampus helps form memories of experiences, including those powerful early encounters with independence. You might forget the weather on the day you first rode alone, yet retain something of the feeling: the person holding your saddle has let go, and you’re still moving. Suddenly, you can get somewhere under your own power.

Perhaps that was what stopped me at the yard sale. Not a memory of owning this particular bicycle, but recognition of what a bicycle can mean before it becomes exercise, equipment, or a way to commute.

The seller wanted twenty dollars. I paid without bargaining. I had no child in mind, no restoration plan, and no sensible answer about where I would put it.

There's no question that the use of connected devices is surging. Tablets, smartphones, and hybrid devices are selling quickly (Apple announced it has already sold 3 million of its new iPad since its launch on March 16). But how is the use of these products affecting us? Are the devices actually changing the way we live?
Perhaps. Data from the Pew Research Center seems to suggest these devices are making us more avid consumers of news. It stands to reason that having access to pretty much every news site in the world at the tips of our fingers might make us more inclined to read news, and the data backs up that assertion.
Pew Research Center says new consumption is a big part of what we do on most consumer electronics devices. Among desktop/laptop owners, 70% receive news on their computers. Half of smartphone owners use their phones for news, and 56% of tablet owners use their devices for news.
But Pew says news consumption on mobile devices is especially heavy. And often, these users are consuming news on multiple devices. For instance, 34% of desktop/laptop news consumers also get news on a smartphone. And 27% of smartphone news consumers also get news on a tablet.
So, using mobile devices appears to correlate with a healthy consumption of news. I'll let readers draw their own conclusions about whether that means connected-device users are better informed. But it does seem to indicate connected devices have the potential to make news reading more of a habit.
This should be of note to educational institutions. Perhaps reading news on a tablet would make it more exciting for school children. Of course, I don't believe we should instantly throw out all the textbooks and worksheets and perform every learning task on a digital screen. But the fact is, mobile devices are increasingly a part of everyday life, and people without access to these devices run the risk of being left behind.

Since coming home from Svalbard, I’ve felt like an old cathode-ray television struggling to find its signal. The picture doubles, flips, then warps at the edges. For a moment everything lines up; then two versions of the world slide across each other again.

There’s jet lag, of course. A nine-hour time shift is enough to make breakfast feel like an administrative error. But sleep isn’t the whole problem. Most of this disorientation is emotional: I’m home, while some stubborn part of me is still in the Arctic, reluctant to catch up.

I hope the next few weeks will help those two perspectives settle into a single picture. Writing about the journey seems a good place to start.

There’s plenty I want to tell you. About our tough female guides, and the particular reassurance of being in their capable hands. About Pyramiden, the abandoned settlement whose emptiness deserves more space than I can give it here. About flying snails, afternoon cake elevated to a daily ritual, and the slightly odd business of collecting dead specimens for a colleague. And about our captain, whose gruffness and geniality turned out to be perfectly compatible.

Much of what I brought back isn’t photographic. During the trip, I mostly recorded audio, gathering material for what I hope will become a downloadable sonic journey to the Arctic. I want to give you something you can listen your way into, rather than simply look at.

Why sound, rather than visuals? That deserves a post of its own, and I’ll return to it.

For now, I’m letting the picture flicker.

The Supreme Court seems to be a lot more savvy than the California lawyers pushing for game restrictions have bargained for. There are plenty of places online with transcript excerpts, and after reading some of those, I've got a whole new respect for some of those justices.
Oh, and Postal 2 was the main example California was using as something that should be restricted? Talk about clueless.
Kinect launched last night, but you didn't find me standing in line for one. The launch software is stunningly unimpressive, on top of the fact that it seems as though every games journalist in the world has forgotten that Sony's EyeToy ever existed.
I own an EyeToy, and I've played the Kinect several times, and the two are basically the exact same thing. Of course, the Kinect is more advanced and (probably) better tech, but the fact remains that the two share the same general concept and perform essentially the same functions. Given this, I find it incredibly puzzling that not a single review or article I've read so far ever compares the two. Someone alert Rod Serling.
Gameplay-wise, I bailed on Red Dead Redemption's campaign for the time being. I might come back to it, but I had too many issues to really get immersed in it. Instead, I loaded up the Undead Nightmare DLC, and although I only put a little bit of time into it, it's been a fun ride so far. I'll probably finish it up and then save the rest of Dead Redemption for some rainy day.
Apart from that, I've been juggling too many things... playing the co-op in Splinter Cell: Conviction with the wife, doing a level or two a day of Defense Grid, and still plinking around with Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker.
I should really pick one or two of these and just power through, but while I'm sort of vaguely enjoying them all, none of them has really captured my attention or has engrossed me to the point that I'd put everything else on hold.
Hopefully something that knocks my socks off will come down the pipe sooner rather than later… can't say that I'm really a fan of feeling mired in the middle of so-so software.

Lately, I’ve been spending my spare time working on gdx-setup-ui, the desktop tool that handles the less exciting side of starting a libGDX game: generating and configuring the Eclipse projects for libGDX and its various backends. My goal is simple. You should be able to spend your time writing your game, not sorting out project settings.

Since version 2, gdx-setup-ui has also supported adding third-party libraries when you create a project. Select the libraries you want, and the tool puts their jar files in the appropriate folders and updates the classpaths automatically. That means less manual setup and fewer opportunities to miss a dependency before you have even started building anything.

The library selection is still fairly small, but I’m planning to expand it. A post-processing library is among the additions I’d like to include, giving developers another useful option without adding more configuration work.

The latest feature takes that same approach beyond project creation. You can now update an existing project to the latest libGDX release and add or update third-party libraries in one step. Rather than treating setup as something that only happens at the beginning, I want the tool to help keep projects current as they develop.

Before I make a stable release, though, I’d really appreciate some help testing it. My free time is limited, and there are only so many project configurations I can try myself.

If you use gdx-setup-ui, please give the beta a try and report any bugs you find. Details about your project and the steps that caused the problem will be especially helpful. Your feedback will help make the next release more reliable for everyone.

As a complete newcomer to the virtual world of Second Life, I recently had the pleasure of attending a grand celebratory event at the newly opened Discovery Educator Network virtual headquarters. The festivities kicked off with an official ribbon cutting ceremony led by the chair of the leadership council. As they cut the ribbon, the chair announced, "This space will truly bring our global educators together." It was a fantastic way to officially open the doors.

The ground floor immediately served as a welcoming social hub for all attendees. Organizers were generously handing out fun virtual giveaways, including branded shirts and glowing necklaces, to get everyone in a festive mood. There was also a raffle, and to my absolute surprise, I won a private tutorial session. This was incredibly welcome news. As a beginner, I have been struggling to follow the fast-paced text chats, navigate my way through dense crowds of avatars, and figure out the mechanics of learning how to fly. Getting some one-on-one guidance is exactly what I need right now.

After mingling downstairs, I made my way upstairs to find a vibrant dance floor. The music was energetic, and the space was packed with lively participants taking advantage of the preset dance moves. It was highly entertaining to watch everyone let loose, especially the attendees who showed up in elaborate and creative avatar costumes. 

The highlight of the tour awaited on the rooftop. We were treated to a mesmerizing demonstration of a holographic emitter. The device seamlessly cycled through various immersive scenes, transforming the space into a theater, a serene park, and even a swimming pool right before our eyes. 

I want to extend a huge thank you to the organizers for putting together such a wonderful experience. I took plenty of screenshots throughout the evening and compiled them using an online slideshow tool so you can all see the magic for yourselves.

Every so often I sit down and take stock of what I'd love to add to my gaming shelf. Call it a wishlist, call it window shopping, call it a slow form of torture. Here's what's currently rattling around in my head.

First up is Joseph Bloch's revised Castle of the Mad Archmage. I've always had a soft spot for megadungeons, those sprawling, level-after-level monsters that can fuel a campaign for years. Seeing this one get a fresh revision has me itching to flip through it and steal shamelessly.

Next is The Dungeon Dozen by Jason Sholtis. It's a book of d12 tables (that's a twelve-sided die, for the non-gamers) packed with weird, inspiring dungeon ideas. I'm a sucker for random tables. Roll a die, get a spark, run with it. My players never know what's coming, and honestly, neither do I.

Then there's the Savage Worlds Horror Companion. Confession time: I've never actually played Savage Worlds. Yet I keep circling back to it, and the horror supplement keeps calling my name. Maybe this is the year I finally give it a shot.

Ben Robbins' Microscope is another one I can't stop thinking about. It's a "fractal" role-playing game with no game master and no prep, where players build a history together, zooming in and out across eras. Even if I never ran a full session, it would be a fantastic tool for creating a campaign setting with my group instead of for them.

I'm also waiting on the next issue of John Stater's NOD zine. His Blood & Treasure rules are what I'm using for my current dungeon campaign, so every issue feels like a care package of fresh material.

Bonus wants? A few GURPS sourcebooks, which are great reading even when you're not playing GURPS, and Tome of Horrors 4, because you can never have too many monsters.

Now for the reality check. I recently bought a custom bass guitar, and my wallet has not stopped complaining. Gaming and music are both hobbies I love, and right now they're arm-wrestling over the same budget. So this list may stay a wishlist for a little while. "Patience," as they say, "is a virtue." I'm working on it.

When things go quiet here, it usually means life has become anything but quiet. I wish this latest silence meant I’d been busy with lovely adventures. Mostly, though, I’ve been trying to get through the days without falling apart in the supermarket.

That smiling photo of me running along the harbor promenade in the rain? Completely genuine. The wind was ridiculous, my socks were soaked, and I laughed all the way back. For a little while, there was nothing to do but splash through puddles and keep moving.

Right now, emotionally, I feel more as though someone has taken a cheese grater to my heart and then suggested a refreshing bath in lemon juice. Subtle, I know.

It feels unfair to wave vaguely at a disaster and refuse to explain it. I understand how frustrating that can be to read. But telling the whole story would be unfair to me, and to other people whose lives overlap with mine. Some things need privacy, even when keeping them private feels terribly lonely.

What puzzles me is how easily I can admit this to strangers. Why is typing into an empty box sometimes easier than answering someone I love when they ask whether I’m okay? Perhaps here I can finish a sentence without having to manage the look on anyone’s face.

To my friends and family who have called, checked in, and quietly stayed close: thank you. My clumsy replies don’t mean your kindness hasn’t reached me.

I hope things get easier soon. Until then, I’d like this little corner to remain somewhere I can come without pretending to be cheerful, and perhaps find something cheerful anyway.

Tonight, I’m borrowing a hopeful chorus:

“Keep on the sunny side,
Always on the sunny side,
Keep on the sunny side of life.”

Two milestones snuck up on me this week, and I celebrated each one in its own fitting way.

The first was my birthday. I spent part of it at thirty-some thousand feet on a JetBlue flight, somewhere over Arkansas, while a lightning storm lit up the clouds outside my window. I ordered a whiskey, raised a quiet toast to another year, and watched the sky flash like a giant, unruly strobe. As a photographer, I couldn't help thinking, "Now that's a light source."

The second milestone is this very post, the 1,700th on the Visual Science Lab blog. For that one I brewed a pot of premium Jamaican coffee, the good stuff I save for special occasions. Many of these posts were written over a steaming cup.

The photo I'm sharing is a behind-the-scenes shot from a three-day shoot in New York with my colleague, Nick. We had a simple but fun system: each of us chose a model from a stack of headshots, and then we took turns photographing. It kept the energy high and gave us a chance to see how differently two people approach the same afternoon.

I loved the bustle of New York, the crowds, the pace, the sheer density of everything. But stepping off the plane in Austin, I felt my shoulders relax. I'll take the calm and the open space every time.

Coming up soon are thoughts on our changing photography market and hands-on reviews of several cameras: the Sony A7 and A7r, the Panasonic G6 and the Olympus E-M1. I'll also be reviewing a monolight and some inexpensive softboxes.

My teenage self would be horrified. Back then, I had very little patience for the monarchy and certainly wouldn’t have imagined myself happily sewing a Jubilee dress. Yet here I am, swept along by the patriotic mood of the summer, watching the Olympic torch go past and finding it all rather lovely.

Perhaps it’s the sunshine, or simply the pleasure of having something cheerful to join in with. Whatever the reason, Storm now has a new dress, and I’ve apparently made peace with a little flag-waving.

The dress is Tallulah, a halterneck sundress from Jenifer Paganelli’s Girls World pattern book. I originally intended it to be a birthday present, but the hot weather persuaded me that keeping a finished summer dress hidden away would be silly. So she’s had it early, with plenty of opportunity to wear it while the sun is actually shining.

I used the bunting print from Moda’s Sweetwater range. Despite being an American fabric, it feels perfectly at home in a British summer: cheerful strings of flags, just right for Jubilee celebrations without making the dress something she can only wear for one occasion. I do like a seasonal sewing project that still has a life beyond the event.

The pattern itself prompted rather less enthusiasm in places. The fabric requirements are decidedly generous, to the point of being overstated. It’s frustrating when you’re planning a project and buying fabric, particularly if you’re trying to keep the cost sensible. Next time, I’ll look much more closely at the pieces before deciding how much yardage I really need.

I also found that the front piece needed trimming. Nothing disastrous, but worth mentioning for anyone else making the Tallulah dress. Once that was sorted, I finished the hems with two neat rows of stitching, a small detail that gives the finished dress a lovely, tidy look.

Storm celebrated her new outfit by playing guitar for the photographs. A halterneck sundress and a musical performance seem a perfectly good combination to me, even if they weren’t quite the birthday reveal I’d originally planned.

And, because apparently there’s no stopping this royal-themed turn of events, there’s a placemat to acknowledge too. Teenage me would definitely have rolled her eyes. Present-day me is enjoying the summer.

Of all the knitting bags I have made (it might be JUST short of 100), Amy Butler's Stash N Dash is one of the top 3. It is perfect for knitting on the go (which I do a lot), small projects (my current obsession), socks and gifts. I made the biggest Toiletry Bag, and it is perfect. I have decided I can use it as a project bag- in which I only have to pull out my needle, zip it and knit. It holds my yarn, tangle-free and keeps it from rolling all over. This is also perfect when just knitting on the couch (keeps my yarn from little fingers) or at the Doctor's office. The strap hangs from your wrist so you can wear your yarn and quickly stash it away. The toiletry bag is also great for notions, a wristlet for quick shopping trips, or a treasure bag for a little lady or man to tote their polished rocks, shiny coins or red marbles around. Oh, and the bag is more spacious inside than it looks on the outside.
The Stash N Dash is quick to cut and sew up. I used a combo of quilting cotton (strap and top of bag) and home dec (lining and bottom of the bag), so I just interfaced the quilting cotton. Some more bags are definitely coming up, and I am thinking of adding the straps or a little loop to hook a strap onto the smaller bags. These bags are a great option for Christmas presents because you can create a set in any fabric to match the recipient: dupioni silk for my sister-in-law, funky cotton for my mom and solids for my mother-in-law. These are also great teacher gifts, neighbors and the friend who has everything.

David Brenner was the first stand-up comedian I recall laughing at. As a kid, I would always get excited when he'd be on The Tonight Show or one of the ubiquitous daytime talkers such as Mike Douglas or Merv Griffin. He just had such an easy, likable way, and his routines made me think about the comedy in everyday life. It made a huge impression on me, even as a kid. I remember he had a bit about his car breaking down. He looked under the hood, even though he knew nothing about cars, waiting for a flashing light that said "Fix me! Fix me!" I asked my mom, "How did you get that job?"
I also felt kinda bad for Brenner when it seemed a new generation of more cynical comics pushed him to the margins a bit in the 1980s. And I recall his late 1980s late-night show, launched amid a crowded herd of such shows. His, like most of the others, was doomed to fail. I remember rooting for the show to work (it mostly didn't) because he was so earnest and clearly loved just being there, having the opportunity to talk to celebrities for a living.
This quote from his obit supports that memory of his glad-to-be-there disposition:
"I come from the slums of Philadelphia, and everything in my life is profit. My downside is what most people would strive a lifetime to get to."
We will miss you, David Brenner. Here's a great clip of Brenner on Letterman from several years back. It's past the prime of his career, but it's a terrific example of his gift of humor in observation of everyday life. It's not Louis CK, but not everything has to be.

There are few things I enjoy more than a good cup of tea. Breakfast tea, something fruity, a warming spiced blend: I’m happy to make room for all of them. But if I have a choice between tea bags and loose-leaf tea, loose leaves win every time. For me, the flavour is fuller and more satisfying, and the little ritual of making a pot is part of the pleasure.

I started with a simple cup infuser, which was a handy way to explore loose-leaf tea without committing to a whole pot. These days, though, the piece of kit I reach for most is my WMF teapot.

I bought it through Teapigs more than three years ago, and it has become one of those purchases I’m genuinely glad I made. It even survived my move to Norway. The same teapot is still available online, which is lovely to know when people ask about it.

What makes it such a favourite isn’t anything complicated. The removable strainer does a brilliant job of keeping the leaves out of my cup, and I can lift it out once the tea has brewed to my liking. That means I’m not leaving everything to get stronger while I work my way through the pot.

Then there’s the tea-light warmer underneath. It keeps the tea at a lovely drinking temperature for hours, making it ideal for a slow afternoon when one cup simply isn’t enough. And the spout pours without dripping, a small detail that makes an enormous difference when you use something regularly.

As for what goes into the pot, Suki Tea is my preferred supplier. My current selection covers most moods: breakfast tea for a familiar, comforting brew, fruit blends when I fancy something different, and spiced teas and chai for those moments when I want a cup that feels particularly cosy.

I still enjoy trying different varieties, but having a reliable teapot makes returning to my favourites even better.

We have all heard the famous rule that guarantees expertise if you just put ten thousand hours into an activity. It sounds like a comforting formula, but the truth is that this popular reading of researcher K. Anders Ericsson drastically misrepresents his actual findings. Accumulating hours on a clock is simply not enough to achieve true mastery in any field.

Think about the mundane things we do every single day. Just repeating a task for years, whether that means walking around your neighborhood or making the same type of sales pitch, does not automatically produce improvement. Casual practitioners eventually hit a performance plateau where they just stop getting better. What actually matters is deliberate practice. This involves intense, highly focused effort aimed specifically at refining your technique and raising your overall performance level.

Deliberate practice is exactly what allows top performers to push past the frustrating plateaus where the rest of us stall out. It is important to note that this kind of work is incredibly demanding on both the brain and the body. In fact, the physical and mental effort required is so intense that some true experts need a period of rest after just one single hour of practice. As experts often remind us, "Mastery comes from quality practice, not accumulated time."

The good news for anyone looking to improve today is that meaningful progress does not need to wait for thousands of hours to pass by. You can begin to build incredible skills gradually through short, focused practice sessions. For instance, you might concentrate fully on improving your approach during a single, everyday sales call, practice truly attentive listening in your next meeting, or commit to writing purposefully every single day. Ultimately, it is the quality of your engagement that changes your trajectory, proving that focused habits are worth much more than mindlessly logging hours on a clock.

France – Today's Tour de France TTT stage was a great inside look at the racing that takes place within a race, especially during a 3-week-long Grand Tour.
At the start of every major stage race, each team will come with a clear set of goals and objectives, many of which do not include winning the overall itself. Realistically, there are only a handful who are competing for the Tour de France GC, with others content to focus on the possibility of stage wins, or one of the other classifications such as the Green jersey points competition, Polka Dot mountain jersey competition or White Best-Young-Rider jersey competition. Aside from that, some teams may be simply shooting for a strong showing to prove that their invite was worthy and thus giving them a platform to build on, or to get in some key breaks and garner a little TV time for their sponsors. It all has very real, very tangible value.
In the case of Team Argos-Shimano, their Tour de France presence is very clearly built with a primary focus on the flatter sprint-finish stage wins, such as Stage 1, which went to Marcel Kittel. This doesn't mean that other opportunities will not present themselves along the way, or that strategy won't shift if circumstances do–but, as long as the race is not dictating any change in priorities, their mission remains true.
In a day like today, while Argos-Shimano does have some of the world's best TT'ers, the 9-man squad as a whole was not really in contention for this stage win, nor will they tell you they are gunning for the Tour de France overall, so how they rode spoke to their total race-long strategy. It was a day to go hard but not take any unnecessary chances. No reason to over-tax anybody. With more sprint stages and opportunities ahead, focus instead on putting in a good effort, getting through safely, and delivering all nine men to the finish line. So, on the surface, it might be easy to look at Team Argos-Shimano's last-place TTT finish and ask, "What happened?", but in truth, the team rode exactly the race they wanted to today.
17 days to go and lots of racing ahead.

I’m starting the 30 Book Challenge, but I’m bending the format a little. Rather than answering one prompt a day, I’ll tackle several in each post. Some questions invite an essay; others need barely a sentence. This seems a happier arrangement for everyone.

First up: my favorite book. Surely that depends on when you ask? What I want from a novel changes with my mood, and comparing books across genres feels faintly ridiculous. A comforting reread and a book that completely changes my perspective earn their places in different ways.

Still, the best thing I read this summer was a biography of Lawrence of Arabia. It’s the one I keep returning to in my thoughts. Beyond that, my favorites include works by Victor Hugo, Roald Dahl, J. R. R. Tolkien, and Alexander McCall Smith. I wouldn’t want to rank them, much less choose a single winner.

My least favorite book is considerably easier: The Time Traveler’s Wife. The romance unsettled me rather than swept me away. More frustratingly, its determinism—the idea that events are fixed and unavoidable—seemed too readily accepted. I kept wanting the book to examine what that meant for responsibility and choice. Instead, the morality and internal logic left me unconvinced.

As for books that make me laugh or cry, I’m a difficult customer. I can be deeply involved without producing either an audible laugh or a tear. Joseph Heller’s Closing Time is an exception, though, and rereading McCall Smith’s 44 Scotland Street series has prompted the sort of laughter most books never quite manage.

Perhaps that’s already the lesson of this challenge: naming favorites is hard; remembering how books made me feel is easier.

Empathy is woven into the very fabric of our everyday lives, showing up in those fleeting, quiet moments we rarely even notice. You might catch yourself reading the intentions of other drivers at a busy intersection to avoid a collision, sensing the anxious urgency of a stranger standing behind you in a grocery checkout line, or simply sitting in silence to keep a good friend company during a difficult time. At its very core, empathy means perceiving and understanding another person's emotions or perspective. It is the profound experience of almost feeling their internal state as your own, whether you are navigating relationships at work, resting at home, or out in public spaces.

When we frame this concept through the philosophy of yoga, empathy becomes a deliberate practice of deep connection. It stands directly opposed to the ego. The ego is exactly what divides us, placing people onto opposing sides and fueling endless cycles of harsh criticism and judgment. Our ego acts as a defensive shield, sparing us from the vulnerability of actually feeling what other people feel. As one teacher says, "Ego loves to separate, but the heart longs to connect." When we let the ego lead, we lose sight of our shared humanity.

Take a moment to imagine a completely different reality. Think of a world where we simply let go of that defensive shield. What would our lives actually look like without the constant heavy burden of blame and gossip? It might seem like a distant dream, but it is a state of being we can actively cultivate right now in our own communities. 

I want to invite you to try a simple daily practice. Consciously choose to suspend judgment today. When you feel the familiar urge to criticize someone else, pause for a moment. Breathe, and purposely widen your emotional view to truly see the other person. By consistently leaning into this kind of empathy, you can genuinely connect with others and ultimately find a beautiful, lasting sense of personal freedom.

I just opened a bottle of El Toqui Syrah, and it was corked. How do you know a corked wine? It's usually fairly obvious if you have any kind of experience with wines, but if you don't, you would probably think it was just a yucky wine. Sometimes you do get "just yucky wines" that aren't corked--they're just yucky.
This one gave no indication by the cork. Sometimes the cork will be cracked, or there will be oozing around the cork. That doesn't necessarily mean the wine will be corked, but it means beware.
What does a corked wine taste like? That's a little more difficult to explain because it depends. This one I just opened had a beautiful color, but after the nice fragrance of fruit in the room, getting closer to the glass, there was a fairly strong odor of mildew, or wet newspaper. But I have had wines that smell pretty funky on opening, but after a few minutes of air, the funk goes away, and the wine tastes fine.
This one tasted like mildew as well. This one was obvious. But other times, a wine may just be really lackluster and flat. About the only way I would know if the wine was corked or just a poorly made wine is by past experience with the wine and or vintner. This is where other reviews can be helpful as well. If I had any doubt about this wine being corked, (NW) reviewed the same wine not long ago. That's always a good check on your suspicions.
Supposedly, up to 15% of wines are corked. I think that is a greatly inflated figure. In over 25 years of wine tasting, I have seen only about 2-3% corked wines, which is why I question the legitimacy of alternative closures, but that debate is pretty well over.
At any rate, I opened another bottle of a different wine, and it was marvelous. That's the wine reviewed above! So raise a glass and remember, life is too short to drink bad wine!

I recently read a suggestion that the anime adaptation of Sailor Moon should have incorporated the manga version of Sailor Pluto. The argument was that showing Pluto openly longing to be with the other Senshi would add a layer of dramatic angst to the story. While I understand the appeal of that kind of overt emotion, I have to disagree.

Personally, I prefer Pluto's sorrow exactly as it is in the anime: a steady, understated melancholy that subtly shapes everything she does. There is something deeply profound about a quiet sadness, rather than loud emotional outbursts about wanting to fight alongside her friends.

My main complaint with the manga is how it handles her background. The text constantly claims that Pluto has endured millennia of absolute loneliness and unwavering duty, but it never actually shows us the weight of that experience. Instead of acting like a timeless, solitary guardian, she frequently gives in to outbursts that make her seem no different from the teenage heroines she is supposed to be watching over. As I see it, this is a serious characterization flaw. As one reader perfectly phrased it during a recent discussion, "How can someone who has stood alone for centuries suddenly act like an impulsive high schooler?"

I do sympathize with Sailor Pluto, but certainly not for the reasons the original story intends. My sympathy lies in the missed potential of her character arc in the manga. A guardian burdened by thousands of years of solitude deserves a quiet, dignified sorrow, not the fleeting drama of a teenager.

Every time a new creative app shows up, I brace myself for the headline. This week it's Microsoft's Acrylic, and right on cue, tech writers are asking whether it's the "Photoshop killer" or the "Flash killer." I get why. Conflict sells, and a cage match makes for a catchier story than "new tool offers interesting options." But as someone who works at Adobe, I've seen what those labels do, and it isn't pretty.

The problem is expectations. Call something a killer and anything short of total victory looks like failure. Remember InDesign? It was branded the "Quark Killer" before it even shipped. When version 1.0 didn't instantly dethrone QuarkXPress, plenty of reviewers declared it a disappointment. Yet over the next few years, InDesign kept improving, won over designers, and became a genuine success. The early verdict said more about the hype than the software.

I have personal history here, too. Before joining Adobe, I was a Flash developer, and I loved the platform. When I signed on with the LiveMotion team, my goal wasn't to wipe Flash off the map. I wanted to give people more ways to create great work, and to make the whole authoring ecosystem richer. It didn't matter. LiveMotion was stamped "Flash Killer" almost immediately, and it was measured against a fight it never picked.

Macromedia's John Dowdell has made this point well over the years: software isn't a zero-sum game. One tool's gain isn't automatically another's loss. Different people work in different ways, and they deserve choices that fit how they think.

So let's give Acrylic, and every newcomer, a fair shot. Judge it on what it does well, not on whether it slays a giant.

I've never seen other people at the grave, but always there are tributes: flowers, coins, and miniature liquor bottles. This book, too, is a kind of tribute, though Fitzgerald, surely, would rather have had the booze.
Maureen Corrigan's book So We Read On: How The Great Gatsby Came To Be and Why It Endures is truly a wonderful tribute. Those who love F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby can't help but get caught up in her passion for the book; however, even those who might not be a fan of Gatsby but are still avid readers will appreciate Corrigan's love of literature and excitement over the continuous discovery that reading brings – and "discovery" is perhaps the best word to describe this book that is part literary analysis, part history and biography, and part memoir.
The reader experiences Corrigan's trip to the deep, dark basement of the Library of Congress to spend a few days leafing through original Fitzgerald letters and drafts, and it's as adventurous as a treasure hunt. The nostalgia is easy to feel as she makes a trip back to her Catholic High School in Queens to see what students think of Gatsby, now. She makes a great case for Gatsby's initial boost in popularity (it was a flop when it was first published), arising from the Armed Services Edition paperback versions distributed to the troops during World War II.
While her portrayal of Scott and Zelda Fitzgerald is sympathetic, Corrigan doesn't sugarcoat their lives nor bypass their faults and hardships. She mentions a group of staunch Zelda supporters who blame Scott for Zelda's tragic life; however, Corrigan doesn't seem to fall into that category herself. I found it interesting that, while she might have respect for Ernest Hemingway as a writer, she doesn't respect him as a person. Her research reveals Hemingway's continuous condescension toward Fitzgerald later in their relationship. By Corrigan's standards, Fitzgerald was a much better friend with Ring Lardner.
Maureen Corrigan is the book critic for NPR's Fresh Air, and she has also been instrumental, along with the National Endowment for the Arts and local public libraries, in establishing the "One Book, One City" programs throughout the United States.
If I could think of a dream job, it would probably be doing research for a book like this.

The performance space at The Barnstable High School holds 1600 seats, and I have to think that every seat was occupied. I chose this event, entitled Passport to Spain, since they were scheduled to play one of my favorites, Concierto de Aranjuez by Rodrigo. It is marked by its fabulous Spanish guitar solo that I never tire of. I was not disappointed. The orchestra played with much love and passion for the music. What I really enjoyed was the way in which the conductor, Jung-Ho Pak, presented the event. There were over 70 students from about 5 or 6 local High Schools in attendance, which may be why the performance was more like a lecture demonstration. We were given information about all the composers and the theme and locale behind each piece. We met the Flamenco guitarist – Juanito Pascual, singer- Alfonso Mogaburo Cid and dancer- Sabrina Aviles. Each of the artists explained the major nuances attributed to each of their Flamenco forms. There was a short film with the Master, Andrés Segovia, explaining and demonstrating the many colors and "dreams" that the guitar can create. The conductor also offered information attributed to Spanish artists through the centuries. Some of the projections included works by: El Greco, Velázquez, Goya, Dali and Picasso. The musical program included works by composers: Torroba, Lara, Tchaikovsky, de Falla, Albéniz, Bizet, Rimsky-Korsakov and of course Rodrigo. The conductor brought much attention to the fact that most of these composers were not Spanish but brought to their work their own interpretations or reflections of what Spain was to them. We have all come to recognize the many flavors of these interpretations as Spanish, although they may not actually be artistically "correct". But love them we still do. The orchestra really was a joy to hear, and I was very pleased to have attended this performance. I will be choosing to go to the CCSO many times again. I only have to hop in the car for a 15-minute drive from the Inn. What a fabulous gem right at my fingertips.

Trying to locate colonial Maryland land holdings has taught me that an old warrant is rarely a straightforward guide. Instead of giving a location I can easily plot, it points toward another tract, which points toward another. Before long, finding one plantation becomes a neighborhood research project.

Benjamin Posey (I) offers a perfect example. His tract, Posey’s Chance, was described in relation to Hornfair and Hopewell, two properties he later acquired. Following those connections reveals more than boundaries. Under the Calverts’ feudal landholding arrangement, Posey leased adjoining parcels and assembled a profitable plantation of more than 300 acres. What looks like a scattered collection of names begins to emerge as a working estate.

One name in the warrants especially caught my attention: “Panquiyah Manor.” I initially assumed it was Native American. That seemed a reasonable explanation for an unfamiliar Maryland place-name, but the search took an unexpected turn.

A 1765 letter to Governor Sharpe described a large “Pancaya Manor” beside Beaverdam Manor. The spelling differed, yet the reference appeared to identify the same estate. It was the kind of discovery that answers one question while making another more intriguing: where had this peculiar name come from?

The only other source I found was Don Quixote. There, the “balsam of Pancaya” appears among impossible literary fantasies. Suddenly, the manor’s name seemed less like a geographical inheritance and more like a knowing joke.

Could colonists have borrowed it to mock the promise of an idyllic colony? I cannot turn that possibility into certainty, but it offers a compelling way to read the evidence. Beneath the formal language of warrants, patents, and leases, there may be a trace of colonial irony: an extravagant name for a place whose rewards required the practical work of acquiring land and making a plantation pay.

Some Saturdays the plan falls apart in the best possible way. Our informal Urban Sketchers meetup was supposed to center on the annual Cherry Blossom and Japanese Cultural Festival, held indoors at Seattle Center. I fully intended to spend the morning capturing kimono silks, taiko drummers, and delicate paper blossoms. Then I stepped into a cloudless sky and warm sunshine, and my good intentions evaporated. In Seattle, you don't waste a morning like that under a roof.

So I wandered outside and pointed my sketchbook at the landmarks instead.

First up was a subject I've avoided for years: the Pacific Science Center's soaring white arches. Their perfect symmetry has always intimidated me. One wobbly line and the whole drawing looks like it's melting. This time I decided to stop fighting for precision. Inspired by Liz Steel, whose loose, lively sketches I admire endlessly, I reached for water-soluble colored pencils and let my lines stay relaxed. A swipe of a water brush softened the color, and suddenly the arches felt airy rather than rigid. For the leafy tree in front, I switched to brush markers, which gave me bold, quick strokes that contrasted nicely with the delicate pencil work. It isn't perfect, but it's the first time I've enjoyed drawing that building.

Next, music drew me across the grounds. Quichua Mashis, the Andean group whose pan flutes and drums practically define summer at Seattle Center for me, were performing. Musicians are tricky subjects because they never hold still, so I sketched in fast gestures and filled in details between songs. I'll admit I'm partial to their traditional pieces over their pop covers. There's something about those breathy flutes carrying an old melody that a cover version can't match. I happily bought one of their traditional CDs before moving on.

With my energy fading, I tried one last sketch: the back of the Experience Music Project, with the monorail track sweeping past. Those crumpled, colorful curves are a challenge on a good day, and I approached them tentatively, roughing in shapes rather than committing to detail. Still, pairing the building's wild forms with the monorail's clean line made a satisfying composition.

I never did see the festival. I don't regret it one bit.

I’m a 27-year-old graduate student, and for the past three years, severe abdominal pain and bloating have shaped nearly every part of my life. Sometimes I have diarrhea; other times, constipation. But the pain is the constant, and lately, it feels like my world is getting smaller around it.

I’ve had endoscopies, a colonoscopy, imaging scans, food intolerance testing, and tests for celiac disease. Everything has come back normal. I know normal results should feel reassuring, but it’s hard to feel relieved when I’m still hurting and nobody can explain why.

I’ve tried several medications, restrictive diets, and alternative therapies, hoping each new approach would finally make a difference. None has brought lasting relief. I’ve been told I have IBS and “leaky gut,” but I struggle to accept those explanations when the treatments offered for them haven’t helped. I’m not looking for a particular diagnosis. I’m looking for an explanation that leads somewhere.

I’ve also spent two years in psychotherapy and taken antidepressants. That experience has left me convinced that my symptoms aren’t simply psychological. I understand that stress and physical symptoms can interact, but addressing my mental health hasn’t resolved the abdominal pain.

The most frightening change is food. At this point, rice and eggs are the only things I seem able to tolerate, and I’m losing weight. Eating has become something I worry about rather than enjoy.

My family is supporting me, and we’re willing to travel anywhere for answers. If you’ve experienced persistent abdominal pain and bloating despite normal tests, how did you find your next step? Was there a specialist or medical center that helped you make sense of it?

I’m exhausted, but I haven’t stopped hoping that someone can help me understand what’s happening.

When I heard the Kindle was finally making its way to Canada, I was thrilled. However, that excitement quickly turned into disappointment once I looked at the actual details. As a Canadian reader, I feel completely let down by this launch.

First, the device ships directly from the United States, which means buyers are slapped with unexpected import duties. We are expected to pay the full American price, yet we receive severely limited wireless features compared to our neighbors to the south. It feels like paying a premium for a downgraded experience.

The frustrations do not stop at the hardware. The Kindle iPhone app is missing from the Canadian iTunes store. If you want to read local news, you will find only a handful of Canadian newspapers available. Furthermore, Kindle books cannot be purchased through Amazon.ca, and it appears Canadian authors are currently unable to publish their work to the platform.

Fortunately, I am coping just fine without it. I have been reading novels on my iPhone using an app called Stanza. I buy the majority of my digital books from Fictionwise, and I am also trying out a great Canadian service called Shortcovers. For my news fix, I recently discovered PressDisplay, which handles my need for local newspapers.

Finally, the issue of Digital Rights Management really bothers me. I deeply resent that DRM prevents me from sharing a great book with a friend. As I told a fellow reader just the other day, I am seriously considering removing the DRM from the files I own, because "restricting how we share stories goes against the very spirit of reading." The current digital reading landscape here leaves much to be desired, but we will find our own ways to adapt.
