I admire France’s determination to give its language a fighting chance against the endless stream of English technology terms. A country with an academy devoted to protecting French was hardly going to let “hashtag” stroll in unnoticed. Still, the officially approved replacement, “mot-dièse,” makes me smile.

For anyone who has managed to avoid Twitter vocabulary, a hashtag starts with the # symbol, followed immediately by a word or phrase without spaces. It makes posts searchable and helps people follow a shared subject. Someone posting from the March for Life rally, for example, could add #MarchForLife so others could find the conversation.

Simple enough. But the French alternative introduces a few entertaining complications.

First, there’s that hyphen. Hashtags need to be unbroken strings, and a hyphen interrupts them. You can discuss a mot-dièse on Twitter, but you cannot turn the complete, officially approved expression into a working hashtag. The name trips over the very tool it describes.

Then there’s the question of turning it into a verb. English speakers can casually say they “hashtagged” something. What, exactly, would I be doing in French? The approved noun doesn’t make the answer obvious.

And “dièse” refers to the musical sharp sign. That symbol and the familiar pound sign look like close relatives, but their lines slant differently. Apparently, even punctuation has a case of mistaken identity.

My first instinct is to suggest “mot de hachage” instead. Yet I’m not convinced that captures the intended meaning of “hash,” either.

Perhaps that’s what I enjoy most here: one tiny symbol has managed to make translation, typography, and national language policy surprisingly complicated.

For the past six months, I have been working on a project close to my heart right here in Sackville. Our town is home to about five thousand permanent residents and roughly two thousand four hundred university students. It is a beautiful and tight knit community, but like many small towns, we need to think carefully about our economic future.

I have been focusing my efforts on organizing independent consultants and small knowledge based businesses in the area. Today, remote work and dispersed client bases mean that professionals can live absolutely anywhere. I strongly believe that small towns like ours can attract these workers without needing to invest in massive infrastructure projects. As I often tell local leaders, "Building a community that appeals to remote workers is the smartest economic development strategy we can pursue."

More importantly, relying on a multitude of tiny firms creates a far more resilient and diverse economy than depending on a single large employer. We all know the devastating impact when a major factory or corporate headquarters closes its doors. A vibrant network of independent businesses provides a safety net against that kind of sudden economic shock.

Over this period, I have identified about ten such businesses operating quietly in our town. To bring us together, I launched an online forum. While the digital engagement has seen little activity so far, our face to face interactions have been wonderful. I started hosting monthly coffee meetups, which have quickly become a valuable space for connection.

Looking ahead, my goals for this group are ambitious but entirely achievable. I want us to demonstrate the true economic impact we bring to Sackville. We plan to build a shared online showcase to highlight our services, provide mutual support for one another, and eventually engage in government lobbying to ensure our voices are heard. Small businesses might be tiny on their own, but together, we are shaping the future of our town.

Is your shopping done? Are the cookies baked? Have you nestled the packages under the tree? Have you shoved aside anyone to get that last Nintendo Wii at Target yet? Is it me, or are people turning into cranky, mean old Scrooges this year? Last week, I let someone in the checkout line ahead of me. I thought that was a nice thing to do, and while I was in a big hurry, I could wait 2 more minutes. Well, the lady in line behind me didn't seem to agree. When I was a bit slow to respond to the clerk beckoning me to take my turn, she said "Hey!" and whacked me too hard with her armload of books! Huh? I started to say something, like "well Merry Christmas to you too," but thought better of it.
I saw more of the same behavior this weekend. Yesterday, my daughter and I had to go to the mall, oh terror of terrors, to get a few last-minute things (actually, I have to go today without Kendall for the last-minute things, but that is a different story). We tried to stay happy and Christmasy, but when we couldn't find anything "healthy" to eat at the mall (yeah, I don't know why this surprised us either), and a little old man shoved us away from the mall directory so he could get a look, we decided it was time to go home. We baked cookies, wrapped our presents and watched some quality holiday television, and our moods changed for the better.
Moral of this story: Please don't smack me with books at Kepler's bookstore in Menlo Park. And shopping and all the other activities that take up our time are necessary, but reserve most of your time to spend with your family and friends during the holiday.
Merry Christmas, Happy Hanukkah, and may you have a wonderful holiday season!

Yellow nail polish takes me straight back to my early teens, when I begged my parents for a Christmas haul of Marks and Spencer makeup. The packaging was all garish colours and Pop Art graphics, and I thought it was the most exciting thing imaginable. Did I know what to do with any of it? Not really. But that hardly mattered when there were such gloriously questionable shades to play with.

Now yellow nails are calling my name again, although I’m hoping my application skills have improved since those first experiments. With Chanel’s upcoming Mimosa polish looking set to become a big summer nail trend, I wanted to see whether I could get on board without committing to the Chanel price tag.

Enter Essence Sundancer, a cheerful little bottle costing roughly €1.99.

Before anyone gets too excited, this isn’t an exact Mimosa alternative. Sundancer is a warmer, banana-like yellow with a creme finish, while Mimosa looks cooler and has that sparkly quality. They belong to the same sunny family, but they’re not twins. If it’s specifically the Chanel shimmer you’re after, this won’t quite scratch the itch.

Application, unfortunately, brought back some of that teenage uncertainty. Sundancer needed four coats before I was happy with the coverage, which is a fair amount of effort for such a seemingly straightforward colour. This is not the polish I’d reach for when I wanted to paint my nails and get out the door.

Still, for €1.99, I find it difficult to stay cross with it. The finished colour is wonderfully bright, and it’s a cheap way to test whether yellow nail polish feels fun or just a bit too banana for your liking.

Then there’s the usual objection: “Yellow doesn’t suit pale skin.” I’m never entirely convinced by blanket rules like that, so I photographed Sundancer on my untanned hands, then again after a tan, to compare the effect.

The difference is interesting, but I’d rather leave the verdict open than declare that one skin tone gets exclusive rights to a colour. Sometimes an unexpected contrast is half the appeal.

What do you think: better before the tan, better after, or yellow nails under no circumstances? Cast your vote and tell me in the comments. I’m curious whether this summer shade has won you over.

When ChathamSTEM's Nabil Mouline was exploring opportunities to leverage the community's expertise and resources to help with the School District's objective to become the Number 1 STEM program in the state – among public school systems - he remembered a conversation with Margaret Holzer.
Holzer is leading a growing Environmental Sciences program at Chatham High School, and she was keen on getting some expertise in practical know-how concerning the expanding field of renewable energy and solar panels in particular. A few phone calls later, Patrick Ryan, energy entrepreneur and his son, Patrick, a Chatham High School Graduate, both ChathamSTEM supporters, stepped in with a donation of Solar Panels and the know-how to be shared with Holzer's class.
"Having materials like that in hand brings a sense of reality to what students read about in a textbook or see online," Holzer said.
"Usually we (the community) are called on to provide financial support either through taxes - supporting our school budget or donations to the PTOs, the Chatham Education Foundation and other groups in town. At ChathamSTEM, we believe that the community also has the responsibility and opportunity to provide know-how, scientific expertise and other in-kind support so as to bring the best to our kids, maybe even more so in the fast-changing world of science, technology, engineering and math. Teachers like Ms. Holzer are on the frontline every day, and we owe them all the support we can get," Mouline said.
Needs like this are pervasive even at the best high schools, and being able to leverage the expertise and connections of the parents is key.
"We have seen that last year, when we rallied the community around the Computer Science program, and it has worked (10-fold the amount of signups). We are now helping with the robotics, science research and soon the engineering programs. Some of us are also looking into tech-entrepreneurship with some early successful experiments," Mouline added.

A Lake Andes man has been reindicted for five counts of killing or injuring his neighbours' horses.
Ray Johanneson, 69, was originally indicted in July this year for allegedly shooting five horses, four of which reportedly died, that belonged to Lori Abdo-Smith and Charlie Smith.
The Smiths claimed the shootings were racially motivated. Johanneson, who pleaded not guilty to the charges on Tuesday, is white, and the Smiths are American Indian.
Abdo-Smith declined to comment on the issue when contacted by The Daily Republic on Thursday afternoon.
Johanneson maintains his innocence, stating on Thursday that he didn't shoot the horses. He said many of the horses were let loose over five or six years and grazed in his corn, bean and wheat fields, destroying his crops.
The same day the horses were discovered dead, Johanneson said he reported about 27 horses eating his crops because they were starving to death. He said the Charles Mix County Sheriff's Office took photos of those horses and the damage they caused to his crops.
Johanneson said Thursday there is no racial issue.
The charges against him were dismissed by the court in March because witness names were not included in the indictment, which is required by law, said Scott Podhradsky, deputy Charles Mix County state's attorney.
The witnesses' names are now included on the indictment, which was refiled on May 22.
Each charge is a misdemeanour, which carries a maximum penalty upon conviction of one year in county jail and a $2,000 fine.
A judge on Tuesday scheduled a jury trial for August.

Fossils of small reptiles discovered near Russia’s Mezen River suggest that sophisticated hearing evolved far earlier than previously thought. The animals lived about 260 million years ago, yet had ears with a surprisingly modern design, pushing back evidence of sensitive hearing on land by roughly 60 million years.

Early land-dwelling vertebrates were generally thought to have been mostly deaf to airborne sounds, with sophisticated hearing emerging around 200 million years ago. But the Russian fossils reveal that at least one much older group had already developed an effective system for carrying sound from the outside world to the inner ear.

The fossils belong to at least six species of parareptiles, an ancient reptile group. These roughly weasel-sized animals, measuring about half a meter long, lived during the Permian period, before dinosaurs appeared. Their skulls preserve evidence of a large eardrum positioned in the cheek, connected to the inner ear by a bone similar to one used in human hearing.

That arrangement matters because an eardrum alone is not enough to provide sensitive hearing. Sound vibrations must also reach the inner ear, where they can be detected. The combination of a broad eardrum and a connecting bone suggests these parareptiles could have heard about as well as living lizards.

Their skulls offer another clue to how they lived: large eye sockets. Together with their well-developed ears, these features suggest the animals may have been active at night. Sharp hearing could have helped them detect movement in darkness, while large eyes may have supported vision in low light.

The findings point to a more complex picture of early terrestrial ecosystems. Rather than a landscape populated largely by animals with limited hearing, the Permian world may already have included small, nighttime specialists equipped to gather information through both sight and sound.

The fossils also complicate the evolutionary story of the ear. Modern-style hearing probably arose independently in several animal lineages, rather than appearing once and passing unchanged to later groups. These parareptiles therefore raise fresh questions about when, how and why sensitive ears developed. Their remains suggest that the history of hearing on land stretches considerably deeper into the past than the conventional timeline allowed.

More details have emerged from Lambeth Palace about the "theological summit" that the Archbishop of Canterbury will attend this week in the Gulf.
The conference entitled "Building Bridges" takes place from April 7-9 in Doha, Qatar. It is being hosted by the Amir of Qatar, His Highness Shaikh Hamad bin Khalifa Al-Thani, and follows on from a similar gathering last January at Lambeth Palace.
Last year's gathering was attended by Tony Blair and Cardinal Cormac Murphy-O'Connor, the head of the Roman Catholic Church in England and Wales.
This year, around thirty Christian and Muslim scholars from across the world will hold detailed discussions over three days.
The gathering will focus on the place of scripture in the two faith communities. Speakers will address issues such as the contemporary interpretation of scripture and scriptural perspectives on those from other faith traditions.
The format of this year's conference includes both open lectures and private sessions. As with the first conference last year, it is hoped that an account of the deliberations will be published in book form.
The conference was planned well in advance of the military conflict in Iraq and is part of a continuing process of engagement between Christian and Muslim scholars. Dr Williams underlined the importance of dialogue;
"Christians and Muslims have much to learn from each other, and much to share, despite all the differences we acknowledge."
"A meeting such as this is a clear demonstration that we do not have to be imprisoned in mutual hostility and misunderstanding when our encounters are shaped by the scholarship and experience of people such as those who will be contributing to this meeting."

The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has urged micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), especially those operating in rural communities, to channel their requests for financial support through the Cooperative Financing Agency of Nigeria (CFAN).

The call was made in Abuja at a pre-seminar organised ahead of the United Nations Day of Cooperatives, which is marked on July 7 each year.

Speaking at the event, an official of the CBN's financial inclusion department described CFAN as the registered umbrella body for cooperatives in the country. He noted that working through the agency would make it easier for small businesses to benefit from the bank's support programmes.

He drew particular attention to the N220 billion MSME fund, explaining that the larger share of the facility has been set aside for women.

"Cooperatives remain one of the most effective ways of reaching small businesses at the grassroots," he said. "When enterprises come together under a recognised platform like CFAN, it becomes easier for them to access credit and for us to support them."

The executive secretary of CFAN said this year's celebration would provide an opportunity to review last year's focus on financial inclusion. It would also introduce the new theme of sustainable consumption and production.

According to him, the theme encourages cooperatives and their members to adopt practices that make better use of resources while building businesses that can last.

"We want our members to grow, but we want them to grow responsibly," he said.

The seminar also brought together several partners of the apex bank, including private firms in the agriculture and housing sectors. Participants discussed value-chain financing, an approach that provides funding at different stages of production, from sourcing raw materials to processing and getting finished goods to market.

Even though the Traverse City Central Invitational was the first match of the year for the Grand Rapids South Christian girls golf team, coach Ron VanDyke said the Sailors' first-place finish in the two-day tournament should prepare his team as it goes for its 17th consecutive trip to the Division 3 state finals.
"I like this tournament because it showcases some of the top talent in the state," VanDyke said. "It gives you a state finals feel with the two-day format and being away from home."
Senior Megan Wierenga led South Christian with a two-day total of 175, and Grace Elenbaas shot a 179 at the Grand Traverse Resort's two courses -- Spruce Run and Wolverine. Sophomore teammate Nicole Hoekwater added a 198, and Rachel Thuele rounded out the South Christian top four with a 200.
Flint Powers Catholic was second in the Division 2, 3 and 4 bracket, finishing seven strokes behind South Christian. Kristen Wolfe led the Chargers with a 167, and Morgan Zloto shot a 177.
Grosse Ile's Emily Bargardi shot a 179 to lead the Red Devils to a third-place finish in divisions 2 through 4, and Megan Moco added a 194.
Farmington Hills Mercy won the Division 1 bracket with a score of 704.
Division 1 teams played the Wolverine course on Day 1 and Spruce Run on Day 2, while teams in divisions 2 through 4 played Spruce Run on Day 1 and Wolverine on Day 2.
VanDyke said the two courses, particularly Spruce Run, provided a challenge for his team in its first match of the season.
"I played Spruce Run 30 years ago, and it seems like the trees have grown a lot," he said. "The fairways we're tight, and they forced the girls to hit good shots."

A POLITICIAN has launched a campaign to fight against any potential downgrading of maternity and children's services at the Conquest Hospital.
Sarah Owen, Labour's parliamentary candidate for Hastings and Rye, set up the campaign this month with Lord Bassam of Brighton.
East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust, which runs both the Conquest on The Ridge and Eastbourne DGH, is currently consulting on six options for the future of paediatric and maternity services in East Sussex, but none of them includes maintaining a consultant-led maternity unit at both hospitals.
Sarah, who was born in the Buchanan Hospital, met with Lord Bassam of Brighton at the Conquest on Tuesday (February 18), where they discussed their concerns.
She said: "I was born in Hastings and want to ensure that the next generation can be born here too.
"We believe our hospitals need excellent quality consultant-led maternity services in place, for the hundreds of women who don't have straightforward births, having to travel across to Eastbourne in an emergency is clearly far from ideal. Please join the campaign to stop the downgrade of maternity services in our local hospital."
Last March, East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust said it had been advised by doctors, midwives and nurses, together with the National Clinical Advisory Team, that maternity and paediatric services at that time could not continue as they were.
As a result, from May 7, the DGH became a midwifery-led maternity unit, and children could no longer stay overnight in the Friston Ward.
Consultant-led maternity was centralised at the Conquest.
In December, the three East Sussex Clinical Commissioning Groups (CCGs) published the six options.
They are currently carrying out a consultation with the public.
Healthwatch East Sussex is organising a series of Question Time-style events on the future of maternity for residents, with the one in Hastings on Monday, March 3. To find out more, go to: www.healthwatcheastsussex.co.uk.
To join Sarah's campaign, visit www.sarahowen.org.uk/maternityservices for more information. To take part in the consultation, visit www.betterbeginnings-nhs.net or attend one of the consultation events listed there.

Seoul-based artist Minjae Lee is preparing a new series that turns his attention to some of the most recognizable women in film, music, and fashion, reimagining them through the dreamlike style that has earned him a devoted following.

Largely self-taught, Lee has built his reputation working with traditional, hands-on materials rather than digital tools. Markers, pens, crayons, and acrylic paints are staples of his practice, and he often layers them to create vivid, textured portraits of female figures that seem to drift between reality and fantasy. His characters are known for their haunting eyes, flowing lines, and bursts of color that give each piece an emotional charge.

The upcoming collection will feature a lineup that mirrors Lee's own background and influences. Korean stars will share the spotlight with classic Hollywood legends such as Marilyn Monroe and Audrey Hepburn, whose famous images will be filtered through his distinctive artistic lens. The series will also include international models, as well as actresses and singers from both Asia and the West.

That blend of East and West is no accident. Cultural fusion has long been a central theme in Lee's work, alongside explorations of emotion and the inner life of the soul. By placing Korean celebrities next to global icons, the series highlights how his art draws from his Seoul roots while engaging with a wider world of popular culture.

Fans can expect the new pieces to stay true to the expressive approach that defines his earlier portfolio. Rather than offering straightforward likenesses, Lee's portraits aim to capture something beneath the surface, giving viewers a fresh, emotionally rich take on faces they thought they already knew.

Two convenience store clerks were hospitalized with multiple gunshot wounds after an armed robbery involving four suspects, police said. One of the clerks is in critical condition and, according to his landlord, is now on life support.

The robbery happened around 7 p.m., when two masked men entered the store carrying guns and demanded money. Two accomplices waited outside in a car. Both clerks were shot several times, and all four suspects escaped in a dark vehicle.

The wounded employees were taken to Cape Fear Valley Hospital. Najib Bouzerda, 44, was listed in critical condition, while Mohamed Ould, 41, was in fair condition. The account of the robbery did not establish how much money, if any, the suspects took before fleeing.

Bouzerda’s landlord said he already worked full time at a hotel and had taken the convenience store job about a month earlier to help make ends meet. The additional work was intended to supplement his income, the landlord said.

According to the landlord, Bouzerda had expressed concern about safety in the area and considered it dangerous. His girlfriend had also urged him not to work at the store. He nevertheless took the second job as he tried to cover his expenses.

Police have released surveillance footage showing two of the suspects as investigators seek information about those involved. The appeal for help comes as Bouzerda remains critically injured and Ould receives treatment for his wounds.

Anyone with information about the robbery or the suspects is asked to contact detectives or CrimeStoppers.

Optical Image Technology, the State College, Pennsylvania-based creator of the enterprise content management product DocFinity, has announced a strategic partnership with Xpertdoc. Xpertdoc is a Canadian company that specializes in document design, output, and distribution. This new alliance brings together two powerful systems to help organizations handle their paperwork and digital files much more efficiently.

The collaboration pairs Xpertdoc’s unique ability to generate high volumes of customized client communications, which is built entirely on familiar Microsoft technology, with the robust organizational tools of DocFinity. Once Xpertdoc creates the personalized documents, DocFinity steps in to handle the secure storage, indexing, retrieval, and overall lifecycle management of those files. By integrating these two systems, modern businesses can seamlessly create, store, and find their most important information.

Leaders from both organizations describe the partnership as a perfectly complementary deal. For everyday customers, this integration is expected to significantly cut operational costs while improving processing speed, document quality, and overall workplace productivity. The president of DocFinity highlighted the natural fit between the two software firms, noting that they share core business philosophies. "We share fundamental values such as a commitment to solid technology, extreme usability, and highly responsive customer service," the president stated.

In a separate but equally important development, the team at DocFinity has also recently launched a brand-new Records Management module. This new operational feature is specifically designed to seamlessly complement its existing enterprise content management and business process management software programs. It is already seeing active use across several major industries, including insurance, healthcare, and higher education, where strict compliance and organized, long-term record keeping are absolutely essential for daily operations.

Many of us who book through travel agencies feel secure being able to book our trips, hotels and flights face to face with a travel expert. The thought of the travel agency closing never crosses our minds, especially not when we're abroad and enjoying our holiday. This happened last week, leaving more than 1000 passengers stranded abroad when Sun4U folded.
Sun4U was a travel agency based in Birmingham and specialised in package holidays and trips to Spain, the most popular travel destination among British vacationers. The company announced on Thursday evening that it would dissolve and that travellers with bookings and currently on holiday would be responsible for finding their own alternative modes of transportation. This includes 1,200 travellers, mostly in Spain.
What went wrong?
Sun4U is believed to have really suffered, like many travel companies, during the flight ban that affected UK airspace in April as a result of the erupting volcano in Iceland. Unable to catch up after the losses, the company informed its staff last week that it would fold.
The travel agency's main tour operator, Goldtrail Holidays, also folded earlier this summer, putting a lot of stress on Sun4U to find other flights/accommodations for travellers to Turkey and Greece.
What to do?
Travellers abroad who have booked a holiday with Sun4U must contact the CAA (Civil Aviation Authority) or their supplier, as indicated on their holiday invoice. Travellers who have booked full-package holidays have some protection with Air Travel Operators' Licensing protection.
Those, however, who merely used Sun4U only to book flights have no protection if they've paid Sun4U for their flights. If, however, the travellers paid for their flights directly with the airline, they should have no trouble.
Travellers on package holidays, expecting to travel in the coming weeks, are advised now to apply for a refund and make alternative holiday plans. If you need to search for last-minute flights from the UK, use liligo.co.uk.
Those who made hotel reservations with Sun4U can still go on their holiday, but might have to pay twice for their rooms and bookings.
Telephone contact for Civil Aviation Authority: 08 445 717 260

AARP has awarded its first “Movies For Grownups” seal to “Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit,” an unexpected choice that highlights the growing importance of older moviegoers to Hollywood. The advocacy group for people over 50 selected a fast-paced franchise reboot for its inaugural endorsement, rather than a more obvious adult-oriented drama.

The decision surprised some because the film gives Tom Clancy’s familiar intelligence analyst a younger, more action-driven treatment. Earlier Jack Ryan films, including “The Hunt for Red October,” have become classics. Yet the character’s long history also gives the reboot a connection to audiences who followed his previous screen adventures.

That familiarity helps explain why a film built to refresh a franchise could also attract mature viewers. A younger lead and quicker pace do not necessarily erase the appeal of an established character. For older fans, “Shadow Recruit” offers both a recognizable name and a new version of the spy thriller.

The seal also carries practical marketing benefits. Films receiving the endorsement can use promotional packages funded by AARP, giving them another way to reach the organization’s audience. The support makes the designation more than a symbolic nod: it provides a promotional tool for films seeking attention from older ticket buyers.

AARP’s broader “Movies For Grownups” initiative has expanded to include awards and festivals, increasing its influence in the movie business. Its activities reflect a market that analysts say deserves greater attention, as mature adults become an increasingly important force at the box office.

Teenagers still go to theaters, but their habits offer a contrast. For many, the trip is primarily a social outing, with the choice of film sometimes left until they arrive. The gathering, rather than a particular title, can be the main attraction.

Against that backdrop, AARP’s endorsement points to the value of targeting audiences through familiar stories and trusted recommendations. Its first selection also suggests that movies for grownups need not exclude action, reinvention or a younger star.

If the government believes its announcement of $107 million in funding to Victorian hospitals has set itself as the knight in shining armour coming in to save the day, voters are seemingly less than convinced.
Amid ongoing finger-pointing between the federal and state governments, there remains little clarity in who was ultimately responsible for the disgraceful circumstances surrounding the health funding debate.
What most people are concerned about is not who funds it but just that it happens. Without support from federal and state governments, beds close, staff disappear, and surgeries cease, and that's not a good outcome for anyone who might be sick.
The strategic manner in which the information was released by the federal government late on Wednesday afternoon was designed to get maximum exposure.
It certainly achieved that goal. Yet, the government also must have believed that it could gain political mileage by providing funding directly to hospitals, thus implying the state government could not be trusted.
Stepping in as it has in this instance is the responsible course of action.
But claiming some sort of moral high ground in the process only serves to further ingrain the notion that the debate was less about patients and more about politics.
Ballarat Base Hospital chief executive Andrew Rowe spoke for the majority in his response to the government's announcement: "We are pleased to get back to what we do best, and that is care for our patients."
It will be of particular relief for Mr Rowe, as his board, some of whom were appointed by the current state government, has been pushing hard on the issue behind closed doors.
There are still considerable elements of future funding arrangements that governments at both levels must clarify.
Firstly, will the federal government now also provide hospital funding directly in other states? Also, will the mode of assessing funding distributions – based in some respects on population movements and forecasts – remain the same? Will the state government reassess how it uses federal distributions in health?
The funding announced this week is welcomed.
That aside, it remains a frustration that the impasse couldn't have been resolved earlier and that future funding remains murky.

The Stawell Gold Mines Future Possibilities project has entered its final stage, with a business case now presented to Northern Grampians Shire Council and the project control group overseeing the work.

The report outlines several potential new uses for the mine site once gold production winds down, including an underground particle physics laboratory, hydroponic farming and a landfill operation.

Getting the site ready for these ventures would require an estimated $2.4 million to $2.9 million in infrastructure, and council officers are now actively seeking investors to help bring the plans to life.

Mayor Kevin Erwin said the proposals were not an either-or choice. "These projects can run side by side," he said. "They don't rely on each other, and they don't hinge on what happens with Big Hill."

The mayor was referring to an upcoming decision on whether open-cut mining will proceed at Big Hill, a matter that has drawn considerable community interest. He stressed that the future possibilities work would move forward regardless of that outcome.

Preparations for the physics laboratory are already under way. Equipment is currently testing whether the mine's underground decline, the sloping tunnel that provides access to deeper levels, is suitable for sensitive scientific research. Physicists value deep underground sites because the surrounding rock shields experiments from cosmic radiation.

Hydroponic farming, which grows plants in nutrient-rich water rather than soil, was identified as a good fit for parts of the site. Because it does not rely on the ground itself, it can be carried out on land free of contaminated soil.

Councillor Wayne Rice acknowledged the transition would not be painless for everyone. "There's no getting around the fact that some miners will lose their jobs," he said. "But new tunnelling work for the lab could create employment, and that's an opportunity we need to grab."

Converting Wonga Pit into a landfill site is considered a longer-term prospect, with the process expected to take several years to complete.

The Toyota 86 will be returning to the Goodwood Festival of Speed a year after it was introduced there. However, this time around, Toyota will be highlighting its TRD Griffon 86 Concept that was created by Toyota Racing Development.
Following its Japan premiere at the Tokyo Auto Salon, the TRD Griffon 86 will be gracing the track at Goodwood with modifications made throughout the car, like weight reduction, chassis strengthening, and race-spec TRD accessories.
The exterior now sports a carbon fiber bonnet, roof, doors, boot lid and rear wing. Carbon fiber reinforced plastic, meanwhile, was used for the bumpers, front wings and rear diffuser. Windows are also replaced by polycarbonate material to further reduce the car's overall weight.
Inside the cabin, it was fitted with a TRD bucket seat, gear shift knob, ignition button, oil pressure and water temperature gauges. The steering wheel was provided by Momo, while the seatbelts are supplied by Takata.
The car's mechanical components are strengthened by replacing the standard LSD with a TRD mechanical LSD, and a coil-over suspension kit was also installed. Brakes are upgraded to a TRD monoblock brake calliper kit with race-spec brake pads. Wheels are replaced with 18-inch TWS wheels with Yokohama Advan Tires.
No modifications were made to the car's standard 2.0-liter normally aspirated boxer engine.
The FT86 Open concept – a working design study for a GT86 convertible – will also be put on display in the UK for the first time.

Borussia Dortmund's rising nineteen-year-old French forward Ousmane Dembele has openly admitted that his ultimate career goal is to play for Barcelona. The talented youngster, who has been making waves in the Bundesliga, recently shared his long-term ambitions while reaffirming his current commitment to his German club.

For now, the Vernon-born attacker insists he is perfectly content continuing his development under manager Thomas Tuchel. Dembele understands the importance of consistent playing time at this crucial stage of his career. "Barcelona is my ultimate goal, but right now I need to keep developing and playing regularly," he explained, indicating that a move to Spain remains a dream for the future rather than an immediate plan.

Dembele has enjoyed a remarkably strong start to life in Germany since his transfer from French side Rennes last summer. Before choosing Dortmund, the highly sought-after teenager was pursued by several top European clubs, most notably reigning Premier League champions Leicester City. Ultimately, the appeal of Dortmund's track record with young talent won him over.

His decision appears to be paying off wonderfully. Dembele has already secured a regular place in Tuchel's starting lineup, contributing an impressive one goal and four assists across ten appearances. This immediate impact highlights exactly why the German side is widely considered the perfect stepping stone for Europe's brightest prospects.

As Dortmund prepares for an upcoming home match against Hertha Berlin, all eyes will once again be on their dynamic French star. While the glittering lights of Catalonia may be calling his name in the distance, Dembele remains entirely focused on delivering results and refining his craft in the Bundesliga.

Fans of stealth action who are counting down the days until the next Metal Gear adventure may have a worthy distraction on the way. Splinter Cell: Pandora Tomorrow, which earned strong praise on the Xbox, is coming to the PlayStation 2, and our hands-on time with the game suggests PS2 owners have plenty to look forward to.

The storyline is identical to the Xbox release. Players once again step into the shoes of Sam Fisher, a seasoned operative working for Third Echelon, a secretive branch of the US intelligence community that handles missions too sensitive to officially exist. This time, Fisher is tasked with tracking down an Indonesian guerrilla leader who has acquired biological weapons and is threatening to unleash them on the United States.

The hunt takes Fisher across a varied set of locations. The campaign begins in Eastern Europe before shifting to the dense, humid jungles of Indonesia, with short missions in France and America along the way. Each environment brings its own challenges, from tightly patrolled compounds to sprawling outdoor areas filled with natural cover.

While the core experience is the same, the PS2 version is not a straight copy. To keep the game running smoothly on Sony's hardware, the developers have reworked some levels. Certain areas have been sealed off, making some maps more compact, and the number of lights that can be destroyed has been reduced.

That second change has a noticeable effect on how the game plays. In the Xbox version, shooting out bulbs and lamps to create pools of shadow was a key tactic for slipping past guards unseen. On the PS2, that approach is far less useful, so players must rely more heavily on the darkness that already exists in each area.

Some longtime fans might see this as a step backward, but in practice we found it made the experience more rewarding. Rather than simply blasting every light in sight, you are pushed to study guard patrols, read your surroundings and carefully plan a route through naturally shadowed spaces. Successfully sneaking through a well-lit room by hugging its few dark corners feels like a genuine accomplishment.

For PS2 players hungry for tense, thoughtful stealth gameplay, Pandora Tomorrow is shaping up to be a strong contender.

It was a double celebration at St Dominic's Grammar School yesterday as two sets of twins received 18 A*s and 17 As between them in their GCSEs.
Aisling and Niamh McGarrity and Seainin and Colleen Maxwell walked into the west Belfast school on Thursday morning, just hoping they'd passed their exams so they could do their A-Levels.
Niamh opened the envelope to find she had seven As and one A*.
"I was so happy. I really didn't expect what I got," she said.
Sister Aisling was equally surprised when she saw she had 5 As and 2 A*s.
"I feel so happy, but I'm shocked, happily shocked and very proud. At least we know that all the hard work we put in has paid off," she added.
The girls, who are not identical, studied different subjects.
The happiness doubled at the Falls Road school when 16-year-old twins Seainin and Colleen Maxwell picked up their results alongside their mother.
Seainin is hoping to go on to study Biology, Chemistry, Physics and French after discovering she had received six A*s and four As in her GCSEs.
Sister Colleen studied the same subjects but also did Spanish as another language, and obtained nine A*s and one A, joking that: "The A was in French, I don't know what happened there."
She also wants to go on to study Biology and Chemistry at A-Level, along with Maths and Further Maths.
Colleen said, "I feel really happy and proud of my results. I really didn't think I would do as well as I have."
Proud mother Sandra Maxwell said, "They have always worked hard and done well. It is a big thank you to the school for how well they have done."

If you picked up the new EA UFC video game, don't be surprised when you see a cleaned-up Carlos Condit.
According to a report over at The Wall Street Journal, a history of legal issues is to blame.
Here's their breakdown:
Phoenix-based tattoo artist Chris Escobedo took an intellectual property rights training course and sued now-bankrupt videogame developer THQ Inc. over a mixed-martial arts game in which one of his tattoos—a large, scowling lion on the right rib cage of Ultimate Fighting Championship star Carlos Condit—makes a cameo appearance.
Last year, he settled the lawsuit for an undisclosed sum, he said.
"They're doing it without consulting the original artists, and that's what makes it illegal," he said. "I'm the little guy in this situation."
Such lawsuits have left a mark. When video game giant EA Sports, a brand of Electronic Arts Inc., developed its own fighting game featuring Mr Condit, which will be released this week, it left out the lion, causing gamers to growl. Electronic Arts declined to comment.
"That tattoo artist must feel he now owns a portion of Carlos Condits rib cage, too, huh?" wrote one fan on an EA online forum after seeing early screenshots.
Mr Escobedo, 35 years old, said gamers sent him hate emails and attacked him on his Facebook page after news broke of his lawsuit. He said he has known Mr Condit since the latter was a teenager, but the litigation has spoiled their friendship. The sports-management company representing Mr Condit declined to comment.

A three-year-old service dog has earned a place alongside students in the yearbook at Stafford High School in Virginia, delighting classmates who have come to know him as a familiar and welcome presence on campus.

Alpha accompanies 16-year-old A.J. Schalk, who has Type 1 diabetes, and has been attending classes with him for about eighteen months. While his yearbook appearance has brought smiles, the dog’s daily role is far more important: helping Schalk recognize dangerous changes in his blood sugar.

When Alpha detects a dangerous swing, he alerts Schalk by pawing at him. Schalk says the dog has saved his life several times, making their partnership an essential part of his school day. The warning gives the teenager a signal that his blood sugar needs attention.

That serious responsibility has not stopped Alpha from becoming a beloved member of the school community. Teachers and students warmly welcome him, and his presence has helped change the way Schalk feels about living with diabetes. Rather than seeing his condition only as a difficulty, Schalk says Alpha has helped make the experience more positive.

The teenager now looks forward to going to school, where the response to his canine companion has been enthusiastic. Alpha’s place in the yearbook reflects the welcome he receives in classrooms and hallways, as well as the bond students have formed with the hardworking dog.

Alpha took part in picture day to get his photograph for the yearbook. He also received a school ID, giving him another marker of belonging at Stafford High. Students were delighted when they spotted his picture among the yearbook portraits.

For Schalk, however, Alpha’s contribution goes well beyond a memorable photograph. The dog offers potentially lifesaving alerts while also helping make school a more welcoming experience. His inclusion in the yearbook captures both sides of that role: a service animal carrying out an important job and a companion embraced by the people who share his days. For students, the portrait is a cheerful reminder of a familiar face in class.

IBM has unveiled the world's smallest computer, which is "smaller than a grain of salt", measuring 1 x 1 mm. This tiny speck of technology is also very cheap to manufacture, costing less than ten cents. This device was unveiled at the IBM Think Conference, which started on March 19.
The world's smallest computer comes with an x86 chip, Mashable reports. IBM says that this computer has around 1 million transistors, which would require microscopic vision to take a look at it. This tiny computer is capable of monitoring, analysing, communicating, and even acting on data. In addition to this, the computer is equipped with SRAM for memory and a photovoltaic cell for power. It is also capable of uplink and downlink communication using an LED and a photo detector.
This device is a part of IMB Research's 5 in 5 project announced at the event. As the name suggests, this project is about IBM's Research team working on five technologies based on Artificial Intelligence (AI), blockchain, encryption and Internet of Things (IoT).
All these technologies are clubbed under crypto-anchors based on blockchain technology. These crypto-anchors can take the form of tiny computers or optical codes that can be embedded into products. IBM says that the purpose of these crypto-anchors is to help eliminate counterfeit products, which are widespread globally. Crypto-anchors can be embedded into something as small as "an edible shade of magnetic ink". Also, crypto-anchors are considered "highly secure", which cannot be cloned.
This tiny computer, with more to come, will be embedded in objects and products used daily. Using blockchain technology, it will identify an object's authenticity "from its point of origin to when it reaches the hands of the customer".
IBM will make the first models of its crypto-anchors available in another 18 months. It also plans to make these products available in the marketplace within the next five years.

Shoppers in downtown will have a new way to navigate the city streets and experience Troy Night Out, the business event held on the last Friday of each month.
A downtown software company, Gavant Software, Inc., has produced a mobile application for smartphones that allows event attendees to see businesses participating in Troy Night Out each month and search for specific restaurants, exhibits or music venues.
"We've printed a paper map every single month for Troy Night Out with over 60 different listings of things that are going on, but now folks will be able to go paperless," said Elizabeth Young, executive director of the Downtown Troy Business Improvement District.
Set over a deep blue background showing the Rice building, the mobile application offers options to "Do!" "Look!" "Taste!" and "Touch!" When selected, each brings up a map showing businesses corresponding to the chosen sense. "Taste!" displays participating restaurants, while "Look!" shows many of the exhibits and galleries that will be open.
The application is available for free download at the iPhone App Store and the Google Marketplace for Android and will be ready for use by the upcoming Troy Night Out on March 29.
"Our tenth anniversary was last year, and we wanted to do something for the community," said Jon Kloptosky, president and founder of Gavant.
Gavant's projects have ranged from producing a web application to allow authorized users to access Contour by Getty, a database of professional and celebrity portraits, to ExpertFlyer, an application providing air travel information to frequent fliers, to work accomplished for chip manufacturer GlobalFoundries. The company's core clients are regional and from New York City, but they are looking to expand beyond the state.

Bennett's Business Systems provides and services imaging equipment, such as copiers, to other businesses. It took a bet that it could get a leap in sales by moving from a small-business IT operation to an enterprise-class one. CEO and CIO Wes Benwick was unhappy with the proprietary OMD accounting package (a Cobol program recently ported to Windows) widely used in the copier/printer industry, and was concerned about diminishing availability of integration tools and experts to tie them into other systems. Moreover, Bennett's had already tried to build its own telesales-management application, but it didn't scale past three users. So Benwick decided to outsource his financial and sales applications to Salesforce.com, which would instantly provide an enterprise architecture and let his staff of four developers and three support technicians focus on aiding the 25 sales staff members directly, including custom development within Salesforce.com's applications and the development of MySQL database queries and reports. Benwick says sales rose 46 percent in the year after the company moved to enterprise-level tools, even though the size of the sales staff didn't change. Sales had been consistent at the lower levels for at least five years, he notes. However, the IT staff has grown from two to five as Benwick has added more developers to work on tools and reports for the sales staff. But the IT support staff has stayed at one person. "We don't believe our expertise is in managing hardware," so it was easy to rely on someone else to host its systems. Initially, Benwick used a Microsoft Exchange server to manage e-mail, but quickly outsourced that, as well as the spam filtering, which runs on an on-site server administered by another company. "Administering it is a major pain in the butt," especially for a company with fewer than 100 employees, Benwick says. In the same vein, Benwick outsourced the company's data center and e-commerce site, both of which reside at the provider. "I'm hoping I never have to own my own, no matter how big I get," Benwick says.

New Zealand has launched a new website that aims to attract New Zealanders who have moved abroad to move back home, by listing job opportunities, relocation information, plus information on the school system and the arts. The site was launched on 1 Nov.
"New Zealand is a great place to live, work and play. We want to remind expats that New Zealand has an incredible amount to offer," New Zealand Immigration Minister David Cunliffe said.
The website is the start of a programme to make it easier for New Zealanders living offshore to come home, and ensure that those people who intend to return have the information they need to help them.
Mr Cunliffe said the programme was set against a background of a strong economy, the lowest unemployment rate in the developed world, increasing international competition for skills and around 500,000 New Zealanders living offshore.
"New Zealanders have always travelled, and we know that three-quarters of our overseas population are either intending to come home sometime or will consider the option of coming home," he said.
"They have the skills our employers are crying out for, and with unemployment at just 3.7 per cent, this is a great time to begin talking to them about living here."
Department of Labour Communications and Marketing Director Richard Ninness said the programme centred around a website, newzealandnow.info, divided into categories around living, working, playing and moving home to New Zealand.
"The website aims to make it easier for New Zealanders to come home by keeping them in touch with what is really happening in New Zealand and the opportunities that are available here now."
The Department's marketing to attract skills to New Zealand would become more important as global demographics like ageing populations and shrinking workforces increase international competition for skilled labour, he said.
"Skilled New Zealanders are going to be in increasing demand offshore. That means it's important that we take new initiatives now to make sure that they know more about what's good about being home."
The website can be viewed at http://newzealandnow.info/.

A Chicago-area mother has made the heartbreaking decision to take her 16-year-old son off life support after he collapsed during a basketball tournament. Now she is turning her grief into a mission to protect other young athletes.

Jermaine Cullum went into cardiac arrest while playing in a suburban tournament. He was rushed to Loyola University Medical Center, where doctors found no brain activity and determined he could not breathe on his own. His mother, Tarcia Patton, chose to remove him from life support.

Doctors later determined that Jermaine had a rare heart condition that had never been detected.

When Jermaine went down on the court, a nurse and a doctor who happened to be in the crowd rushed to help. They performed CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation, the chest compressions and rescue breaths used when someone's heart stops) and were able to restore his pulse. Patton said their quick actions gave her something precious.

"They gave me the chance to say goodbye to my son," she said.

Patton is donating Jermaine's heart to Loyola for research. She hopes doctors can learn more about the condition that took his life and use that knowledge to help other children.

"If his heart can save another child, then he is still doing good in this world," she said.

Both Patton and a Loyola physician are urging parents and young athletes not to treat sports physicals as a formality. They recommend thorough exams and, if any warning signs appear, an electrocardiogram, or EKG. This quick and painless test records the heart's electrical activity and can reveal hidden problems.

Warning signs can include fainting, chest pain, shortness of breath during exercise, or a family history of heart problems. The United States does not have a mandatory national heart screening program for young athletes, which means families often have to ask for these tests themselves.

"Don't wait," Patton said. "Ask the questions. Push for the test."

More than £5 million of extra government money is to be spent fixing potholes on Norfolk's roads, the Government has revealed.
The news has been welcomed by council leaders who, though they admit they have yet to see the details of the offer, say they want to start work as soon as possible.
Toby Coke, chairman of the county council's environment, transport and development committee, who represents the Gayton and Nar Valley division, said: "This is a very welcome offer from the Government and urgently needed in Norfolk.
"We still need to see the details and ensure we can meet the conditions of the offer, which we'll be doing over the next few days, but I'm very keen to secure this money and start using it on the ground at the earliest opportunity."
In April, the Department for Transport called on councils to apply for a share of a £168 million fund, for which they will have to sign a "pothole pledge", detailing how many potholes they will fix by next March.
On Friday, officials announced that Norfolk had been awarded around £5.4 million from the fund. That money is on top of £3.7 million of funding for the repair of weather-related damage, which was announced in March.
Ministers claim that the extra funding will be enough to fix three million potholes on roads across the country.
And they say that making councils sign pothole pledges will help to reassure residents that the money is being used to fix problem sites in their areas.

Elizabeth Colbert Busch, the Democratic candidate running in the highly anticipated special election for South Carolina's First Congressional District, has publicly distanced herself from President Obama regarding his latest federal budget proposal. As she prepares to face off against Republican former governor Mark Sanford in the upcoming May 7 race, Colbert Busch is making it entirely clear to voters that she intends to chart an independent course on federal fiscal policy.

Drawing heavily on her extensive professional business background, Colbert Busch argued that the president's economic plan ultimately falls short of what the country needs right now. She stated that the proposal fails to actually balance the federal budget and relies far too heavily on raising taxes. Furthermore, she expressed serious concern that the plan does far too little to cut down on wasteful government spending or to adequately ease the significant tax burden currently placed on local small businesses. For a candidate looking to appeal to moderate and conservative voters in South Carolina, emphasizing fiscal responsibility and small business growth remains a central focus of her congressional campaign.

Beyond her concerns over taxes and spending, Colbert Busch strongly objected to the proposed reductions in Social Security benefits that were included in the president's budget. She insisted that the retirement program is not the primary driver of the national deficit. Pointing directly to her recent meetings and conversations with retirees across the district, she emphasized the profound importance of keeping promises made to older Americans who rely on these vital benefits for their daily financial security.

In addition to rejecting the president's budget proposal, she also firmly dismissed the alternative budget plan put forward by Republican Representative Paul Ryan. Seeking a pragmatic middle ground that prioritizes sensible spending without sacrificing the social safety net, she promised voters that she will actively support a balanced budget amendment if elected to Congress. By taking a firm stand against both the Democratic and Republican budget blueprints, Colbert Busch is positioning herself as a fiercely independent voice determined to balance the books while protecting the senior citizens.

As the cyclone-fuelled tides kept large parts of the mangrove forest inundated amid rising fears about the fate of tigers and prey animals, the forest department launched an emergency assessment survey in the Sunderbans on Wednesday.
Forest guard teams and members of the local forest protection committees (FPS) fanned out in search of animal carcasses. The east range and sanctuary range of the Sunderban Tiger Reserve are the worst affected. Hundreds of prey animals, including a dozen tigers, are feared to have been washed away.
''I would be surprised if tigers manage to escape this. Going by the all-round damage, the casualty figure could be high,'' said S S Bist, wildlife expert and managing director of Forest Development Corporation.
The only way tigers could have withstood the 'Aila' onslaught is by escaping to higher, drier parts of the forest. But experts said there weren't enough dry parts of them to shelter the entire tiger population. Actually, there are very few high areas. During a calamity like this one, it's unlikely that all animals would find refuge.
Tigers are tougher, but they are bound to get swept away if water gushes into the forest as it did. Chances of recovering the carcasses are low since they would be lost by the time the forest guards go deep into the forest,'' added Bist.
Apart from the possibility of being swept away, tigers now face the challenge of surviving on a reduced prey base with increased chances of their straying out into the neighbouring villages. A primary survey of the forests in the east and west ranges shows that water is still very high, and there is no trace of prey animals. This is the area that has a heavy concentration of big cats. They will now have to starve and might stray,'' the beat officer added.
Best agreed. ''This is a strong possibility now. It will be easier for tigers now to swim into the villages which have merged with the rivers.''

A widespread disruption hit several Google services on the morning of Monday, December 10, interrupting access to Gmail, Google Drive, Google Talk and the Play Store. Service began recovering soon afterward, but the incident initially left the scale of the problems unclear.

Gmail repeatedly went offline and returned, rather than remaining unavailable throughout the disruption. Reports also linked the problems to crashes in the desktop version of Google Chrome, suggesting that the effects extended beyond users being unable to open individual Google services in their browsers.

The outage drew heavy public attention, pointing to a broad disruption, although the number of affected users was not immediately established. With several products experiencing problems at the same time, the early reports presented a wider picture than a straightforward interruption to email alone.

As access began to return, Gmail’s status page acknowledged that Google was investigating the issue. The intermittent nature of the Gmail failures meant that the service’s return at any one point did not necessarily mark the end of the morning’s difficulties: users had already seen it go down and come back.

Google later apologized and said its engineers had identified and fixed the root cause. According to the company, many users’ web requests failed for about 18 minutes across two brief windows that morning, measured in Pacific Time. That account described two periods of failures, rather than one uninterrupted 18-minute outage.

The company’s apology, however, focused solely on Gmail, even though the reported disruption had also affected Drive, Talk and the Play Store. Its explanation confirmed a fix for the failures it described but left a gap between the Gmail-focused statement and the broader set of problems reported during the incident.

In a posting to Microsoft's RSS Team blog, Jack Ozzie, vice president of development at the software giant's Groove Networks subsidiary, said the firm has made significant progress with the SSE specification. Ozzie also introduced the update, slated to be Version 0.91, which claims improvements in the area of "independent replication of hierarchical items," among other additions. First introduced by Microsoft Chief Technology Officer Ray Ozzie last year, the objective of SSE is to define the minimum software file extensions necessary to allow applications to share data for publishing RSS feeds, and for use with OPML (Outline Processor Markup Language). RSS is a system for identifying news or other online content made available to users by a publisher. OPML is an XML format for data outlines commonly used to exchange lists of RSS feeds between aggregators of such content. Microsoft also launched a "SSE 101" tutorial meant to help people begin working with the technology, which offers documentation, sample code and XML files that claim to demonstrate working implementations of the specification. Jack Ozzie said in his post that Microsoft has received significant support from outside developers in pushing SSE forward. "We've received lots of requests both from the community and from within Microsoft for samples, samples, samples of SSE code in action," Ozzie wrote. "We heard you." When Ray Ozzie, who is Jack's brother and a co-founder of Groove, introduced SSE last fall, he described the technology as "the RSS of synchronization" and said it would greatly improve the ability of calendaring applications to share information to help process news feeds. "Using RSS itself as is for synchronization wasn't really an option," he said. "That is, RSS is primarily about syndication or unidirectional publishing, while in order to accomplish the mesh sharing scenarios, we'd need bidirectional synchronization of items. But RSS is compelling because of the power inherent in its simplicity."

The 59th Houston International Boat, Sport and Travel Show is making waves at the Reliant Center this year, drawing bigger crowds as more people discover, or rediscover, life on the water.

Organizers say the show truly has something for everyone, no matter the size of their wallet. More than a thousand boats fill the exhibit halls, ranging from simple kayaks that cost a few hundred dollars to a luxury vessel carrying a price tag of roughly $1.5 million.

"You can walk in here with a modest budget or a very generous one and find something that fits," a show representative said. "That's what makes this event special. It's not just for people with deep pockets."

One noticeable trend this year is the number of smaller boats on display. According to the representative, there are more compact and affordable options on the floor than ever before, helping newcomers get started.

The exhibitor floor itself tells a story about the economy. After several years of unsold booth space, every spot is now filled. The representative credits the turnaround to improving economic conditions and growing consumer confidence.

"For a while, we had empty spaces we just couldn't fill," he said. "Now the floor is full, and that's a good sign for the whole industry."

He added that many current boat owners are ready to trade up. Newer models offer improved technology, such as advanced navigation and electronics, along with better fuel efficiency, which can mean real savings over time.

For those looking for a simpler and cheaper way onto the water, kayaking remains a popular choice. A kayak advocate at the show pointed to the sport's low costs and convenience.

"There's no fuel, no slip fees, and you don't need a big truck to haul it," the advocate said. "You can throw a kayak on top of your car and be on the lake in an hour."

Whether visitors are seasoned captains or first-time paddlers, the show offers a chance to compare options and talk with experts.

An inspection into Glasgow Royal Infirmary found nursing staff on several wards had to repeatedly challenge medical staff to obey strict rules over dress code and infection control.
Three separate doctors were seen wearing a wrist watch, having long hair untied and wearing an outdoor jacket at bedsides.
Inspectors issued the hospital requirements to improve its performance in preventing hospital-acquired infections.
The report said in general there was good compliance with the dress code policy, but said some medical staff did not comply.
The inspection team from Healthcare Improvement Scotland gave the hospital one month to ensure staff stick to the code.
It issued four requirements, including ensuring all patient equipment was stored and cleaned in one ward to reduce contamination risk, after three commodes and other equipment were found to be contaminated.
The report said inspectors checked another 17 commodes and found them and the majority of patient equipment to be clean.
The chief inspector said the board was making good progress to protect patients, staff and visitors from acquiring an infection.
Health bosses said a plan has been devised to address dress code compliance.
Rory Farrelly, NHS Greater Glasgow & Clyde Acute Director of Nursing, said: "We were pleased to note the number of positive findings by the HEI inspectors since their last visit.
"In particular, we were pleased that the inspectors noted the good communication between nursing and domestic staff in all wards, and the effective communication and support between the infection control team and ward staff.
"There was also clear evidence of good hand hygiene practice, and overall, the areas inspected were found to be clean. However, we recognise there are still areas we need to address."

Damon Dash, the well-known co-founder of Roc-A-Fella Records, has officially expanded his cultural footprint beyond the music industry. Recently, Dash hosted the opening of a new art exhibition titled Kinetic. The lively event took place at the gallery located inside his expansive DD172 media complex, drawing a diverse crowd of music and art enthusiasts alike.

Never one to shy away from bold statements, Dash fully embraced his well-documented love of controversy to introduce a show that pushes creative boundaries. According to gallery director Nyssa Frank, the exhibition draws a unique parallel to music. She explained that the collection finds its drama in history, noting that it blends the past, present, and future "much as hip-hop does." This thematic connection made the exhibition feel right at home in Dash's venue.

The multidisciplinary event featured several standout pieces that captivated attendees. A major highlight was an interactive installation by artist Andrew Russell Thomas. Thomas created a fascinating totem constructed entirely from found objects and speakers. The piece was brought to life by a swinging microphone that generated dynamic audio feedback, engaging the audience in an unexpected sensory experience.

Equally compelling was the work of Shani Peters. Her contribution included a thought-provoking video installation that seamlessly spliced footage of classic Black sitcom characters with historical clips of a Black Panther leader. Alongside this visual piece, Peters displayed custom-etched records featuring poems written in direct response to the Sean Bell verdict, adding a profound layer of social commentary to the room.

Ultimately, the Kinetic exhibition proved to be a major success. The vibrant gathering clearly demonstrated Dash's ongoing commitment to supporting fine art just as passionately as he has championed music throughout his legendary career.

BioWare has heard the complaints about Dragon Age II, and the studio says the next chapter in its fantasy series will take them to heart.

When Dragon Age II launched, it quickly drew fire from some of BioWare's most devoted fans. Many felt the sequel didn't live up to the high bar the studio had set with titles like Dragon Age: Origins, arguing that it traded away the depth and complexity that role-playing game (RPG) enthusiasts crave. For what it's worth, this writer found Dragon Age II to be a good game, just not an exceptional one, and that seems to be where many players landed as well.

In a recent interview with PC Gamer, BioWare CEO Ray Muzyka addressed the backlash and offered a glimpse at the road ahead. According to Muzyka, Dragon Age III will blend the strongest elements of both Origins and its follow-up. He promised that the next installment will hold surprises for longtime fans who have been with the series from the start, as well as for newer players who discovered the franchise through the second game.

Muzyka also explained why he thinks Dragon Age II received such a mixed reception. He pointed to a gap in expectations, noting that the game earned plenty of high review scores. The lower marks, he suggested, tended to come from critics who were hoping for another Origins and judged the sequel against that standard.

Still, Muzyka was clear that BioWare isn't brushing off the criticism. He stressed that the studio places real value on player feedback and intends to tackle the concerns of its core fans directly. The goal, he explained, is a game that satisfies dedicated veterans and newcomers alike.

Dazed and Confused has relaunched its website with an image-led design and an unusual opening event that required 10,000 visitors to gather before the site unlocked.

The fashion and culture magazine, founded by Jefferson Hack and Rankin, unveiled the redesign on 7 September, reinforcing its reputation as an innovative British publication and putting its digital presentation firmly in the spotlight.

Before the reveal, visitors were greeted by a countdown and a live tally of people arriving at the site. Early arrivals waited about twenty minutes for the audience to reach the threshold. The approach turned a routine website launch into a shared event, building anticipation before readers could explore the new layout.

At the centre of the redesign is an HTML5 mosaic combining images and text, a first for a UK magazine. Rather than presenting stories in a conventional list, the layout gives photography and written content space within the same visual display. Infinite scrolling allows readers to keep browsing without moving through separate pages, while image optimisation supports the picture-heavy experience.

A fixed navigation header provides a consistent route through the site. It expands to reveal content categories, featured articles, popular stories and social links, giving readers several ways to discover material beyond the items immediately visible on screen. The combination balances a striking visual identity with practical tools for finding content.

The commercial elements have also been folded into the design. Advertising and newsletter sign-ups sit neatly alongside editorial content, offering potential routes to greater online revenue. For a magazine with a strong social media following, the prominent social links also connect the redesigned website with its wider online presence.

The relaunch puts digital design at the heart of Dazed and Confused’s identity, rather than treating the website simply as an extension of print. It also raises the question of how sister titles AnOther and AnOther Man, along with rival i-D, will respond through their own digital strategies as fashion and culture publications compete for readers’ attention online.

Researchers from Stanford University and the Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have successfully captured the most detailed picture to date of the Fermi bubbles. These colossal, gamma-ray-emitting structures extend tens of thousands of light-years both above and below the center of our Milky Way galaxy.

The cosmic phenomenon was first identified approximately four years ago by a research team at Harvard University led by Douglas Finkbeiner. That initial, groundbreaking discovery relied heavily on data gathered by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope's Large Area Telescope. Now, a new comprehensive study, which has been officially accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal, is shedding more light on these mysterious galactic formations by combining recent Fermi data with results from various other experiments.

Despite having a much clearer image today, the Fermi bubbles continue to present several major puzzles for astronomers. The recent study highlights three primary mysteries: the remarkably sharp edges of the bubbles, their unexpectedly uniform brightness across vast distances, and their immense overall size.

Extracting this detailed cosmic view was a monumental challenge for the research team. Co-lead researcher Anna Franckowiak, who worked closely alongside colleague Malyshev on the project, explained the unique complexities involved in mapping the structures. "This was a very difficult process," Franckowiak noted, emphasizing the extensive effort required to isolate the correct data. Because the massive bubbles have no known counterparts at other wavelengths of light, the team had to meticulously identify and strip away heavy foreground gamma-ray emissions just to see the structures clearly.

As scientists continue to study our galaxy, the Fermi space telescope is still actively gathering valuable data from orbit. Researchers remain highly optimistic that these ongoing space observations will eventually resolve these lingering questions, helping us finally understand the true origin and nature of these glowing bubbles towering over the Milky Way.
