A deep-sea sonar vehicle searching for missing Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 was lost after striking a 2,200-meter-high mud volcano on the floor of the Indian Ocean, interrupting work by one of the vessels involved in the search.

The vehicle, known as a towfish, was being pulled behind the Fugro Discovery when the collision snapped its tow cable. The sonar equipment and 4,500 meters of cable fell to the seabed, according to the Australian agency coordinating the search on Malaysia’s behalf.

No one was injured in the incident. The coordinating agency said it expected the equipment to be retrieved later. The towfish was part of the underwater search operation involving Fugro, a Dutch survey company working under contract.

A towfish carries sonar equipment beneath the surface, allowing search teams to examine the ocean floor for objects that could be aircraft wreckage. Unlike equipment mounted directly on a ship, it travels behind the vessel on a long cable. In this case, the collision severed that connection, leaving both the vehicle and a substantial length of cable on the bottom.

The accident highlights the challenges of searching deep ocean terrain, where large underwater features can complicate efforts to survey the seabed. The mud volcano struck by the vehicle rises 2,200 meters from the surrounding ocean floor; that measurement describes its height, rather than the depth of the water above it.

Flight MH370, a Boeing 777 carrying 239 people, disappeared while flying from Kuala Lumpur to Beijing after inexplicably diverting from its planned route. The Indian Ocean search has sought to locate the missing aircraft and establish where it came down.

Separately, a large piece of metal debris discovered on a beach in Thailand was judged likely to have come from a Japanese H-2 rocket, rather than the missing airliner. That assessment distinguished the beach discovery from the search for MH370 and offered no new aircraft wreckage to guide the underwater operation.

The first Chord Hugo TT, essentially a larger Hugo with a display and a full range of hi-fi connectivity, was launched a few years ago. It stands for 'table top', which in itself tells you a lot about the product. It's bigger than the Hugo and is a desktop-oriented version.
This sequel – launched today at the Munich High End Show – has, as you'd expect, been subject to a number of upgrades, both inside and out.
Fundamentally, it's founded on the new Artix 7 FPGA chip, which has been coded by Chord's digital design consultant, Rob Watts, and claims to offer five times the processing power of the original Hugo TT.
There's also a new power supply, designed to play ball with even the most demanding headphones, and the promise of improved noise-shaping over the original.
The Hugo TT 2 eschew the battery supply used in its predecessor and instead uses six super caps in the power supply unit, capable of delivering huge, linear dynamic currents: peak output currents of 5A and 9.3V RMS.
The digital input count has increased, and now includes two optical (24-bit/192kHz-capable) and two coaxial (24-bit/768kHz-capable) sockets, as well as a USB-B connection capable of decoding 768kHz PCM and DSD 512 files. There's also aptX Bluetooth for wireless streaming.
Outputs deliver just as much versatility. There's balanced XLR, unbalanced RCA and three headphone outputs (two 6.33mm and one 3.5mm, which can be used simultaneously), as well as dual BNC DX outputs for use with Chord devices.
There are now buttons on the front (menu, set and power) for manual switching between filtering and crossfeed modes, and there's a remote (which also works with the Hugo 2) in the box too.
The new Hugo TT 2 also offers user-selectable audio controls, including an advanced four-stage filter giving you a choice of sonic signatures.
It can be used in pure DAC mode, enabled for high-power when headphones are connected (including low and high gain modes), or used in amplifier mode for use as a digital preamp or when directly connected to speakers.
The Chord Hugo TT 2 will be available in the autumn, priced at £3,996.

A North Charleston woman was arrested late Monday night after she got into an argument that led to a stabbing -- and it all started with classic rock. According to a North Charleston police report, 54-year-old Vernett Bader was charged with criminal domestic violence of a high and aggravated nature after officers showed up at her Brossy Circle home to investigate reports of an assault with a knife. When officers arrived, Bader was standing outside the house with another man, who told police the victim had several cuts on his arms and hands. Bader caused all of the cuts, the report states. When police talked to the victim, he said he had been listening to The Eagles when Bader told him that she did not want to hear the classic rock band's songs. So the man told her to shut up, the report states. Bader responded by allegedly getting a 14-inch serrated bread knife and swinging it at the man repeatedly, the report states. The victim wrestled the knife away from Bader, but she came back with another knife before the victim could run and lock himself in the bathroom. The victim said he and Bader used to date, but said that while the relationship had ended, they still lived together, the report states. According to Bader, the victim was choking her, which led to her getting a knife. However, officers did not see any handprints on Bader, and the neighbor corroborated the victim's story. Officers noted in the report that everyone involved in the altercation was intoxicated at the time of the assault. The report did not detail which Eagles songs were being played. As a result, Bader was arrested and taken to the Al Cannon Detention Center.

A recent study suggests that attention problems in adults may be linked to disrupted sleep, particularly obstructive sleep apnea, a condition that affects about 30 million Americans. The findings point to a possible connection between nighttime breathing difficulties and symptoms associated with attention deficit disorder.

Obstructive sleep apnea occurs when muscles in the throat collapse during sleep, repeatedly blocking airflow. These interruptions can cause snoring, fragmented rest and daytime drowsiness. The condition is also linked to heart disease, high blood pressure and diabetes, as well as smoking, making its effects a concern beyond poor sleep alone.

Among 34 patients with sleep apnea examined in the study, nearly half showed possible or probable symptoms of attention deficit disorder. That finding suggests that difficulties with attention can accompany sleep-related breathing problems. It does not establish that every patient with those symptoms has a separate attention disorder, or that apnea explains all adult attention difficulties.

After patients received treatment with continuous positive airway pressure, commonly called CPAP, both their daytime sleepiness and attention scores improved markedly. CPAP delivers air through a mask to keep the airway open during sleep, helping prevent the repeated breathing interruptions that disturb rest.

The improvement raises the possibility that treating sleep apnea could ease attention-related symptoms in some adults. Rather than viewing daytime drowsiness and difficulty concentrating as unrelated complaints, the findings suggest they may sometimes reflect the same underlying sleep problem. The study’s small group of apnea patients, however, leaves questions about how widely the results apply.

The lead researcher also noted that attention problems may not disappear completely after apnea treatment. Other conditions, including anxiety or depression, could contribute to ongoing symptoms. That distinction matters because improved breathing during sleep may address one source of difficulty without resolving every factor affecting a person’s attention.

The research team also examined patients with insomnia, extending its investigation beyond sleep apnea. Together, these lines of inquiry highlight the role sleep may play in understanding adult attention complaints and why persistent concentration problems warrant consideration alongside sleep quality.

Four United States senators recently concluded a significant three-day visit to the Philippines aimed at strengthening bilateral relations and addressing ongoing territorial disputes in the South China Sea, a vital maritime region that Manila officially refers to as the West Philippine Sea.

The bipartisan congressional delegation, which included prominent Senators John McCain, Joseph Lieberman, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Kelly Ayotte, engaged in high-level discussions heavily focused on regional stability. As maritime tensions with China continue to simmer over competing territorial claims, the senatorial visit served to reassure a long-standing and important ally in Southeast Asia.

During the diplomatic trip, Senator McCain specifically ruled out the possibility of an armed conflict with China over the contested waters. Instead, he emphasized the critical need for diplomatic cooperation with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations to peacefully protect freedom of navigation. Ensuring that these vital commercial sea lanes remain fully open to international shipping is a top priority for Washington and its regional partners.

Highlighting the significant economic stakes, Senator Lieberman pointed out the immense importance of the disputed waterway to global trade. He expressed his strong opposition to any single nation dominating the vital region. Delivering a message of reassurance to Philippine leaders, Lieberman promised to strengthen the Philippine military to help maintain a balanced and secure environment in the area.

Despite this commitment to regional military support, Washington does not plan to reopen the large military bases in the Philippines that were closed in the early 1990s. Instead, the current defense strategy involves conducting joint military exercises and transferring surplus ships and modern equipment to bolster the defensive capabilities of the Philippine armed forces.

On the diplomatic front, the visiting senators voiced strong support for a multilateral negotiating approach led by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. This inclusive strategy encourages all involved countries to work together to establish fair maritime rules. However, this collective approach faces continued resistance from China, which strongly rejects multilateral negotiations in favor of pursuing one-on-one bilateral talks with individual claimant nations.

Archaeological finds described as 'the most important' to be discovered in North Somerset for 100 years have been unearthed in Banwell.
Bristol Water has been laying a seven-kilometre, £3.6million main between Banwell and Hutton, and archaeologists employed to investigate remains along the work route discovered a horde of Roman artefacts in the village.
Bristol Water's Jeremy Williams said of the discovery: "We are told that the finds rewrite the known interpretation of Roman Banwell and are of regional significance."
Among the discoveries was what appears to be a Roman cemetery containing several human burials, 9,000 pieces of pottery, several copper brooches and a coin from the reign of Roman emperor Constantine the Great.
As well as the cemetery, which seems to show a shift in Roman practice from cremating the dead to burying them, there is also evidence of earlier, possibly Iron Age, agricultural activity around the site.
It is thought that the cemetery was linked to the villa of a wealthy landowner, as opposed to a larger settlement.
Mr Williams said: "The archaeologists are very excited about their finds, which they have made despite bad weather turning the area into a sea of mud at times.
"The excavation has been described as potentially the most important for 100 years in North Somerset."
Many of the finds will be on show at an event hosted by the Banwell Society of Archaeology at the village hall in Westfield Road at 7.30 pm on November 19.

Mercedes has signed 15-year-old Estonian Paul Aron to its Formula 1 junior programme, adding one of karting’s standout graduates to its roster as he builds momentum in his first season of single-seater racing.

Aron joins the Mercedes development scheme after a dominant karting campaign in which he won the CIK-FIA European OK Junior title. He also claimed victories in other major junior events and finished third in another prominent series, establishing the credentials that preceded his move into cars.

The teenager is now racing for Prema in both the German ADAC and Italian Formula 4 championships. He has already secured his first single-seater victory at the Red Bull Ring and ranks among the leading rookies in both competitions.

Those early results mark a promising transition from karting to Formula 4, an entry-level category where young drivers begin adapting to the demands of car racing. Competing in two championships gives Aron opportunities to build experience against fellow emerging prospects.

Aron also has a family connection to the junior single-seater ladder: his older brother, Ralf, previously competed in Formula 3. Paul’s arrival at Mercedes adds a new development opportunity as his own career takes shape.

He is the team’s third junior signing this year, following the recruitment of karters Antonelli and Powell. The additions join a programme that also includes Esteban Ocon and George Russell.

The latest intake suggests Mercedes is placing greater emphasis on recruiting younger talent rather than adding drivers already competing in Formula 2 or Formula 3.

That apparent shift may reflect the difficulties Mercedes encountered in securing a Formula 1 race seat for Ocon. For Aron, however, the immediate focus remains on developing in Formula 4 and building on his breakthrough victory.

In a highly anticipated television event, worlds collided when the Teutul family from TLC's hit reality show American Chopper traveled to the Gosselins' Pennsylvania home for a special crossover episode.

An ambitious effort to revolutionize student health in the Los Angeles school district has encountered a significant roadblock. Inspired by the First Lady’s nationwide campaign for healthier children's meals and newly revised federal dietary guidelines, the district completely overhauled its lunch menus. However, officials are now discovering that the well-intentioned initiative has backfired badly.

Since the introduction of the new, health-conscious menus, far fewer students are choosing to eat school lunches. Many students have openly dismissed the new food offerings as unappetizing or poorly prepared. Instead of eating the provided nutritious meals, a growing number of children are opting to bring items like chips and soda from home. The situation has even sparked an informal campus trade, with an underground market for junk food emerging among the student body. 

The fallout extends beyond dietary choices to serious waste and unexpected health concerns. Local principals describe witnessing massive amounts of discarded milk and untouched healthy entrees ending up straight in the garbage. "We are seeing unprecedented amounts of food waste every single day," noted one school administrator. Furthermore, some students are reporting health complaints such as lethargy and stomach pains simply because they are skipping meals altogether. 

The financial toll of the sweeping menu overhaul has also been severe. District costs climbed sharply during the transition, with spending on fresh produce alone rising tenfold over just a four-year period. 

Now, facing mounting backlash from hungry students and concerned parents, the Los Angeles school district is being forced to reverse course. To encourage students to actually eat the meals provided, officials are bringing back familiar, traditional lunchroom favorites. Moving forward, menus will once again feature popular items like hamburgers and pizza to strike a realistic balance between nutritional value and student appeal.

Researchers at Texas A&M University are fighting social network spam with a clever trick: fake accounts designed to lure spammers into revealing themselves.

The project, funded in part by a grant from Google, uses decoy profiles known as "honeypots" on Twitter and MySpace. Like a pot of honey that draws in insects, these accounts are built to attract spammers who spread malicious software, known as malware, or who try to "phish," tricking people into handing over passwords, bank details and other personal information.

To look convincing, the Twitter decoys post updates automatically, drawing on a large pool of real tweets collected from genuine users. That recycled content helps the fake accounts blend in with ordinary members of the network.

When another account contacts a honeypot, monitoring software goes to work. It examines the messages sent, the sender's profile, demographic details and posting history. By comparing these traits across many accounts, the researchers can identify patterns that separate spammers from legitimate users.

So far, 61 honeypots have caught more than 30,000 spammers. One common pattern stands out: many of the spam accounts pose as young women from California, and they typically target men.

Social networks are especially attractive to spammers for two main reasons. First, users tend to trust the people they connect with, making them more likely to click a link or reply to a message from a "friend" or follower. Second, shortened web links, widely used on Twitter because of its character limit, hide the true destination of a link until someone clicks it.

Google's involvement may surprise some, since Twitter and MySpace are not Google services. However, the company regularly funds outside research, and efforts to curb spam benefit the entire internet, including Google's competitors. Fewer scams and less malware make the web safer for everyone.

The researchers are now setting their sights on Facebook, the largest social network, as the next place to deploy their honeypots.

This summer I set myself a little kitchen challenge: cook more Mexican-inspired food at home, and finally learn to make a salsa I'm truly proud of. Store-bought jars have their place, but I wanted something fresh, bright, and mine.

For guidance, I've been leaning heavily on Rick Bayless's website. He's a chef who has spent decades exploring and teaching Mexican cooking, and his recipes are wonderfully clear for home cooks like me.

My first attempt was his Salsa Mexicana, the classic chopped mix of tomato, onion, chile, and cilantro. It was good, but I could tell the tomatoes were holding it back. Grocery store tomatoes in early summer just don't have much flavor. So I'm calling that round one. Once my garden tomatoes ripen, I'll be making it again, and I suspect the difference will be dramatic.

Of course, salsa left me with that familiar problem: half a bunch of cilantro wilting in the fridge. Rather than let it go to waste, I tried Bayless's Avocado-Cilantro Mayonnaise, and I'm so glad I did.

It could not be easier. Combine about half a cup of good mayonnaise, one avocado, and a quarter cup of chopped cilantro in a food processor. Pulse until smooth, then season with salt. That's it.

The result is creamy, fresh, and tastes a lot like guacamole in spreadable form. It's also a gorgeous pale green, which makes it feel fancy for something that took five minutes.

My plan is to slather it on sandwiches all summer long. Next time, I might swap in plain yogurt for some or all of the mayo to lighten it up. "Healthier guacamole spread" has a nice ring to it, doesn't it?

What is it about a little red bicycle? This one, parked at a yard sale in front of an aged, shingle-style house one weekend, predates my own vintage, and yet, it evokes memory. None specific to my world, but rather a general sensation of nostalgia.
I was reminded when I saw it of a question posed by Rob Penn in his cycling classic, It's All About the Bike. In his exposition of the neuroscience behind why people never forget how to ride a bicycle, Penn notes that certain neurons in our brains encode all our motor skills — biking, as well as walking, dancing or rowing. He wonders why the bicycle has become the benchmark. After all, "It's like riding a bike" is the phrase we most commonly use with reference to remembering a skill.
"It may be to do with the relationship between the bicycle and childhood," Penn writes. "Most of us now learn to ride a bike early in life, 'before the dark hour of reason grows.' Perhaps, in youth, the cerebellum sends out stronger electrical signals, which are in turn encoded very carefully and stored in a secure place — the cerebral equivalent of a safe-deposit box in a steel vault beneath a bank in Zurich."
Penn's exploration focuses on the brain's keen development of motor skills in youth. But the brain also has a place, in the hippocampus, where memory and spatial relationships are consolidated, including early experiences of a transcendent kind. The ones that die hard, even as others fade with age. Elemental memories of freedom — of the transformative moment when we escaped our driveways or city blocks to a new independence, untethered from parents. Perhaps they surface from there in an almost magnetic attraction to a little red bicycle.
Despite rust and ruin, innocence and possibility reside in a stalwart steel frame and dense rubber tires. That's why I dismounted from my road bike and bought this little beauty for $20 straight up. No idea what I'll do with it.

I'll be honest: I didn't need a new tablet. But when Apple's latest iPad sold millions of units within days of hitting shelves, I couldn't help wondering what all of us are actually doing with these things. Tablets, smartphones, and hybrids (laptop-tablet combos) are flying off store shelves. So how are they changing the way we spend our days?

It turns out one answer is surprisingly wholesome. According to research from the Pew Research Center, connected devices seem to nudge people toward reading the news. Most computer owners say they read news on their machines, and roughly half of smartphone and tablet owners do the same. Mobile news reading is especially strong, and plenty of people don't stick to just one screen. They check headlines on their phone over breakfast, skim articles on a tablet during lunch, and catch up on a laptop at night.

I used to think of "reading the news" as something I did once a day. Now it happens in little bursts, whenever there's a spare minute and a screen nearby.

Does this make us better informed? I'm not sure anyone can say yet. Scrolling headlines isn't the same as understanding an issue. Still, I think there's something to the idea that constant access turns news reading into a habit.

That got me thinking about schools. If tablets can make adults more curious about the world, why not use them to engage students? I'm not suggesting we toss out textbooks, notebooks, and library books. Traditional materials still matter. But a tablet in a classroom could make current events feel immediate and interactive rather than dusty and distant.

There's a catch, though. Not everyone owns one of these devices. If connected gadgets really do shape how we learn and stay informed, people without them risk falling behind. "Access" shouldn't become another word for privilege.

So yes, I'll probably keep my old tablet a while longer. But I'm glad it keeps me reading.

When I was a kid, we had a cathode-ray tube TV. Sometimes, when the antenna signal got deflected, or the vertical and horizontal were messed up, all the people and images on the screen would suddenly spasm into several versions of themselves, or the picture would start flipping top-to-bottom on the screen, or bend and zig-zag. That's sort of how I feel right now, returning from Svalbard. It's not so much a physical sensation as an emotional one… though re-adjusting to a nine-hour time difference is probably part of it. I know my body will figure out how to match the cues from nature soon enough. I'm not so sure about my images on the screen, though. For the next few weeks, I'm hoping to tweak the dials and bring these two visions into alignment. There are lots of stories from the journey I will try to do justice to here in coming posts, including adventures with our understatedly-badass guides, Theres, Sara, and Åshild; the ghosts of Pyramiden; flying snails; it is not 4 pm if there's no cake; if it's dead, drag it back to Kate; and the convivial wrath of Captain Jo. Much of what I did on the journey was to record audio, which I will be putting together into a larger project that will be available for download in a few months. My ultimate goal is to offer a journey to the Arctic in sound that anyone can take by listening. Why sound and not video and photos? I'll devote an entire post to that in the upcoming weeks…

Lately, I have been keeping a close eye on the Supreme Court hearings regarding video game restrictions, and the outcome has been fascinating. The justices actually seem much better informed on the nuances of the gaming industry than the California lawyers arguing for state censorship. It is almost comical that the state decided to use Postal 2 as its primary example of a game that warrants strict legal oversight. Pointing to such an outdated and intentionally absurd title to make a sweeping legal argument about modern video games feels completely out of touch with reality.

In other news, the much anticipated Kinect launch recently took place, but I completely skipped it. Looking at the launch lineup, the games just seem remarkably weak and lack the depth I usually look for in a new platform. What truly puzzles me, however, is the gaming media coverage of the device. I keep reading reviews and watching tech demos, but no one seems to mention its glaring similarity to the Sony EyeToy. As someone who remembers playing those early motion games, the parallel is impossible to ignore. I am surprised the critics are giving it a pass without at least acknowledging the history. "It feels like we are pretending motion tracking cameras were just invented," as a friend recently pointed out, and I could not agree more.

As for my personal playlist, my attention has been a bit scattered. I recently put the main campaign of Red Dead Redemption on pause. It is a fantastic experience, but right now, I am finding myself much more invested in its zombie themed expansion, Undead Nightmare. There is something incredibly fun about wandering the wild west and battling the undead.

Beyond that, my gaming time is currently divided among a few different titles. I am having a great time playing Splinter Cell: Conviction in cooperative mode with my wife, which always makes for an entertaining evening. When I am playing solo, I usually bounce between Defense Grid and Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker.

While they are all good games, none of them truly grips me or holds my undivided attention right now. I am mostly just passing the time, hoping a truly standout game comes along soon to completely capture my interest.

These last days, I spent all my spare time on the gdx-setup-ui tool you may know. This desktop application is used to quickly create and set up the different Eclipse projects required to use libgdx and all its backend, so you can concentrate on useful stuff, such as coding your game. Since version 2, you can also include some third-party libraries in your projects during creation, and everything is handled for you: jar files are put in the correct folders, and the project classpaths are edited to include the libraries. While there are not a lot of libraries available for now, this will change in the future. Expect the post-processing library (contributed by dudez), for instance, and many more.
Following this aim, I wanted to add a new functionality for a long time: being able to update the projects to the latest libGDX version with the same ease of use. This is easy to implement; the different jar files of the libgdx distribution just need to be copied to the correct folders, and that's all. However, what I thought would be really cool was to add this update support to the third-party libraries, i.e. to be able to select any third-party library in the list, and the tool would add it if it was not already present, or update it instead.
Since I barely have a few hours of spare time per week currently, this took quite a long time to implement, but it is now done! Therefore, I need you, really: I don't want to ship a broken release, so I need a real beta-test on this. Please report any bugs or inconsistencies you find.

If you’ve been wondering what’s behind “This is Your Life, Archimedes Jackson,” here’s a little background on the roleplay story and an invitation to get involved. In a City of Heroes-style community, a reunion between former allies seems like a good starting point for trouble.

This story is partly a parody of an earlier piece, “Archie’s Transcendence.” It also gives me a chance to relaunch a second storyline that began on another forum. Rather than leave that thread stranded, I wanted to bring it into this setting and see where a fresh round of collaboration could take it. Both older works will be archived and posted later, so the background will be available for anyone interested in tracing the connections.

At the center of the trouble are Gigyatron and Exyle, two villains played by my wife and me. They were once allies of Archie, our unfortunate empath. Now they’re looking for revenge, and this isn’t just a case of villains making dramatic threats: they’ve already killed one version of him.

That detail naturally raises a few questions. Why have former allies turned so completely against Archie? What do they actually want from him now? And when things get ugly, will anyone step forward to help him?

I’d rather let those answers emerge through the roleplay than explain everything before the story has room to breathe. The uncertainty is part of the fun, especially when other players bring their own characters and perspectives into the mix.

That’s where you come in. If you have a villain who might fit, a hero willing to get involved, or a character you’d like to put in the spotlight, I’d love to hear your ideas. There’s room here for more than the central confrontation, and collaboration is a big part of why I’m revisiting this material.

My one request is that you check with me before introducing major plot changes. I want everyone to have space to contribute while keeping the main storyline coherent.

For now, Archie has old friends with lethal intentions. What happens next is where we get to play.

As a prolific maker of knitting bags, I am constantly on the lookout for the perfect design. Recently, I discovered what has quickly become one of my absolute favorites: the Amy Butler Stash N Dash pattern. While this pattern is traditionally meant for toiletries, I decided to sew the largest size and repurpose it as a dedicated project bag for my portable knitting, small projects, and socks.

What I love most about this bag is how it completely transforms my crafting experience. It keeps my yarn perfectly contained and untangled, which is a massive bonus. Even better, it protects my precious materials from curious children at home. When I am out and about, the convenient wrist strap is a lifesaver. I can easily carry my yarn on my wrist and stow my work quickly when I need my hands free. As I often tell my knitting friends, "This little bag holds surprisingly more than it appears to on the outside."

The construction process is an absolute joy because the pattern is so quick to make. For my version, I decided to combine interfaced quilting cotton with some sturdy home decor fabric. This combination gives the finished bag a beautiful structure and long-lasting durability.

The versatility of the Stash N Dash goes far beyond holding yarn. I have realized it works perfectly as a notions pouch, a quick shopping wristlet, or even a little treasure bag for a child. Because it sews up so fast and looks professional, I am already planning to make several more versions. I just learned that David Brenner has died, and I've been sitting with that news longer than I expected. Brenner was the first stand-up comedian who ever made me laugh. I don't mean chuckling politely because the grown-ups were laughing. I mean really laughing, the kind that makes your stomach hurt.

When I was a kid, he seemed to be everywhere. He was a regular on The Tonight Show, and he turned up constantly on the daytime talk shows hosted by Mike Douglas and Merv Griffin. If I was home sick from school, there was a decent chance Brenner would wander onto the screen at some point, lanky and grinning, ready to tell a story.

What hooked me was how easygoing he was. He never seemed to be attacking anyone. He just talked about everyday life and the little absurdities we all share. I still remember a bit about his car breaking down. He lifted the hood and simply stared at the engine as if it might explain itself. He had no idea what he was looking at, and neither did any of us. That was the joke, and it was perfect. Watching him, I started paying attention to how comedy worked, and I never really stopped.

By the 1980s, the comedy world had shifted. Edgier, more cynical comics took over, and Brenner's gentle style started to look old-fashioned to some people. I felt bad for him. When he launched his own late-night show, I rooted hard for it, even though it didn't last long.

Brenner grew up poor in Philadelphia, and he always seemed genuinely grateful for the life comedy gave him. That gratitude came through in everything he did.

Here's a clip of him on Letterman years later. He was still funny. Rest easy, David.

K. Anders Ericsson's research doesn't prove that to become an expert at anything, you need only do that thing for 10,000 hours. It doesn't suggest anything of the sort. In fact, one of my favorite quotes from Ericsson is "Just because you've been walking for 55 years doesn't mean you're getting better at it." And just because you've been selling for as many years doesn't mean you're getting better either.
Ericsson's 10,000-hour rule says that you need to do what he calls "deliberate practice" for all of those hours. Deliberate practice is very different from mindlessly repeating the same activity over and over. Instead, you focus intently on improving your form, your competency, dialing in your performance. It's this intense level of practice that allows the master to break through the plateaus where amateurs get stuck.
Ericsson suggests that some masters have to take a nap after an hour of deliberate practice. It's taxing on the system.
This is why the 10,000 rules don't work. It's not because you haven't done something for 10,000 hours. It's because you haven't been engaged in deliberate practice for all of those hours. But fortunately, you don't have to wait to accumulate all of those hours to improve your competency.
You can improve little by little, day by day, by giving your focus over to the one sales call that you are going to make. You can deliberately practice listening for 20 minutes when you sit down with your client, your team, or your spouse. You can deliberately practice writing for 20 minutes a day and, over time, you will become a better writer (even if you are not Hemingway).
It never hurts to go for the first chair. Mastery is worth pursuing. But mastery isn't found in the 10,000 hours. It's found in deliberate practice. You get better when you focus on getting better. Practice doesn't make perfect. Perfect practice does.

Every morning when I was a child, my mother stood at the door as I grabbed my backpack and said the same thing: "Make it a good day." Not "have" a good day. Make one. It took me years to understand her. She was teaching me that my attitude was mine to choose, no matter what the day handed me.

I think about her words often now, especially when I look at the world around us. News of wars, political battles, and conflicts in our communities and even our own homes can leave us anxious and unsettled. In the middle of all that noise, I have found one choice that brings peace and protection: the choice to have faith.

Some people think of faith as a gift that lands on certain lucky souls. I don't see it that way. Faith requires desire and effort. Notice how the Savior speaks to us. He says, "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." He says, "Knock, and it shall be opened unto you." Those are active words. Coming means moving toward Him. Knocking means lifting our hand and trying. He is waiting, but we have to take the step.

That means each day we decide. We can choose faith over doubt, faith over fear, faith over uncertainty, and faith over pessimism. Just like my mother said, belief is something we make.

I love the promise that if we have faith "as a grain of mustard seed," we can say to a mountain, "Remove hence to yonder place; and it shall remove." I have seen mountains move in my own life, though not the rocky kind. I have watched doubt become hope. I have felt sin give way to repentance. I have known pain to turn into peace.

So today I am grateful. I feel secure, even when the world does not. And I feel a quiet, steady joy, because I have chosen to believe.

I'll admit it: when I first saw Argos-Shimano sitting at the very bottom of the team time trial results, my gut reaction was disappointment. Last place? At the Tour de France? But the longer I thought about it, the more I realized I was reading the result the wrong way.

Here's something about a three-week Grand Tour that took me years of watching to really understand. Not every team is there to win the yellow jersey. Only a handful of squads genuinely have the riders and depth to fight for the overall title, known as the general classification. Everyone else is chasing something different.

Some teams want stage wins. Others are hunting the green jersey for the points classification, the polka-dot jersey for the best climber, or the white jersey for the best young rider. And some smaller teams simply need to prove they deserved their invitation. That often means sending riders into long breakaways so the sponsor's logo spends hours on television. Each of those goals demands a different way of racing.

Argos-Shimano built its entire Tour around sprint finishes, and it was already paying off. Marcel Kittel won Stage 1, putting the team in the spotlight from day one. With a sprinter that fast, every flat stage becomes a genuine opportunity, and protecting that opportunity matters more than almost anything else.

That's what made the team time trial so interesting. Argos-Shimano actually has some strong time trialists, so it could have pushed for a respectable placing. Instead, the team rode hard but cautiously. There was no reckless cornering, no burning riders into the ground, and no unnecessary risk. All nine riders crossed the line together and safely.

A friend texted me afterward: "Did they just give up?" I told him no, they just did the math. A crash during a high-speed team effort could end a lead-out rider's Tour. Wasting energy on a day they had no plan to win could cost them a sprint later in the week.

So that last-place finish wasn't a failure. It was a choice. Argos-Shimano was saving its legs for the days that actually mattered to its goals.

It's a good reminder for any cycling fan. The results sheet only tells you who was fastest on a given day. It doesn't tell you who raced smartest.

Every day when we move through our lives, we are practicing empathy. Watching at an intersection to see who goes or who gives way, maybe feeling in a supermarket queue someone's urgency to go first, or simply sitting with a friend. The skill of tuning in to what others' needs are is the practice of empathy.
Empathy can be described as the capacity to receive and understand emotional states or the ability to understand things from someone else's viewpoint. When we practice empathy, we can be with someone and embody the state they are in. It is almost as if we receive and feel what is being felt by those we are in touch with. We can experience empathy at work, at home or on the street with strangers.
Yoga is the practice of connection; the opposite of connection is ego. When we can't see someone else's point of view, what we do is step into separation. We step into our camps and take our sides. We disagree, criticize or scrutinize the actions of others. We separate others from us and see them as against us, as the other. When we are like this, it saves us from feeling and helps us to justify our positions.
How do you think the world would be if we were empathetic to all the people around us? If instead of taking sides, we were all sides? If instead of judging and gossiping, we felt for the other person? How would your life be and the life of your co-workers, friends, colleagues and family if, for one moment, we all stopped looking for who was right but really stepped inside the others' shoes and became one with how it must be for them?
Practice for today: Reserving your judgment and taking a broader view with your emotions is a way to connect to all of the human race. Empathy is the practice of seeing beyond your borders into another's emotions. Practicing empathy is a way to set yourself free.

I was looking forward to a quiet evening with a bottle of El Toqui Syrah last weekend. I pulled the cork, poured a glass, and admired the color, a deep, inviting purple that promised plenty of dark fruit. Then I took a sniff. Instead of blackberries and pepper, I got a damp basement. The wine was corked.

If you've been drinking wine for a while, you probably recognize cork taint almost instantly. Newer wine drinkers, though, often just assume they've bought a bad wine and move on, never realizing the problem was a contaminated cork rather than the winemaker. To be fair, some wines really are just poor, and no cork is to blame. So how can you tell the difference?

Sometimes the cork itself offers a clue. If it's crumbling, soaked through, or wine has leaked down the neck of the bottle, be suspicious. My El Toqui showed none of those warning signs. The cork looked perfectly healthy, which is a good reminder that appearances can deceive.

The real giveaway was the smell and taste. A corked wine typically reeks of musty cardboard or wet newspaper. As I muttered to myself, "It's like drinking last week's paper after it sat out in the rain." That mustiness carried right through to the palate, flattening whatever fruit should have been there.

Be careful not to jump to conclusions, though. Some wines open with odd, funky aromas that blow off after a few minutes in the glass or a decanter. Give it some air before you pass judgment. Milder cases of cork taint are trickier, since the wine may simply taste dull and lifeless. That's where experience helps. If you've had the wine before and it tasted vibrant, or other reviewers rave about it, a flat bottle is probably corked.

You'll sometimes read that as many as 15% of bottles are affected. I'm skeptical. In 25 years of regular drinking, I'd put my own rate at around 2 to 3%. Still, when it happens, trust your nose.

I thought Oregon’s bye week might offer a chance to catch my breath. Instead, injuries, Pac-12 developments and the Ducks’ climb to No. 1 kept the news rolling. Now UCLA arrives, and I’m ready to trade the headlines for some football.

My biggest question isn’t whether Oregon has more talent. It’s whether the time off has interrupted the rhythm that made this offense so difficult to stop. Momentum can be a funny thing, especially when your quarterback spends the break resting a sore shoulder.

Darron Thomas doesn’t need to win this game with his arm alone, but I’ll be watching his timing early. Are the throws crisp? Does the offense move with its usual confidence? With Kenjon Barner likely unavailable, the Ducks have one fewer option for turning an ordinary play into a big gain.

That makes the plan straightforward: give LaMichael James plenty of work. Let him establish the running game, then use screens to keep UCLA moving sideways. When the Bruins start leaning toward the line of scrimmage, take some shots downfield against their injured cornerbacks. There’s no reason to get elaborate when Oregon’s strengths fit the matchup this well.

UCLA should have a few moments. Its running game is good enough to sustain drives and perhaps put points on the board before Oregon settles in. But it’s also a one-dimensional attack, and Kevin Prince’s probable absence makes it harder to imagine the Bruins finding enough balance to keep pace.

Over four quarters, I expect Oregon’s depth to become the story. The Ducks can keep applying pressure long after UCLA’s early energy begins to fade.

If the Bruins have a route to making this uncomfortable, it starts with their kicking game: win field position and collect points whenever the opportunity appears. Even then, they’ll need Oregon to help.

I can picture a rusty opening. I have a much harder time picturing a close finish.

My pick: Oregon 45, UCLA 13.

What a summer it has been! Our crew has logged more miles than we can count, from shady trail hikes to early-morning runs along the river, and we've welcomed a whole new class of puppies who are learning to sit, stay, and (mostly) not chew our shoelaces. Some of our regulars even discovered a love of splashing in the shallows. Watching those little ones grow more confident every week has been one of the highlights of our season here on the South Shore.

As we head into the hottest stretch of the year, we wanted to share a few friendly reminders to keep your pups happy and healthy.

First, check that your dog's flea, tick, and heartworm prevention is up to date. Ticks aren't just a deep-woods problem anymore. We're finding them in backyards, parks, and even on neighborhood sidewalks. And the mosquitoes? They've been especially fierce this year, which matters because mosquitoes are what spread heartworm. If you're not sure when your last dose was, give your vet a quick call.

Second, think hydration and cooling. Humid days are tough on dogs, since they cool off mainly by panting rather than sweating. Bring water on every outing, even short ones, and leave full bowls at home. Make sure your dog always has access to shade or air conditioning. As one of our walkers likes to say, "If it's too sticky for you, it's too sticky for them."

Third, get moving together! Summer is a great time to bond through exercise. Try a morning walk, an easy jog, a few sprint intervals in the yard, or a good old-fashioned game of fetch before the heat sets in.

Finally, a word on etiquette. Keep your dog leashed wherever it's required, and don't assume every stranger (or every dog) wants to say hello. Ask first. And please, always pick up after your pup. Nobody enjoys a surprise on the sidewalk.

Fall will be here before we know it, so soak up these long, sunny days with your best friend. We'll see you out on the trails!

The Killing's Gotta Stop
Has anyone else had enough of these "Microsoft Acrylic is the [Photoshop/Flash/Illustrator/FreeHand/Fireworks/etc] Killer!" articles? Is the technology press so bored that they have to invent conflicts?
If I were Microsoft, I'd be deflecting these assertions like crazy. Why? They set unrealistic, misleading expectations that end up reflecting poorly on new products.
Background: When InDesign 1.0 was in development, it got dubbed by some at Adobe as "Quark Killer." (This was before my time here, so I don't know the origin of the phrase, but I do know that I've never heard anyone here use it.) When the 1.0 product shipped and didn't "kill" an app that had been established for more than a decade, it was assumed to be a failure. Well, 5+ years later, InDesign is doing just fine, thanks.
It's also false to assume that new apps need or want to kill others. I was a Flash developer in the late '90s, so when Adobe offered me the chance to work on LiveMotion, I jumped at the chance. Did I want to "kill" Flash? Of course not! I enjoyed working with the format enough that I wanted to make the ecosystem of authoring tools bigger and better. But hey, sure enough, LiveMotion got dubbed the "Flash Killer," setting up conflict and disappointment. (And now, that unfortunate moniker has passed to another unreleased product.)
So, back to the subject at hand. I think Macromedia's John Dowdell said it well: of course, Microsoft will create tools to target its next-gen OS; it's not a zero-sum game; and different strokes serve different folks.
As Max Fischer would say, "The killin's gotta stop, ese."

I’ve never felt that loving The Great Gatsby should be a requirement for loving literature. Some books find us at the wrong moment; others simply leave us cold. That’s why I found the appeal of Maureen Corrigan’s So We Read On so refreshing. Her affectionate tribute to F. Scott Fitzgerald’s novel makes room for something more inviting than compulsory admiration: the pleasure of discovering what a book can hold.

Corrigan, the book critic for NPR’s Fresh Air, combines literary analysis with history, biography, and memoir. That mixture keeps her enthusiasm from becoming a lecture. She wants to understand not only how Gatsby works, but also how it survived, reached new readers, and became a novel people continue to argue about.

The research passages have the energy of a treasure hunt. Following Corrigan among Fitzgerald’s papers at the Library of Congress, I was reminded that scholarship can begin with the same impulse that sends any curious reader down a rabbit hole: surely there’s one more detail worth finding. Her delight in the search makes the archival material feel alive rather than dutifully assembled.

Just as appealing is her return to her Catholic high school in Queens to hear what students think about Gatsby. The visit brings nostalgia into conversation with fresh responses. There’s something touching about returning to a place that shaped your reading life and discovering that the books are still there, meeting entirely different people.

Corrigan’s account of Gatsby’s changing fortunes also gives its familiar status a useful jolt. The novel was initially a commercial failure, not an instant monument. She argues that its circulation through wartime Armed Services Editions helped build its readership. That history makes literary endurance seem less inevitable and more dependent on books actually finding their way into readers’ hands.

Her portraits of Scott and Zelda are sympathetic without smoothing away their difficulties. I also appreciated her impatience with Hemingway’s condescension and her warmer treatment of Fitzgerald’s friendship with Ring Lardner. These relationships matter because they restore a human scale to a writer so often surrounded by legend.

What stayed with me most, though, was Corrigan’s belief in reading as a shared adventure. Having helped launch “One Book, One City” programs, she clearly values conversations beyond the critic’s desk. You don’t have to finish So We Read On adoring Gatsby. Feeling newly curious about reading is reward enough.

Have you ever noticed how incredibly fast trends in style and social media photography shift? It feels like overnight, entire communities of creators adopt the exact same warm vintage filters or start styling their outfits with the exact same chunky footwear. Keeping up can feel like a full time job. Lately, I have been working hard to grow my Instagram following, which means spending hours researching effective hashtags and analyzing what actually captures attention.

During my research, one thing became abundantly clear. Outfit of the day shots and flat lays completely dominate the fashion blogger tag. If you want to stand out, mastering the flat lay is an absolute must. Recently, I stumbled across a wonderful lifestyle blog that featured a cheerful, practical guide to perfecting these overhead shots. Their tutorial covered all the essentials of setup, emphasizing that natural lighting is the most critical element of any flat lay. They also shared brilliant tips on arranging items so the eye dances across the image.

I want to add a few of my own tips to that excellent advice. First, you do not need an expensive photography studio to create a beautiful aesthetic. I highly recommend improvising your backdrops. A simple white bed sheet, a textured blanket, or even inexpensive colored paper from a craft store works wonders. Once your background is set, do not be afraid to climb on a chair and try various angles. You want to fill the frame with your favorite accessories and clothing pieces without overcrowding the composition. As they note in the guide, "Always give your items enough room to breathe."

After you snap the perfect picture, the real magic happens in the editing process. Take some time to play around with different filters and saturation levels. A little boost in saturation can make your outfit colors pop beautifully against a neutral backdrop.

I would love to hear about your own creative process. What are your favorite props or photography tricks for social media? Leave a comment below to share your experiences, and be sure to follow my Instagram account for more daily style inspiration.

Instead of tossing it, I tucked a doily behind the opening and backed it with mustard cardstock. I love how that empty space became a focal point.

Next came texture. I misted color through a tree mask (a mask is just a stencil you spray or paint through), then dipped an old toothbrush in yellow paint and flicked it across the page for a speckled look. To finish, I layered in some Prima packaging pieces and canvas leaves for a little dimension.

The photo itself makes me laugh every time. It's my infant twins sitting in a pile of leaves, and one of them looks thoroughly worried about the whole situation. I'm calling it his first official fall face.

I didn't want to crop out all that gorgeous fall scenery, so rather than trimming the picture down, I framed the boys by wrapping jute around the photo. It draws your eye right to their sweet faces while keeping the background intact. If you don't have jute on hand, twine works just as well.

Ripe oranges on the trees in Sacramento had me convinced we’d arrived in Northern California just in time for spring. Then we drove to Lake Tahoe, and winter made a fairly convincing comeback. Snow piled up around us, replacing my visions of sunshine with something better: fresh powder and two weeks of adventure.

In Tahoe, our host families made us feel immediately at home. There was something especially comforting about coming back from skiing to such a warm welcome. Hot tubs helped, too. After a day on the slopes, sinking into steaming water while surrounded by snow felt like the perfect reward.

We also caught Tahoe City’s Snowfest, which gave us plenty of reasons to stay out after skiing. A torchlight parade, fireworks, and laser shows lit up the evenings. The firefighters’ pancake breakfast was more my speed than the polar bear plunge, though watching people brave that freezing water was unforgettable. An ice-cream contest added another unlikely winter activity to the mix.

On our way to San Francisco, we stopped at the Jelly Belly factory. From there, the trip shifted into city mode: winding Lombard Street, cable car rides, Union Square, Chinatown, and North Beach.

One of the biggest surprises was having a local NFL player guide us to Alcatraz and take us to an arena football game in San Jose. Those outings made an already busy itinerary feel wonderfully unpredictable.

Biking across the Golden Gate Bridge was another highlight, and spotting whales gave us yet another reason to keep looking toward the water. Between Pier 39, an improv show, birthday celebrations, and shopping, we rarely ran short of things to do.

Looking back, I’m struck by how much variety we packed into fourteen days. I loved the famous sights, but the welcome we received in Tahoe stays with me just as clearly as the view from the bridge.

I'll admit it: I had never been to a Cape Cod Symphony concert until last weekend. What finally got me out the door was the program title, "Passport to Spain," and one piece in particular, Rodrigo's Concierto de Aranjuez. I've loved the guitar for years, so I couldn't pass up the chance to hear that famous slow movement performed live.

I expected a decent turnout. I did not expect a sold-out house of roughly 1,600 people packed into Barnstable High School. The energy in the room was wonderful, and I noticed plenty of younger faces scattered through the seats. It turned out a lot of local high school students were in attendance, and that shaped the entire evening in the best way.

Conductor Jung-Ho Pak didn't just raise his baton and launch into the music. He treated the concert almost like a lively classroom presentation. Before each piece, he turned to the audience and explained who the composer was and what we were about to hear. It never felt like a lecture. It felt like being let in on a secret.

He also brought out a flamenco guitarist, a singer, and a dancer, and each of them took a moment to describe their art form. Hearing the dancer talk about rhythm and then watching her footwork made the whole tradition click for me. There was even a film of the legendary guitarist Andrés Segovia. Throughout the night, Spanish paintings were projected above the stage, from El Greco all the way to Picasso.

One point Pak made has stuck with me. Many of the composers on the program, including Tchaikovsky, Bizet, and Rimsky-Korsakov, weren't Spanish at all. They were outsiders who dreamed up their own version of Spain, and somehow that imagined Spain became the one most of us recognize today. In other words, a visitor's postcard became the picture everyone remembers. I loved that idea, and I'll never hear those pieces quite the same way again.

I walked out humming and genuinely delighted. Better yet, the venue is just a short drive from home, so I have no excuse. I'll definitely be back for the next concert, and I might even bring a friend or two along.

It's difficult to pinpoint property locations from Colonial warrants and patents. The location of a tract of land is described in reference to another previously established tract of land. In Benjamin (I)'s case, his tract Posey's Chance, for example, was described in relation to Hornfair and Hopewell, two other tracts that he'd also eventually own. What is immediately clear, though, is that he managed to lease (it was a feudal system, so ownership was a fiction really) numerous adjoining tracts from Lord Calvert's "esquires." By doing so, he built a profitable plantation of 300+ acres.
Looking closely at early warrants for Posey's Chance and other tracts, the eye wanders to a strange name… "Panquiyah." William Henson, the author of the warrants, described the tracts as being part of Panquiyah Manor. It's a strange name. First, I thought it was an Indian name, but my searches led me to only one definite reference – a 1765 letter to Governor Sharpe from his Calvert lords describing a vast expanse of acreage that they recommend for immediate lease. They mention a 10,420-acre site called "Pancaya Manor," next to Beaverdam Manor – absolutely the same place as Panquiyah.
Digging a little deeper, I found that "Pancaya" is mentioned in only one other place… in a 1605 book called Don Quixote! It's not the first time I've seen the Colonists mock themselves (Maddox's Folly is the name of one relative's plantation), but this goes a step further. Don Quixote explains to his readers on page 249 that he's been duped… he fell early on in life for a fantasy of literature, and among those fantastical literary descriptions was "balsam of Pancaya" – an impossible poetic promise, like gold from the Tiber and pearls from the South Sea. Or a Colony of milk and honey.

The 38th annual Seattle Cherry Blossom and Japanese Cultural Festival in the Seattle Center's Armory was supposed to be the purpose of this morning's ad hoc Urban Sketchers gathering. But the day turned out warm and sunny enough that it seemed a shame to stay indoors, so I spent most of the morning sketching some of the Center's many attractions.
The Pacific Science Center's iconic arches have long been something I've wanted to sketch, but didn't dare. I knew that if I attempted their beautifully symmetrical webbing and intriguing shape with a precise pen point, I would get the perspective, angles and curves all wrong, if I had the courage to begin at all. So I took a cue from Liz Steel, whose blog I study regularly, who has been experimenting with water-soluble colored pencils to make loose, expressive drawings. Paradoxically, I used brush markers – my usual medium of choice when I need a loose line – to sketch the finer-stroked tree in front of the arches.
Performing outside the Armory was Quichua Mashis, a Seattle-based group that plays traditional music from the Andes Mountains. These Quichua Indians of northern Ecuador have become such a mainstay at outdoor events that I associate their lively music with scones, strawberry shortcake, flip-flops and everything else that is summer in Seattle. Today they played a few traditional tunes, but also "Hotel California," "The Sound of Silence", and "Let it Be." I don't know if their repertoire contains contemporary numbers because they like that kind of music or because they think we do, but I'll take their traditional music over the Eagles any day. (In fact, I did: After I finished my sketch, I bought a CD, specifically asking for one that contained traditional music.)
On my way back out to the bus stop, I decided to confront one more Seattle Center icon I've avoided previously. When the Urban Sketchers met last June to sketch a Habitat for Humanity demo site under construction, a number of sketchers took on the shining, amorphous blob that is the Experience Music Project. I chickened out, saving it for a braver day. Apparently, that day was today, although I took a baby step by sketching its back end, along with the monorail track.

This year, I made a quiet promise to myself: we are not going to do it all. Not every tradition, not every craft, not every invitation. And honestly? It has been one of the most peaceful holiday seasons our family has had in a long time.

For years I treated December like a checklist, and by the twenty-fifth everyone was frazzled, including me. This time we left some things undone on purpose and built real downtime into our days. Lazy mornings in pajamas. Afternoons with nowhere to be. The kids are calmer, the grown-ups are calmer, and the celebrations we do choose actually feel like celebrations instead of chores.

One of our favorite low-key activities has been making homemade gingerbread playdough. It smells like a bakery and keeps little hands busy for ages. If you try it, here's my best tip for messy crafts: pick up a few of those inexpensive clear plastic desk blotters from IKEA. They cover the table, wipe clean in seconds, and let you stop hovering over every crumb and smear. I keep ours stacked by the craft bin, and they've saved our table more times than I can count.

The kids also had their school Christmas parties this week. One came home proudly carrying a frosted graham cracker house, slightly lopsided and absolutely covered in candy. "Don't eat the roof," I was told firmly. It now has a place of honor on the counter.

I'll confess I didn't bake a single cookie this year. Instead, I made two batches of caramel corn, and it is dangerously irresistible. The first batch barely survived the afternoon, which is exactly why I made a second.

As the season winds down, I'm wishing you the same gift I've been given: a little less rushing and a little more resting. May you be surrounded by the people you love, and may your home be filled with peace. Merry Christmas from our slightly undone, very happy house to yours.

The French government is redefining the hashtag with a Gallic touch. The country that has an academy devoted solely to the use of the French language has given its official seal of approval to a new word for the Twittersphere: mot-dièse. For those of you not versed in the ways of Twitter, a hashtag is this little number-sign symbol — # — and when you put it in front of a word, it takes on several special functions, the chief of which is that the whole term becomes searchable. The hashtag is a versatile little tool that lets you find posts on a certain subject or centered around a certain event. For instance, those who were at March for Life in Washington, DC could tag their photos and tweets with the #MarchForLife hashtag and…voila! There they are. The funny thing, though, is that a hashtag has to be an unbroken string of letters, so mot-dièse could not, itself, be a hashtag. If you hashtagged (wait..how do you turn that French phrase into a verb?) the term, you'd get a nicely-broken tag that ended at the dash. Lastly, a hashtag isn't a sharp sign, which is what mot-dièse actually means. This (?) is a sharp symbol. A hashtag, which you probably also know from your phone as a pound sign, leans the other direction. Perhaps a better term in French would be mot de hachage, which is the rough French translation of "hash word", though I don't think that's the right "hash". Maybe we need to get some French social media nerds on the case.

I have been trying to organize a group of independent consultants and micro-businesses here in Sackville. This is a small town with a population of 5,000, plus the 2,400 students at Mount Allison University. I think that micro-businesses are very important because many of us have options on where we can live, as our clients are distributed, and the Internet has made distant/virtual work much easier. We could attract more "free agents" to our area, without significant infrastructure additions.
Having a number of micro-businesses in a small community provides a diverse and more stable economic base than having larger, single-focus firms. The closure of a few micro-businesses would not have the destructive effects as the closure of a single distribution centre, as happened here a few years back. As in nature, diversity in economies helps with adaptation and growth.
My aim over the past six months has been to find out how many people in our area work as non-retail, externally focused knowledge workers. I've set up a discussion board, but there hasn't been too much activity to date. I have a list of about 10 people/companies, but I'm sure that there are more.
I think that, as a group, we can do a few things:
1. Show that we are significant contributors to the local economy (anywhere from $500K to $2M, is my estimate)
2. Share information on being free agents, and help each other. So far, our monthly coffee meetings have generated some good conversations.
3. Look into creating a virtual storefront to share our stories, and perhaps attract others who would like to move to a lovely small town, with heritage homes and a great community to raise kids and enjoy the arts.
4. Lobby the three levels of government. If they are going to continue to play the economic development game, then we should have some input.
I'd love any comments or ideas on how to grow the Sackville SOHO Society.

Is it just me, or has everyone gotten a little grumpy this year? I love the Christmas season, I really do, but my recent shopping trips have left me wondering whether the holiday spirit got lost somewhere between the parking lot and the checkout counter.

Last week I was standing in line at the bookstore with a few gifts. A young man behind me was holding a single item and looked like he was in a hurry, so I waved him ahead. When he finished, I paused for maybe two seconds before stepping forward, and that was apparently two seconds too long. The woman behind me jabbed me in the back with a stack of hardcover books. "Some of us have places to be," she snapped. I was so stunned I just laughed.

A few days later, my daughter and I braved the mall together. We were hungry, so we went looking for something healthy to eat. Nothing. Just pretzels, cinnamon rolls, and fried everything as far as the eye could see. Then, while we were studying the directory, an elderly gentleman nudged us aside with his elbow so he could get a better look. My daughter turned to me with wide eyes and whispered, "Mom, what is happening to people?"

That was our cue. We gave up, drove home, and declared the rest of the day a holiday. We baked a batch of sugar cookies, wrapped presents at the kitchen table, and curled up on the couch to watch our favorite Christmas specials. By the time the credits rolled on the last one, we were giggling about the book lady and the elbow man instead of grumbling.

Here's what I took away from it all. The errands matter, and the gifts will get bought one way or another. But the moments with the people we love matter so much more.

Merry Christmas, happy holidays, and may your checkout lines be short and kind.

A community group in Chatham is leveraging local expertise with a highly ambitious goal: transforming the local school district into the top public STEM program in the state. Recently, ChathamSTEM organizer Nabil Mouline facilitated a powerful connection for Margaret Holzer, who directs Chatham High School's rapidly expanding Environmental Sciences program. Mouline introduced Holzer to energy entrepreneur Patrick Ryan and his son, a recent graduate of the high school.
