With residents and educators working hand in hand, Chatham is steadily building a premier model for modern science and technology education.

A 69-year-old Lake Andes man is once again facing criminal charges in connection with the shooting of horses belonging to his neighbors.

Ray Johanneson has been charged with five misdemeanor counts of killing or injuring horses owned by Lori Abdo-Smith and Charlie Smith. According to reports, four of the five animals died.

The new charges come after an earlier indictment against Johanneson was dismissed because it failed to list the names of witnesses, a procedural requirement. The charges have since been refiled.

The Smiths, who are American Indian, believe the shootings were driven by racial hostility toward their family. Johanneson, who is white, denies any racial motive and also denies shooting the horses.

Johanneson has said the dispute with his neighbors stretches back years. He maintains that the Smiths' horses repeatedly wandered onto his farmland and damaged his crops. He also says that on the same day the horses were harmed, he contacted the sheriff to report that horses in the area appeared to be starving.

The case highlights how a long-running property dispute between neighbors has become entangled with questions of race. For the Smiths, the loss of the animals represents more than a financial blow; they see it as a targeted act against their family.

Each of the five counts carries a maximum penalty of one year in jail and a $2,000 fine. If convicted on all counts, Johanneson could face significant combined penalties.

A jury trial is scheduled for August, when both sides will have the opportunity to present their accounts to jurors.

The first backboned creatures to conquer land were largely deaf, lacking anatomical features where tiny bones help transmit airborne sounds into the inner ear. Advanced hearing was assumed to have evolved shortly before the emergence of dinosaurs, roughly 200 million years ago.
Now, scientists have found that weasel-sized prehistoric reptiles from Russia apparently possessed the first modern ears 260 million years ago — perhaps the first-known specialized trait for living in the dark.
Paleobiologists uncovered large-eyed fossils of these reptiles with surprisingly advanced ears near the Mezen River in central Russia. They are a kind of now-extinct reptile called a parareptile.
The outside of the cheek in the reptiles was covered with a large eardrum. This structure was connected with the inner ear and the brain with a bone comparable to that in human ears.
The scientists estimate the reptiles of the Permian Period — numbering at least six species that reached roughly 1.5 feet (50 centimeters) in length — were able to hear at least as well as modern lizards.
"Animals with an excellent sense of hearing, such as cats, owls, or geckos, are all active at night or under low-light conditions," said researcher Johannes Mueller, a vertebrate paleontologist at Humboldt University in Berlin. "And maybe this is what these Permian reptiles did too."
The comparatively large eye sockets found in the new fossils, another typical feature of vertebrates living in the dark, suggest these reptiles might indeed have been among the first backboned land creatures to pursue a specifically nocturnal lifestyle.
These findings suggest early terrestrial animals and ecosystems were not as primitive as once assumed. "Although efficient hearing abilities and a nocturnal lifestyle seem to be nothing unusual in our modern world, they might have had revolutionary effects at this early time," Mueller told LiveScience.
These reptiles are part of a completely extinct lineage distantly related to turtles, lizards, snakes, crocodiles, birds and dinosaurs. The advanced ears we see today are thought to have evolved mostly independently of each other, Mueller explained.
"It would be interesting to investigate how often and when exactly modern ears evolved. For example, do the ears of modern lizards, crocodiles, and birds have a common origin or not?" Mueller said.

Lambeth Palace has released new details regarding an upcoming interfaith meeting in Qatar, where the Archbishop of Canterbury, Dr Rowan Williams, will join global scholars to discuss religious understanding. The highly anticipated three-day event in Doha, titled Building Bridges, is being hosted by the emir of Qatar. It serves as a continuation of an inaugural session held last year at Lambeth Palace, which saw the participation of prominent figures including Tony Blair and Cardinal Cormac Murphy-O'Connor.

Over the course of the gathering, approximately thirty Christian and Muslim scholars will deeply examine the role of scripture within both faiths. The agenda focuses on modern interpretations of sacred texts and specifically explores what each religion's writings say about the other. The comprehensive program is designed to include a thoughtful mix of public lectures and private, closed-door sessions to foster open and honest conversation. Following the event, organizers plan to publish a book that will formally record these vital discussions for wider public benefit.

Event coordinators have been careful to point out to the public that this meeting belongs to an ongoing scholarly dialogue. It was arranged well before the outbreak of the Iraq war, rather than being a reactionary measure to recent geopolitical tensions. The core focus remains strictly on long-term relationship building between the two major world religions.

Dr Williams highlighted the critical importance of this ongoing conversation. He emphasized that the primary goal of the gathering is "mutual learning and overcoming hostility." By engaging directly with each other's sacred scriptures, participants hope to build a robust foundation for lasting peace and deeper mutual respect and understanding in our increasingly interconnected world.

The Central Bank of Nigeria has urged MSMEs, especially in the rural areas, to partner with the Cooperative Financing Agency of Nigeria (CFAN) to benefit from some of its financial interventions.
A staff member of the Financial Inclusion Secretariat of the CBN, Mr George Ogudu, stated this yesterday in Abuja at a pre-seminar held towards the United Nations Cooperatives Day, which will hold on July 7.
"The CBN has a lot of interventions to help the poor come up to the level where they can live better, and one way they can key into this intervention is through CFAN, which we know as the registered body of cooperatives.
"We have our Micro and Small, Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) fund of N220 billion, 60% of which is earmarked for women," Ogudu said.
The Executive Secretary of CFAN, Mr Emmanuel Atama, spoke on the essence of the United Nations Day of Cooperatives, saying: "Saturday, the 7th of July, has been set aside by the United Nations through our global body, the International Cooperative Society, as the day of Cooperatives.
"On that day, we will talk to our members on how we have spent the last year, which dwelt on financial inclusion, and how we are going to spend the new year, where we will dwell on 'Sustainable Consumption and Production of Goods and Services', which is the theme for this year."
Atama said the pre-cooperative day seminar was a forum to meet with partners, like the Central Bank of Nigeria and others in the value chain, like the Sweet Mama Farms Ltd and Abagyi Housing Ltd, to rub minds with the apex bank on the direction of financing the value chain.

Grand Rapids South Christian’s girls golf team opened its season with a victory at the two-day Traverse City Central Invitational, giving the Sailors an early boost as they pursue a 17th consecutive Division 3 state finals appearance.

Senior Megan Wierenga led South Christian, while Grace Elenbaas, Nicole Hoekwater and Rachel Thuele also contributed to the team’s winning score. The Sailors finished ahead of runner-up Flint Powers Catholic and third-place Grosse Ile in the invitational’s Division 2–4 bracket. Farmington Hills Mercy won the Division 1 competition.

For South Christian coach Ron VanDyke, the tournament’s value extends beyond the final standings. He views the event as an important opportunity to prepare his players for the competition and demands they would encounter at the state finals.

The invitational attracts top talent from across Michigan, giving teams an early chance to measure themselves against strong opponents. Its two-day schedule and away-from-home setting also create an atmosphere similar to the season’s biggest tournament, making the trip a useful test for a program seeking to extend its long run of state finals appearances.

Teams alternated between the Spruce Run and Wolverine courses at Grand Traverse Resort. Narrow, tree-lined fairways challenged players on both layouts, placing a premium on accurate shots and careful decisions. Switching courses added another element to the competition, requiring golfers to adjust while maintaining their performance across two days.

Flint Powers Catholic’s second-place effort was led by standout Kristen Wolfe, whose play helped the team emerge as South Christian’s closest challenger in the Division 2–4 field. Grosse Ile rounded out the bracket’s top three.

For the Sailors, the opening victory combined a successful start with the kind of tournament experience VanDyke values: strong statewide competition, unfamiliar surroundings and two days of golf with a team result at stake.

A new campaign has been launched to protect essential medical services at Hastings Conquest Hospital. Sarah Owen, the Labour parliamentary candidate for Hastings and Rye, has officially teamed up with Lord Bassam of Brighton to firmly oppose any potential downgrading of local maternity and children's services.

The East Sussex Healthcare NHS Trust is currently holding a public consultation to review six proposed options for the future of paediatric and maternity care in the region. However, a major point of concern for local campaigners is that not a single one of these six options would maintain consultant-led maternity units at both the Conquest Hospital and Eastbourne District General Hospital.

Owen, who is a Hastings native, has voiced strong concerns about the severe impact these proposals could have on expectant mothers in the area. She argues that women experiencing complicated births should never be forced to endure a lengthy journey to Eastbourne during a medical emergency.

"Women dealing with complex deliveries need immediate, expert care close to home," Owen stated. "Forcing them to travel to Eastbourne in a high-stress emergency situation is unacceptable and puts both mother and baby at unnecessary risk."

The current debate surrounding these important medical facilities follows temporary changes made last year based on strict clinical advice. Under those previous adjustments, consultant-led maternity services were centralised at the Conquest Hospital, while the Eastbourne facility transitioned into a midwife-led unit. The new proposals aim to find a permanent solution for the region's healthcare provision, but residents are worried about losing specialized local care.

To ensure community voices are heard, a series of public consultation events are currently underway across the area. Local residents are being strongly encouraged to attend and openly share their views on the long-term future of these vital healthcare services. Among these events is a dedicated question-time session hosted by the independent health watchdog, Healthwatch, taking place in Hastings. Campaigners like Owen and Lord Bassam are actively urging the general public to participate and help safeguard local hospital services for future generations.

Minjae Lee is a mostly self-taught artist who uses seemingly old-fashioned tools, such as markers, pens, crayons, and acrylics, to create art that focuses on ethereal women. His newest works will focus on iconic women who range in celebrity from actresses to singers to models. The chosen women to be featured in this series of artwork reflect both his Korean and worldwide influences.
Minjae Lee is originally from Seoul, Korea, and this upbringing has dramatically influenced the art that he creates. His Korean roots have not been forgotten in his latest project. Korean stars, actress Bae Doona and singer Sora Lee, will grace his upcoming artwork.
Recognizable celebrities of glamour, such as Marilyn Monroe, Audrey Hepburn, and Elizabeth Taylor, will also be featured in Minjae's forthcoming work. However, these latest pieces will portray these Hollywood starlets like never before, in true Minjae style. In addition, Canadian Cover Girl Jessica Stram, Russian supermodel Natalia Vodianova, and Victoria's Secret's own Chanel Iman will be captured in Minjae's newest drawings.
Also to be spotlighted in this upcoming series of artwork are Japanese actress Yū Aoi, Italian model Monica Bellucci, Chinese singer Zhou Xun, American actress Devon Aoki, and Freida Pinto, star of the Academy Award-winning film Slum Dog Millionaire. Another exciting addition to this list of outstanding and iconic women is acclaimed Chinese singer Wong Faye.
Many of Minjae's past works have included ethereal female forms that are highly expressive and focus on human emotion, the blending of cultures, and the concept of the soul. These new pieces aim to continue in Minjae's signature style while portraying these iconic starlets.

Police told ABC11 that two armed suspects wearing masks went into the store around 7 p.m. and demanded cash, while two other men waited outside in a car.
During the robbery, two employees at the convenience store were shot. Both were taken to Cape Fear Valley Hospital to be treated for their injuries. Najib Bouzerda, 44, was in critical condition, and Mohamed Ould, 41, was in fair condition.
A store employee who worked a different shift told ABC11 that the two clerks were shot multiple times.
Walter Jaworski, who rents a room to Bouzerda, said the man works full-time at a hotel and just started working at the convenience store last month to make ends meet.
"He's in condition very bad actually on the life support machine [sic]," Jaworski said. ".. He was a very, very good guy and I pray to God that he's going to survive, everything's going to be alright."
Jaworski said Bouzerda felt the quick stop's location was a dangerous place.
"He knew when he started, even his girlfriend said, 'You better stay away from that area and don't work there, because the money's not that important risking your own life,'" Jaworski said.
After the shooting, all four suspects fled the scene in a dark colored vehicle. Police are still searching for the suspects.
Tuesday morning, authorities released surveillance video of two of the men during the robbery. They are asking anyone who recognizes the suspects or has information about the shooting to call detectives at (910) 433-1856 or CrimeStoppers at (910) 483-TIPS (8477).

DocFinity recently entered into a partnership with Xpertdoc, a Canada-based provider of document design, output and distribution services. The partnership will allow DocFinity to streamline the process of document production, reducing costs while increasing productivity, speed and quality. Xpertdoc President Varsha Bhat said it's a synergistic opportunity for them and for their customers. "Given that we provide high-volume generation of custom client communication documents – and since DocFinity provides storage, indexing, access, retrieval and complete lifecycle management of those documents – this alliance enables us to more effectively transform the way our customers do business and helps our clients easily realize significant productivity gains across their firms," she said. Xpertdoc solution accesses the full power of the Microsoft (News - Alert) platform for expressive, professional and compliant client communications. Ron Prichard, president of DocFinity, said Xpertdoc holds the same values as their company. "They're constantly working to ensure that they have sound technology, that their software is easy to work with, and that their customers get responsive, consistent service," he said. "The fact that we'll be able to work with them to make even greater strides in helping our customers streamline operations and improve productivity is a welcome opportunity." Headquartered in State College, PA, DocFinity is a product of Optical Image Technology, Inc. (OIT), a developer of business-improving products and services. Related news reports that DocFinity announced it has introduced its new Records Management module – a complementary addition to its enterprise content management (ECM) and business process management (BPM) software. The module is currently used by a number of companies in insurance, healthcare, higher education and a number of other markets.

Around 1,200 holidaymakers have been left stranded abroad after Birmingham-based travel agency Sun4U suddenly ceased trading, with many told they must now arrange their own way back to the UK.

The firm, which specialised in package holidays mainly to Spain, collapsed without warning, leaving customers scrambling for information about flights, hotels and refunds.

The company's failure has been blamed on heavy financial losses suffered during April's flight ban, when ash from Iceland's volcanic eruption grounded aircraft across Europe for days. Sun4U's problems were made worse by the earlier collapse of its main tour operator, Goldtrail Holidays, which had already caused widespread disruption to bookings for Turkey and Greece.

Travellers currently overseas are being urged to contact the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) or the supplier named on their booking invoice for guidance on getting home.

Whether customers are protected depends on what they bought. Those who booked a full package holiday, typically flights and accommodation sold together, are covered by the Air Travel Organiser's Licence scheme, known as ATOL. This government-backed scheme is designed to make sure package holidaymakers are not left out of pocket or stranded when a travel company fails.

However, customers who bought flights only through Sun4U are not covered. This is a key difference from travellers who paid an airline directly, who are generally in a stronger position if a booking agent collapses.

"If you booked a package, you should be protected, and you should keep hold of all your paperwork and receipts," said one consumer adviser. "Unfortunately, people who bought only flights through the agent may find themselves facing extra costs."

There may also be problems for holidaymakers already staying in hotels. Some accommodation providers may not have been paid by Sun4U, meaning guests could be asked to pay again for rooms they believed were settled. Anyone in this situation is advised to keep receipts so they can pursue a claim later.

Customers with upcoming trips booked through Sun4U are being advised to request refunds and make new arrangements as soon as possible, rather than waiting and risking further disruption to their travel plans.

The collapse is the latest blow to a travel industry still recovering from the chaos caused by the volcanic ash cloud earlier this year.

We all know the rating system for films; from G to X to everything in between, the combination of letters and numbers helps us determine what is appropriate for which age group. But a lot of people don't realize that there's a way to choose movies for people over 50, and "Jack Ryan: Shadow Recruit" has made the cut.
The AARP, an organization that advocates for adults over the age of 50, has given the film the first-ever "Movies For Grownups" seal, which came as a surprise to those who see the film as a younger, snappier version of the Jack Ryan films in past years; "The Hunt For Red October" is now a classic.
Of course, Jack Ryan is a Tom Clancy character, and Tom Clancy is very popular with adults, so it's not hard to see why the AARP would bestow their seal on "Shadow Recruit". Films with the seal have the option of choosing different promotional packages paid for by the organization, an added bonus. The "Movies For Grownups" idea has sparked awards shows and film festivals, giving the AARP bigger clout when it comes to their recommendations.
"From Paramount's side, it makes total sense to target mature adults because they're becoming a bigger and bigger force at the box office in terms of ticket sales," says Gitesh Pandya of BoxOfficeGuru.com.
The move to get more adults into theaters may be due to the declining number of teens and young adults queuing up at the box office. But a recent study by Morgan Stanley says that while many teens are still willing to pony up their cash to see a movie--rather than download it, like they do their music--the choice of films is often not high on their list of priorities. Young people, the study says, will gather at a theater for a group encounter and often won't even choose which movie they're seeing until they get there.

The federal government recently announced a significant intervention in public health, bypassing the state to provide 107 million dollars in direct funding to Victorian hospitals. This move comes after a prolonged and increasingly bitter dispute between federal and state leaders over healthcare funding responsibilities.

While stepping in to ensure hospitals remain operational was widely seen as the responsible choice, the execution of the announcement raised eyebrows. Federal officials appeared to time the release for maximum publicity. Furthermore, the decision to send money directly to hospitals rather than through state channels carried a clear implication: the Victorian government could not be trusted to distribute the funds properly. This approach has reinforced public perception that the standoff was driven more by political maneuvering than a genuine focus on patient care.

For the general public, the political games are entirely secondary. Patients and taxpayers simply want their local hospitals adequately funded and fully functional. When health budgets face shortfalls, the real world consequences are immediate and severe. Communities suffer through closed hospital beds, the loss of crucial medical staff, and the cancellation of vital elective surgeries.

Healthcare administrators on the front lines are breathing a sigh of relief. The chief executive of Ballarat Base Hospital publicly welcomed the financial injection, noting how critical the support is for regional health services. "We are incredibly grateful for this direct funding, as it allows us to keep beds open and maintain the high quality of care our community relies on," the chief executive stated, reflecting the sentiment of hospital leaders caught in the crossfire of the dispute.

Despite the immediate relief this financial boost provides, several major questions remain unanswered. Health policy experts are now watching closely to see if this direct federal funding model will be extended to hospitals in other states experiencing similar budget pressures. There is also uncertainty regarding exactly how these direct funding allocations will be calculated moving forward. Finally, the public is left wondering how Victoria will adjust its use of standard federal health money now that the federal government has set a precedent of stepping in directly. Ultimately, patients hope this signals a return to prioritizing care over political battles.

Particle physics research, hydroponics and landfill are among the potential future uses for the Stawell Gold Mines site.
The Stawell Gold Mines Future Possibilities project is in its final stage after the business case was presented to the Northern Grampians Shire Council and the project control group.
Between $2.4 million and $2.9 million of infrastructure investment is needed to prepare the site for the projects.
Council officers are seeking to attract investors for the upgrades.
Northern Grampians Mayor Kevin Erwin said all the projects could proceed simultaneously.
He said a decision to mine Stawell landmark Big Hill, which would be made at the end of the month, would not affect the future possibilities for the existing mine site.
"All those options can go forward even if the open cut at Big Hill does not or does go ahead," he said.
Cr. Erwin said progress was being made at the particle physics laboratory.
"They've got equipment down at depth testing the suitability of the decline for a lab in the future," he said.
The business case also recommends a proposed hydroponics enterprise on the site.
Cr Wayne Rice said the land suited hydroponics because it would not use contaminated soil.
"It was about working out what we could do with that land in the way of farming – there's some land on the northern side of the hill," he said.
Cr Rice said it was inevitable some mine workers would struggle to find work in Stawell after the mine's closure.
But he said some workers might find jobs with the new projects identified by the business case.
"The particle physics lab won't be happy with the existing underground network," he said.
"It will need new work done. There will be future jobs there to dig new pathways."
Cr. Erwin said using the Wonga Pit as a site for landfill would take years.

Toyota is bringing the 86 back to the Goodwood Festival of Speed, a year after its debut at the event, with a concept that puts weight reduction ahead of extra horsepower.

The TRD Griffon 86 Concept, developed by Toyota Racing Development, will take the spotlight after first appearing at the Tokyo Auto Salon. Its approach centres on a lighter body, a stiffer chassis and a selection of track-focused components.

Carbon fibre and reinforced-plastic body panels help cut weight, while polycarbonate windows replace conventional glass. Inside, the cabin adopts a racing-style layout, with specialised seating, controls and gauges. A Momo steering wheel and Takata belts reinforce the car’s competition-inspired character.

Underneath, the Griffon receives a mechanical limited-slip differential, designed to help manage traction at the driven wheels. Coilover suspension combines springs and dampers in adjustable units, while monoblock brakes form part of the upgraded braking package. The concept rides on 18-inch wheels fitted with Yokohama tyres.

Despite those extensive changes, Toyota has left the 2.0-litre boxer engine in standard form. Rather than seeking more power, the Griffon demonstrates how reducing mass and upgrading chassis components can reshape the priorities of a sports car built for track use.

Toyota’s Goodwood appearance will also include the UK debut of the FT86 Open convertible study. Alongside the stripped-back Griffon, the open-top concept offers visitors a different interpretation of the 86 formula, pairing the sports car’s familiar appeal with the prospect of roof-down driving.

The teenage wonderkid of Borussia Dortmund, Ousmane Dembele, has revealed his dream of playing for La Liga giants Barcelona one day. The 19-year-old French forward has termed the Catalan club as his ultimate destination.
Despite claiming to ultimately end up in Barcelona, Dembele has claimed that he is happy to currently feature for Dortmund in the German Bundesliga. He has revealed his desire to develop as a player in Germany before making his dream move to Spain.
"Not now, because I want to grow and be a protagonist every Sunday. But one day I will play for Barcelona." Dembele said, as reported by Mail Online, via Mundo Deportivo.
The man from Vernon, France, is already a regular starter in the Dortmund team. His start to life in Germany has been perfect, and he has already scored one goal for his club, including four assists in ten appearances in all competitions, according to Squawka.
Ousmane Dembele was scouted by a number of big European clubs before he chose to join Dortmund last summer. Among those big clubs chasing for the player's signature, Claudio Ranieri's Leicester City, who are the reigning Premier League champions, were also involved.
However, the former Rennes man decided to commit his recent future to Thomas Tuchel's Dortmund. Based on his initial performances for the German club, it seems that the player has made the correct decision.
If Dembele wants to ultimately play for Barcelona, Dortmund could be the perfect stepping stone for him. Dortmund and Dembele will be involved in Bundesliga action this week on October 14 against Hertha Berlin at the Westfalenstadion.

When it comes to stealth action on the PS2, all people want to talk about is Snake, Snake, Snake. The latest Metal Gear offering is one of the most anticipated games on the console, but you don't have to wait until November if you're jonesing to tiptoe through the shadows. The PlayStation crowd got a little taste of Tom Clancy's Splinter Cell franchise last year, but it was nothing compared to the buffet that will be coming in a few weeks. A smash hit on the Xbox, Splinter Cell: Pandora Tomorrow is sure to make some people forget about a certain snake eater.
Plot-wise, Pandora Tomorrow is the same on both consoles. You again play as Sam Fisher, a secret agent for Third Echelon, an ultra hush-hush government agency charged with saving the free world from terrorists, maniacal dictators, and a broad range of ne'er-do-wells. Of course, evil has a tendency to spread rapidly across the world, and the latest version of Splinter Cell escapes the dreary Eastern European locales of the last game and transports Sam to the steamy jungles of Indonesia, with some brief side jaunts to France and America. It seems that a charismatic Indonesian guerrilla leader has gotten his hands on some particularly nasty bio-weapons (how topical!), and he's getting ready to show the U.S. of A that he means business. We all know that Sam's not going to let that happen, though.
In order to keep the game running smoothly, the developers had to do a bit of tweaking on some of the stages. While the majority of the levels are the same on both consoles, there have been a few changes made for the PS2 version. I noticed that certain rooms and areas that were accessible in the Xbox version were locked or blocked off, and that there weren't as many destructible lights. This actually changed the gameplay in many of the levels, since you couldn't simply shoot out all of the lights and lure the unsuspecting guards to their deaths. In many ways, this actually made getting through the levels more satisfying, since you had to rely more on sneaking between patches of darkness, and less on creating your own shadows.

Two sets of twins at St Dominic's Grammar School in west Belfast have earned a combined 18 A* grades and 17 As in their GCSEs, far exceeding their hopes of securing the results needed to continue to A-levels.

Niamh and Aisling McGarrity, alongside Seainin and Colleen Maxwell, were celebrating at the school on the Falls Road after discovering how well they had performed.

For non-identical twins Niamh and Aisling, who studied different subjects, opening their results brought both delight and surprise. Niamh achieved one A* and seven As, while Aisling secured two A*s and five As.

The sisters had arrived hoping to pass well enough to take the next step in their education. Instead, they left with a collection of top grades, contributing three A*s and 12 As to the four girls' combined total.

Sixteen-year-old twins Seainin and Colleen Maxwell collected their results with their mother, who joined them as they discovered their achievements.

Seainin earned six A*s and four As. Colleen received nine A*s and one A, joking about the French result that stood out as her only grade below an A*.

Between them, the Maxwell sisters achieved 15 A*s and five As. Both now plan to study science subjects at A-level, with their GCSE results providing a strong foundation for that next stage.

Their mother credited the girls' hard work for their success and thanked the school for its support.

For all four pupils, results day turned expectations of simply doing well enough to progress into a celebration of exceptional achievement. Although the McGarrity sisters had taken different subjects and each pupil received her own mix of grades, both pairs of twins had plenty to celebrate together.

Gamers eagerly awaiting the next generation of console gaming finally have a clear look at what to expect right out of the box. Microsoft recently published an exclusive Xbox One unboxing video on its official Xbox Wire blog. Hosted by Larry Hryb, better known to the gaming community as Major Nelson, the video showcases the highly anticipated limited Day One Edition of the console. This special release rewards early adopters with unique packaging, a commemorative controller featuring exclusive branding, and a special digital achievement to mark the occasion.

Diving into the packaging, Major Nelson reveals an impressive array of hardware. Front and center is the fully redesigned Kinect sensor. Built for enhanced precision, the new Kinect features a stunning 1080p high-definition video camera, an infrared blaster for seamlessly interacting with your television, and a four-microphone array to clearly capture voice commands. Also included is the new wireless controller. In a convenient upgrade from previous generations, this controller can now connect and recharge using a standard Micro-USB cable, ensuring players never have to worry about abruptly losing power during an intense multiplayer match.

Audio enthusiasts will be pleased to learn that a dedicated chat headset is confirmed and included in the package. Microsoft stated that this new headset provides roughly triple the audio quality of the standard Xbox 360 earpiece. It is designed for maximum comfort with a reversible fit, and it features easily accessible volume and mute controls directly on the controller base. Rounding out the included accessories are a standard HDMI cable, the external power supply, a basic instruction manual, and an exclusive branded sticker.

The star of the show, of course, is the glossy black Xbox One console itself. The sleek entertainment hub is equipped with dual-band Wi-Fi for a reliable wireless internet connection, a modern slot-loading Blu-ray drive, and high-speed USB 3.0 ports. Turning the system around reveals a robust selection of rear ports designed to make it the ultimate center of your living room. These include both HDMI in and out ports, optical audio, infrared connections, an Ethernet port for wired networking, and a security lock.

Fans of mixed martial arts who pick up EA Sports' new UFC video game may notice something missing from Carlos Condit. The digital version of the fighter appears without the scowling lion tattoo that covers his right side, an omission tied to an earlier legal dispute, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The artwork was created by Chris Escobedo, a tattoo artist based in Phoenix. Escobedo, who had studied intellectual property law, took action after THQ, the developer behind a previous mixed martial arts game, reproduced his lion design on Condit's in-game character without asking his permission. He filed a lawsuit against the company, which has since gone bankrupt.

The case was eventually settled for an undisclosed amount. Escobedo has said the dispute was not just about money. He wanted recognition that artists deserve to be consulted when their original work is copied and used in commercial products.

EA declined to comment on its decision to leave the tattoo off Condit's character in the new title.

The fallout has been personal for Escobedo. Many gamers and fight fans blamed him for the change, and he has faced mockery and harassment online from people upset that a familiar part of the fighter's look disappeared. Escobedo also says the dispute cost him his longtime friendship with Condit.

The episode highlights a growing question for the video game industry as developers push for ever more realistic athletes. Who owns the ink on a player's skin, and is permission from the person wearing it enough?

A dog may just be voted most popular pup at a Virginia high school after his photo appeared in the school yearbook.
Alpha, the 3-year-old dog, is 16-year-old Andrew "A.J." Schalk's service dog that has been attending school with him at Stafford High School for the past year and a half.
Schalk suffers from Type 1 diabetes, and Alpha alerts his owner if his blood sugar is dangerously high or low.
"It's been absolutely fantastic," Schalk told InsideEdition.com. "He's turned into such a positive thing for me to have, being diabetic and to take around the school."
And everyone else loves him, too.
"[He] brightens everybody's day. All the teachers I have look forward to seeing him, just seeing this adorable little puppy walk around," Schalk said.
Schalk said Alpha gives him a paw to notify him if he is in danger and has saved his life on multiple occasions.
"Being diabetic and having a disability, you wouldn't think that'd be something positive, but taking him to school every day and having everyone react so positively to him has had a positive effect on my life," Schalk said. "It's changed it into something for me where I am excited to take him to school."
Students were happily surprised when they noticed the pup in the yearbook.
"Well, I had just gotten my yearbook and was flipping through when I noticed a dog. I realized it was AJ's service dog, and I thought it was so cute," Diana Bloom, a student at the school, told InsideEdition.com. "He has a very important job and works just as hard as any other student, so he deserves it."
Alpha wasn't the happiest about having his photo taken in front of the giant yearbook camera, Schalk said, but his picture was priceless. Alpha also received a school ID card.
"On picture day, I went and took my picture. I moved out of the way. They lowered the camera a little bit and took his picture," Schalk said. "He did fantastic. He's a great dog."

At its annual Think Conference held this past March, IBM unveiled a technological marvel that pushes the boundaries of modern microelectronics. The company showcased what it is officially calling the smallest computer in the entire world. Measuring just one millimeter by one millimeter, this microscopic device is smaller than a single grain of salt and costs less than ten cents to manufacture.

Despite its incredibly tiny size, the device packs a serious punch. It features an x86 processor equipped with approximately one million transistors, along with built-in SRAM memory. To operate without traditional batteries, the computer relies on a microscopic solar cell for continuous power. It also utilizes an LED and a photodetector, which allow it to achieve two-way communication. This means the tiny machine is fully capable of collecting, processing, transmitting, and acting on highly valuable data.

This groundbreaking device is a major component of the "5 in 5" initiative launched by IBM Research. This ambitious program seeks to merge artificial intelligence, blockchain networks, advanced encryption, and the Internet of Things to solve complex global challenges. Company researchers describe this specific computer as a "crypto-anchor." A crypto-anchor is essentially a highly secure, tamper-proof digital fingerprint that can be embedded directly into everyday goods.

By embedding these microscopic computers into consumer products, companies can reliably verify authenticity at every step of the global supply chain. Experts note that this innovative approach creates a highly secure future where widespread product counterfeiting is nearly impossible, as the new technology guarantees that the products consumers buy are exactly what they claim to be.

Consumers will not have to wait decades to see this technology in action. IBM anticipates that the first working prototypes will be ready for testing within the next eighteen months. Furthermore, they expect to see these tiny computers integrated into commercial products within five years, completely transforming how we track and secure manufactured goods worldwide.

Finding your way around Troy Night Out just got easier. Gavant Software, a technology company based in downtown Troy, has created a free smartphone app for the popular monthly event, which takes place on the last Friday of every month and invites visitors to explore the city's shops, eateries and cultural spaces.

The new app takes the place of the printed map that organizers have distributed each month, a sheet that has grown to include more than 60 listings. Instead of unfolding paper on a street corner, visitors can now use their phones to locate participating businesses and search for restaurants, galleries, exhibits and live music venues.

What sets the app apart is its playful, sensory-based design. Rather than sorting listings in a traditional directory, the interface groups them into categories such as Do, Look, Taste and Touch. Tapping any one of these opens a map showing the venues that fit that description, so someone craving a bite to eat or hoping to browse local artwork can quickly see what is nearby.

The app is available now for both iPhone and Android devices, giving users time to download it before the next Troy Night Out on March 29.

Gavant's founder described the project as a gift to the community, timed to celebrate the company's tenth anniversary. For a firm rooted in downtown Troy, supporting an event that draws people to local businesses was a natural way to give back to the neighborhood it calls home.

While the Troy Night Out app has a hometown focus, Gavant has built software for well-known clients including Getty, ExpertFlyer and GlobalFoundries. Looking ahead, the company hopes to grow its reach and take on work beyond New York State.

Bennett’s Business Systems has turned a shift to enterprise-grade technology into a sharp sales gain, reporting a 46 percent increase without expanding its 25-person sales force after five years of flat sales.

The company, which sells and services copiers and other business imaging equipment, made the change under Wes Benwick, its CEO and CIO. His approach was to replace difficult-to-integrate systems with a platform that would let a small technology team focus on tools for the business rather than maintaining hardware.

Benwick had grown dissatisfied with the copier industry’s proprietary accounting software, built on the Cobol programming language. As integration became more difficult, the software presented an obstacle to connecting business functions. Meanwhile, an internally developed telesales application had failed to scale, limiting its usefulness as the company sought to improve sales performance.

Rather than continue building around those constraints, Benwick moved financial and sales functions to Salesforce.com. The shift freed the IT team to develop custom tools and create reports using MySQL, a database system. That work supported the company’s existing salespeople, giving the technology operation a more direct role in helping the sales force.

The resulting sales increase was especially notable because Bennett’s did not add sales representatives. After a five-year stretch with no sales growth, the company achieved its 46 percent jump with the same size team. For Bennett’s, the move showed that enterprise-grade systems could support growth without a corresponding increase in sales staffing.

Benwick did add developers, but kept technology support staffing to a minimum. He outsourced email, spam filtering, data center operations and e-commerce hosting, avoiding the burden of managing the underlying hardware internally.

That division of responsibilities put outside providers in charge of routine infrastructure while leaving Bennett’s developers to concentrate on applications and reporting tailored to the company. The strategy was not simply to buy larger-scale software: it was to redirect limited IT resources toward work that could help the business sell more, while reducing the time spent supporting the systems behind it.

On 1 November, New Zealand took a major step toward bringing its overseas citizens back home with the launch of a highly anticipated, comprehensive new website. Designed specifically to lure expatriates back to the country, the online platform offers a wealth of resources. These useful features include extensive job listings, practical relocation guidance, and detailed information on local schools and the vibrant arts scene.

Immigration Minister David Cunliffe officially announced the launch, emphasizing the government's commitment to reconnecting with its global diaspora. He described the website as the "first step in a wider programme" designed to help the approximately 500,000 New Zealanders currently living overseas make a smooth return. According to Cunliffe, the timing could not be better. He pointed to the nation's remarkably strong economy and an unemployment rate of just 3.7 percent as key indicators of a thriving job market. Because of this economic growth, local employers are experiencing a high demand for skilled professionals across various industries.

To back up the exciting initiative, Cunliffe cited recent survey findings which revealed that the majority of expatriates either actively plan to return home or are seriously considering the possibility. The new website aims to turn those intentions into reality by simplifying the transition process.

A dedicated marketing official from the Department of Labour explained the user-friendly layout of the platform. He noted that the site is carefully organized around four main pillars: living, working, leisure, and moving home. This intuitive structure allows returning citizens to easily navigate the logistical and lifestyle aspects of relocating to New Zealand.

The official also provided a broader context for the initiative, warning that the global landscape for talent acquisition is shifting. He explained that ageing populations and shrinking workforces worldwide will inevitably intensify the global competition for skilled workers in the coming years. By launching this dedicated website now, New Zealand is proactively positioning itself to attract its own homegrown talent before other nations can recruit them. This strategic move highlights the country's dedication to securing a robust and skilled workforce for the future.

Surrounded by family, Tarcia Patton hasn't left Loyola University Medical Center since her son Jermaine Cullum was rushed here last weekend after the 16-year-old collapsed while playing in a suburban basketball tournament.
While Patton came here hopeful, reality has set in. She has made the difficult decision to take Jermaine off life support.
"It was so hard, I couldn't think right, I just wanted him to get up, I just knew he wasn't going to get up," she said.
Doctors told Patton that Jermaine had lost all brain activity and he could not breathe on his own.
Jermaine collapsed after going into cardiac arrest. Patton says her son had an unexplained, rare heart condition that no one knew about until it was too late.
Two spectators at the basketball game, a nurse and a doctor, performed CPR on Jermaine. Their aid helped the teenager regain a pulse, something his mother is grateful for.
"If they did not do what they did at the basketball court, I wouldn't be able to say goodbye to my son," Patton said. "He would have passed away on that court."
And now Patton wants to give back by donating Jermaine's heart to Loyola for research, not only to find answers about her son, but for others.
"I made the decision because I know his condition is rare," she said. "I want to help other kids out there that might have the same rare disease he might have with his heart."
"Anytime anything happens that is inexplicable, we have to have the opportunity to pursue tissue diagnosis to learn something," said Dr Jeffrey Winterfield, Loyola University Medical Center.
Dr Winterfield and Patton also encourage high school athletes to get thorough physical exams from their paediatricians. Winterfield says if there are any red flags, he recommends taking the screening one step further with an electrocardiogram.
Right now, there is no nationwide mandatory screening program for high school athletes.

Norfolk is set to receive about £5.4 million in extra government funding to repair potholes, with county council leaders welcoming the announcement as an urgently needed boost for the county’s roads.

The allocation is part of a £168 million national fund launched by the Department for Transport. Councils receiving a share must sign a “pothole pledge”, committing them to carry out an agreed number of repairs by next March.

Toby Coke, chairman of Norfolk County Council’s environment and transport committee, said officials would need to examine the terms of the funding and establish whether the authority could meet the conditions attached. However, he said he hoped repairs could begin quickly.

The additional money comes on top of £3.7 million already allocated to Norfolk for weather-related road damage. Together, the two allocations amount to roughly £9.1 million, although the latest award carries its own requirements for pothole repairs.

Ministers say the national scheme will allow councils to repair three million potholes across the country. They also hope the programme will reassure residents that action is being taken to improve roads.

For Norfolk, the announcement offers the prospect of more funding to address a problem council leaders have described as pressing. The immediate task will be to review the government’s conditions before moving ahead with work supported by the new allocation.

The pledge makes the March deadline central to the scheme, requiring councils to commit to a defined number of repairs rather than simply receive an extra contribution towards road maintenance.

Elizabeth Colbert Busch, the Democratic nominee in the special election in South Carolina's First Congressional District, said in a statement released Wednesday that she's opposed to the budget that will be put forth by President Barack Obama, citing the proposal's lack of spending cuts and tax breaks for small businesses.
Colbert Busch is squaring off with former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford (R) in the special election, which is scheduled to be held on May 7.
"I respectfully disagree with the budget that President Obama is expected to present today because it simply doesn't take the right steps to put our fiscal house back in order – especially from my perspective as a businesswoman. The fact is, we have to balance our budget, cut our spending and lower taxes for small businesses to create jobs. Unfortunately, this budget takes the opposite approach; it raises taxes, doesn't balance and doesn't cut enough – when we should be laser-focused on slashing wasteful and duplicative spending.
"Not only does President Obama's plan fail to put our finances back in order, but it would also cut benefits for our seniors, which is wrong. I believe that our seniors earned their Social Security by putting money away every single paycheck for a lifetime, knowing that they could count on Social Security when they retired. Just this week, I met with seniors at Island Oaks Living Center, and they told me how much they worked and depend on Social Security – and I will stand with them. Simply put, Social Security doesn't contribute to the deficit, and politicians should keep their hands off the trust fund.
"Between President Obama's budget and Representative Paul Ryan's plan, neither one has a fiscal approach that is acceptable to South Carolina families. The people of the 1st Congressional District need a representative who will fight for those values in Washington – restoring fiscal responsibility without throwing our seniors under the bus. As a tough and independent businesswoman, I'll fight for a balanced budget amendment, cut wasteful spending and lower taxes on small businesses."

Forest officials in the Sunderbans have launched an urgent survey to assess how many tigers and prey animals may have died after Cyclone Aila sent tidal waters surging across large parts of the world's largest mangrove forest.

Teams of forest guards, joined by members of local forest protection committees, have fanned out across the tiger reserve to search for carcasses. Their efforts are concentrated in the east and sanctuary ranges. These areas bore the brunt of the storm surge, and the damage to wildlife there is feared to be greatest.

Early estimates suggest that hundreds of prey animals, including deer and wild boar, may have been swept away by the floodwaters. Officials are also worried that as many as a dozen tigers could have been lost. That would be a serious blow for one of the most important habitats of the endangered Royal Bengal tiger.

"We are combing every creek and island we can reach," said a senior forest department official involved in the survey. "Our priority is to understand the scale of the loss as quickly as possible so we can plan the next steps."

A wildlife expert familiar with the region warned that the death toll could be high. The Sunderbans, a low-lying maze of islands and tidal channels, offers very little high ground where animals can seek safety when water levels rise sharply.

"When a surge of this size comes in, there is simply nowhere for the animals to go," the expert said. "Many bodies may have been carried out to sea or buried under mud, so we may never know the true number."

Beyond the immediate losses, officials fear a dangerous knock-on effect. With prey suddenly scarce, surviving tigers may be driven by hunger to stray out of the forest and into nearby villages. Many of those villages are themselves still under water after the cyclone.

Forest staff have been asked to remain on high alert along the reserve's edges. Villagers are being urged to report any tiger sightings immediately to help prevent dangerous encounters between people and the big cats.

Microsoft is making it easier for software developers to build applications that share and synchronize data seamlessly. According to Jack Ozzie, a development executive at Microsoft's Groove Networks unit, the company has officially updated its Simple Sharing Extensions specification to version 0.91.

Often referred to simply as SSE, this networking technology was first introduced last year by Microsoft Chief Technology Officer Ray Ozzie, Jack’s brother. SSE defines a set of minimal extensions that allow software applications to share data using standard RSS feeds and OPML outlines. While traditional RSS is widely known across the web for one-way publishing, allowing users to conveniently subscribe to news and blog updates, SSE transforms this familiar process into true bidirectional synchronization. This means data can flow both ways between applications and connected devices, keeping information perfectly updated across different platforms without relying on complicated backend infrastructure.

When introducing the technology to the public last year, Ray Ozzie famously referred to SSE as "the RSS of synchronization." The recent update to version 0.91 brings several key technical improvements, most notably enhancing the independent replication of hierarchical items within the sharing structure.

In addition to the specification update, Microsoft is addressing a growing demand from developers who want practical ways to implement the technology in their daily projects. The company has officially released a comprehensive "SSE 101" tutorial to help programmers get started quickly and easily. This educational package includes detailed documentation, practical sample code, and ready-to-use XML files.

Jack Ozzie noted that the technology is already seeing exceptionally strong support from the outside developer community. By providing these helpful new tools and clarifying the exact specification, Microsoft hopes to encourage even broader adoption of SSE. For developers looking to build interconnected software applications, this recent update represents a significant step forward in making two-way data sharing as simple and universal as reading a daily news feed.

The sky's the limit for what you can find at the 59th Houston International Boat, Sport and Travel Show. The event has seen a surge in attendance because of the rising interest in boating.
"This is a boat sport and travel show."
Dave Foulkrod with the Boat Show says there's something for everyone.
"This year's show, I think they probably start at a couple of hundred dollars, in terms of a kayak or what you can buy there, all the way up to, as I understand, there's probably a million and a half dollar boat in the show, but there are more small boats in the show this year. Camille NulI says if kayaking is your preference:
