An inspection of Glasgow Royal Infirmary has found that nurses on several wards repeatedly had to remind doctors to follow dress code and infection-control rules, despite most staff complying with the standards. The hospital was given four improvement requirements, including one month to enforce its dress code.

Healthcare Improvement Scotland inspectors saw medics at patients’ bedsides wearing watches or outdoor jackets, or with long hair left loose. Their findings highlighted a need for consistent compliance across staff groups, rather than nurses having to keep correcting colleagues during their work on wards.

Another requirement focused on the storage and cleaning of equipment on one ward, where inspectors found three contaminated commodes. Most other equipment examined was clean, but the findings identified an area where further action was needed to meet the hospital’s infection-control standards.

Despite the shortcomings, the chief inspector acknowledged good overall progress at the hospital. The assessment presented a mixed picture: widespread adherence to infection-control measures and evidence of improvement, alongside specific concerns about doctors’ dress and the condition of some equipment.

NHS Greater Glasgow & Clyde welcomed the inspection’s positive findings, including praise for staff communication, hand hygiene and cleanliness. The health board said it had a plan to address the remaining problems. Its response recognised both the progress highlighted by inspectors and the work still required following their visit.

The one-month deadline applies to enforcing the dress code, making compliance an immediate priority for the hospital. The findings also draw a distinction between generally clean equipment across the areas inspected and the contaminated commodes on one ward, where storage and cleaning were singled out for improvement.

Descending from the elaborate spiral staircase at the center of his DD172 media compound last night, Roc-A-Fella founder Damon Dash greeted a crowd to introduce 'Kinetic' – his gallery's current art show that comments on history in a multitude of pieces. "I'm all about controversy," he explained to a knowing crowd. "Where's the drama in this show?"
According to the Dash Gallery director, Nyssa Frank, the show's drama is in history. The exhibit mirrors the pastiche of past, present and future that often makes hip-hop so enjoyable. In one piece, artist Andrew Russell Thomas has created a totem structure out of found materials, floor speakers and a microphone that freely swings, creating a hypnotic feedback loop spurred on by physical interaction from the audience. Another favorite was a video from Shani Peters that nostalgically samples characters from 'The Cosby Show' and 'Good Times' and splices them into conversations with former Black Panther founder Bobby Steale (who is also sampled on 'Tears of Joy' off of Rick Ross' new album, 'Telfon Don'). There is a series of vinyl records next to the screen that feature poems written in response to the Sean Bell verdict. Each record sports an etched diagram of Africa.
Much has been made of Dash's recent evolution, but it's fascinating to actually see his new venture in action. As the show's artists explained their work, guitar notes fluttered throughout the building, a tap dancer prepared to perform, and various artists, musicians and photographers buzzed around the space. Recently, hip-hop fans are most familiar with Dash's patronage of Curren$y, Ski Beatz and last year's Blakroc project, but he's equally focused on fostering a creative environment for the fine art world, too.

The hardcore fans will always have some criticism for BioWare, but that negative feedback seemed to reach a boiling point after Dragon Age II arrived.
We maintain that the game was still great, but it wasn't elite. It wasn't vintage BioWare in terms of overwhelming quality, and it wasn't a role-playing lover's RPG. But the developers say they plan to take the best parts of Dragon Age: Origins and DAII, and create one heck of a game in Dragon Age III. In speaking to PC Gamer, BioWare CEO Ray Muzyka talked about the team's plans:
"The team is going to have some things that are going to surprise both sets of fans, both core fans and new fans, with a marriage of the best from both games, Dragon Age: Origins and Dragon Age 2."
Muzyka said there were lots of 90+ reviews for DAII, but the scores would decline if a critic had expected Origins, so "there was a misalignment of expectation there." But they take their core fans very seriously, and they fully intend to make 'em happy. Added Muzyka:
"One of the core values of Bioware is that we take feedback really seriously, and we know that the core fans who were expecting more Dragon Age Origins – we have to respond to that – we're not willing to ignore that, we're going to take that head on."
The bottom line is that BioWare will take feedback from both sets of fans - those who were disappointed with DAII and those who weren't - and incorporate all of it into the next entry. So ideally, we'll receive the best of both worlds...and that's appealing, isn't it?

One of the world's biggest fashion publications has recently revamped its online presence. Dazed and Confused, founded by Jefferson Hack and photographer Rankin, has already built up a large, diverse following amongst a loyal international group of the culturally inclined. With their new site, which went live on the seventh of September, after a period of hiatus with nothing but a countdown visible, they've cemented their position as one of the most advanced and forward-thinking British publications. The launch, which presented a splash screen and a simultaneous user counter, explaining that the new site would be revealed when the counter reached 10,000, was a clever way of pushing people to the site's launch. Those who were there from the beginning faced a 20-minute wait; whether that builds frustration or anticipation is up for debate. A comprehensive navigation bar as the header gives access to different categories, promoted content, Facebook and Twitter buttons, as well as the most viewed and newest articles. This can also be brought up at any time by clicking the 'show navigation' bar, which is fixed to the top of the screen; the bottom is occupied by smaller Twitter, Facebook and mailing list icons. The pieces below, crafted in HTML5 (a first for a British magazine), are a mosaic of text and pictures. Dazed's content is of a high calibre, and the infinite scrolling coupled with an image optimisation engine ensures the presentation is complementary. The layout allows for neat integration of other elements, such as the newsletter subscription bar and adverts. With the aesthetic being so refined, Dazed could be making increased online revenue, which can only serve to further their, thus far, unparalleled approach. Dazed has handled social media with aplomb, with over 140,000 followers on Twitter and over 3 million page impressions per month. With AnOther and AnOther Man under the same ownership, it will be interesting to see their future online strategy as well as, of course, Dazed's competitors – such as i-D.

At the moment, there are various representations on different search engines depicting Fermi bubbles towering above and below the galaxy.
Stanford Scientists, along with the Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory, analyzed the data of NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which was gathered around four years earlier. Along with this data, the scientists also found the other data gathered from experiments to create the most detailed portrait of two towering bubbles that spread and stretch tens of thousands of light-years below as well as above our galaxy.
The bubbles that shine brightly in energetic gamma rays were found almost four years ago by a Harvard astrophysicists' team, led by Douglas Finkbeiner, the man who combed through data from the main instrument of Fermi, the Large Area Telescope.
According to the new portrait that has been explained in a paper, there are various puzzling features of the towering bubbles. The portrait has been accepted for publication by the Astrophysical Journal editors.
The outlines of bubbles are very sharp, and the bubbles themselves glow in uniform gamma rays over their surfaces. The size of these bubbles is another puzzle.
Malyshev's co-lead, KIPAC postdoctoral researcher Anna Franckowiak, stated that the work of researchers is very challenging when it comes to studying these bubbles. She said, "Since the Fermi bubbles have no known counterparts in other wavelengths in areas high above the galactic plane, all we have to go on for clues are the gamma rays themselves."
She even said that creating the portrait was an extremely difficult task for the researchers. "We had to remove all the foreground gamma-ray emissions from the data before we could clearly see the bubbles."
The scientists, as well as researchers, are looking forward to having their questions answered by Fermi, which is still gathering everything it can for them.

HTC appears to be preparing to enter the crowded tablet market, and if the latest rumors hold true, its first slate will run Google's Android operating system on Nvidia's Tegra 2 processor. That pairing is hardly unique. Roughly a dozen tablets built around the same chip and software have been announced, though none has yet reached store shelves.

According to reported specifications, the HTC device would feature a 1280×720 multi-touch display, 32GB of solid-state storage and 2GB of RAM, a generous amount of memory for a mobile device. Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and GPS are also said to be included. There has been no word on whether the tablet will carry a camera.

What could set HTC apart is not the hardware but its relationships. The Taiwanese manufacturer has built strong ties with North American wireless carriers, supplying popular smartphones to several of the biggest networks. Those partnerships could give its tablet prominent placement in carrier stores and help drive sales. Carrier subsidies, in which a provider lowers the upfront price of a device in exchange for a service contract, could also take a bite out of the rumored price of about US$790.

Industry watchers point to Nokia as a company that could learn from HTC's approach. Despite its global reach, the Finnish phone maker has struggled to secure the kind of carrier backing in the United States that HTC enjoys.

Competition will be fierce. Samsung's Galaxy Tab is set to launch on all four major U.S. carriers by Christmas, giving it a significant head start. Meanwhile, Notion Ink's Adam is drawing attention for its Pixel Qi display, a screen technology designed to remain readable in bright sunlight while conserving battery life.

With so many similar devices vying for attention, success this holiday season will come down to execution and features. For HTC, a strong carrier lineup may be its best advantage.

A deep-sea sonar vehicle searching for missing Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 has been lost after colliding with a submerged volcano in the Indian Ocean.
The sonar vehicle -- known as a towfish -- collided with a 2,200-meter mud volcano on Sunday. The vehicle and 4,500-meter cable attaching it to the Fugro Discovery search vessel are now on the ocean floor.
Australia has been leading the search for MH370 at the request of the Malaysian government. Fugro, a Dutch company that provides deep-sea surveys, later received a contract to join the search.
The Boeing 777 disappeared after leaving Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, en route to Beijing with 239 people on board. During the flight, the plane veered off course over the Indian Ocean between Malaysia and Vietnam. Investigators are unsure why the plane went off route.
"The towfish collided with a mud volcano, which rises 2,200 meters from the seafloor, resulting in the vehicle's tow cable breaking. The towfish and 4,500 meters of cable became separated from the vessel and are now resting on the seafloor," the Australia's Joint Agency Coordination Center said in a statement. "There were no injuries to the crew, and it is believed it will be possible to recover the towfish at a later date."
Meanwhile, a curved barnacle-encrusted piece of metallic debris weighing more than 200 pounds found Saturday on a beach in Thailand has been identified as likely a piece from a Japanese H-2 rocket -- not from MH370 -- due to the placement of bolts and numbers etched on it resembling the rocket's honeycomb launch fairing.
"It is very likely that the debris which has been discovered in Thailand is part of a rocket which [Mitsubishi Heavy Industries] launched from Japan in the past," Kengo Tatsukawa, public relations manager for Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, told VOA News.
Malaysian officials and a Thai aviation team will head to the Nakhon Si Thammarat province, where it was found, to inspect and collect the metal debris.

Audio enthusiasts and tech lovers have a new reason to celebrate as Chord Electronics officially unveiled the highly anticipated Hugo TT 2 at this year's Munich High End Show. Serving as the direct successor to the widely popular original Hugo TT, this new model takes everything fans loved about the desktop oriented, larger version of the portable Hugo DAC and elevates it to entirely new heights. With a clear display and full high fidelity connectivity, the latest iteration is designed to be the ultimate centerpiece for any serious home audio setup.

At the heart of the new device is a powerful Artix 7 FPGA chip, custom programmed by renowned digital design consultant Rob Watts. This advanced internal architecture delivers an astonishing five times the processing power of the original model. According to the company, this massive leap in processing capability results in vastly superior noise shaping and an overall cleaner, more detailed audio performance.

One of the most significant upgrades found in the new unit is its power delivery system. Chord has completely bypassed the old battery supply in favor of cutting edge supercapacitors. This innovative change allows the device to deliver the massive peak currents required to effortlessly drive even the most demanding headphones on the market.

When it comes to connectivity, the device leaves nothing to be desired. The rear panel is fully loaded with inputs, including optical, coaxial, high resolution USB, and aptX Bluetooth for those who prefer high quality wireless streaming. On the output side, users will find balanced XLR, standard RCA, and BNC connections, alongside three separate headphone sockets on the front panel to accommodate a variety of listening setups.

User experience has also been refined. The device now features tactile front panel buttons and comes with a dedicated remote control for easy adjustments from across the room. Listeners can customize their experience using selectable audio filters and a crossfeed function to simulate a traditional speaker presentation through headphones. Furthermore, it operates in three distinct modes, functioning seamlessly as a standalone DAC, a dedicated headphone amplifier, or a digital preamp.

The new device is officially scheduled to arrive this autumn with a retail price of £3,996.

A North Charleston woman is behind bars after police say an argument over music escalated into a knife attack against her former boyfriend.

Vernett Bader, 54, was arrested Monday night and charged with high and aggravated criminal domestic violence. Under South Carolina law, this serious charge can apply when an assault involves a deadly weapon or causes significant injury.

According to a police report, the trouble began when the man, Bader's former boyfriend who still shared her home, was playing songs by The Eagles. Bader reportedly objected to the music. When the man told her to be quiet, the situation quickly turned violent.

Police say Bader repeatedly attacked him with a large serrated bread knife. The man suffered cuts to his arms and hands as he tried to defend himself. After he managed to take the knife away from her, Bader reportedly grabbed a second one. The man then fled into the bathroom to escape.

When officers arrived, Bader told them the man had choked her. However, according to the report, officers found no marks on her consistent with that claim. A neighbor also gave police an account that supported the victim's version of events.

Investigators noted that everyone involved had been drinking.

Bader was taken into custody and booked into the Al Cannon Detention Center. Information about a bond hearing or whether she has an attorney was not immediately available.

South Carolina treats domestic violence cases involving weapons with particular seriousness. The state has long ranked among those with the highest rates of women killed by men, and advocates encourage anyone experiencing abuse to seek help early.

Anyone who needs support can contact the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233. The hotline offers free, confidential assistance 24 hours a day.

Sleep disorders are associated with numerous health consequences, and now a new study shows that a link may exist between sleep difficulties and attention deficit disorder in adults.
People with sleep disorders may also have mood disorders, neuromuscular diseases, and other problems, according to Clifford Risk, MD, PhD, director of the Marlborough Center for Sleep Disorders in Marlborough, Mass.
Approximately 30 million Americans suffer from obstructive sleep apnea. The most common complaints are loud snoring, disrupted sleep, and excess daytime sleepiness.
Obstructive sleep apnea causes repetitive blockage of the airways during sleep. The muscles that keep the airways open collapse, and air cannot get to the lungs. Medical conditions such as cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, and diabetes are associated with obstructive sleep apnea. Smoking is also linked to this sleeping disorder.
The researchers studied 34 people with obstructive sleep apnea. Nearly half of the group (16 people) showed signs of possible or probable attention deficit disorder.
All the participants were then given continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), the most widely used treatment for obstructive sleep apnea.
CPAP uses a machine that delivers forced air through a mask over the nose (and sometimes also the mouth) to keep the airway open.
After CPAP treatments, the participants' daytime sleepiness score improved. Average scores dropped from a 12 to around 3 on a scale of 0-24, with 24 being the most severe rating. The same group reported improvement in attention deficit scores from 17 to a score of 10, a significant change according to the researchers.
In addition, nine of the 16 patients with possible or probable attention deficit disorder, based on having moderate to severe attention deficit scores, improved their attention scores after CPAP.
In an interview with WebMD, Risk says sleep apnea is "highly correlated" with attention deficit disorder and that treating apnea can improve attention deficit. However, some apnea patients may continue to have attention deficit problems after CPAP due to "anxiety, depression, or other disorders," he says.
Risk and colleagues also studied smaller groups of people with insomnia.

A US delegation of 4 senators - John McCain, Joseph Lieberman, Sheldon Whitehouse and Kelly Ayotte - began a three-day visit to the Philippines, designed to promote bilateral relations and discuss the issue of the South China Sea (which Manila calls the West Philippines Sea) and the conflicting territorial claims between China and the Philippines.
McCain, while discounting the possibility of a confrontation with China, insisted that the US would collaborate with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) to preserve freedom of navigation. For this reason, he said, the US and the Philippines had to foster greater collaboration.
Joseph Lieberman emphasized the US interest in the issue because the waterway was a valuable trade route to Asia and impacted the global economy. "We simply cannot allow one nation, in this case China, to exercise disproportionate control over these waterways," he said to the obvious approval of his hosts.
Lieberman again scored with his hosts by pledging to bolster the Philippine military, "Somebody once said that the best way to secure peace is to prepare for war, which is to say to remain strong."
The US will not reestablish military bases in the Philippines. These were shut down in the early 1990s. The US expects to signal its support via joint military operations and the supply of modern American ships and equipment to the Philippines.
Another area where the guests sided with the Philippines against China was in their support for multilateral diplomacy by the ASEAN nations against China. The Chinese have insisted that bilateral diplomacy that maximizes Chinese preponderance was the best route. The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei and Taiwan all favor the multilateral approach that allows them to pool their strength when confronting China.
Joseph Lieberman said, "We're not gonna let those claims to be settled by force or by bullying," he said. "We're going to make sure to the best of our ability that they're settled as a matter of negotiations, multilateral negotiations and international rule of law."

Archaeologists working alongside a Bristol Water pipeline project in North Somerset have uncovered Roman remains described as the most significant discoveries in the Banwell area for a century.

The finds came to light as the company laid a new seven-kilometre water main between Banwell and Hutton, part of a £3.6 million investment in the local supply network. Archaeologists monitoring the excavation work realised the route passed through a site of historical importance.

Among the most striking discoveries is what appears to be a Roman cemetery containing multiple burials. Experts believe the graves reveal a change in funeral customs over time, with the community moving away from cremation towards inhumation, the practice of burying the body intact. The cemetery is thought to have served a villa belonging to a wealthy landowner who once farmed the surrounding countryside.

The team also recovered around 9,000 fragments of pottery, along with copper brooches and a coin dating from the reign of Constantine the Great, the emperor who ruled during the early fourth century and was the first Roman emperor to embrace Christianity.

Despite working in challenging, muddy conditions, the archaeologists identified traces of earlier activity on the land. Evidence of farming, possibly dating back to the Iron Age, suggests people were cultivating the area long before the Romans arrived in Britain.

Residents will soon have the chance to see the artefacts for themselves. The finds are set to go on display at an event organised by the local archaeology society, offering a rare glimpse into Banwell's ancient past.

Mercedes has announced the addition of karting champion and Formula 4 (F4) racer Paul Aron to its F1 junior programme.
Aron is currently racing for Prema Powerteam in the ADAC (German) and Italian F4 championships, which is his first year in single-seater racing. Prior to that, Aron had a sensational season in the karting arena with multiple titles.
He won the CIK-FIA European OK Junior Championship, along with wins in the South Garda Winter Cup – OKJ and also the WSK Champions Cup – OK Junior. In addition, the Estonian finished third in the WSK Super Master Series – OKJ.
In his first year in single-seater competition as a rookie in the ADAC F4 series, Aron sits fifth in the standings after two rounds with his maiden win at Red Bull Ring. He is second in the rookie standings with 93 points to the leader's 103 so far.
In the Italian F4 series, the 15-year-old is ninth in the drivers' standings after two rounds, with the best of fourth with 22 points. He is third in the rookie standings with 53 points to the leader's 83 so far. Paul is the younger brother of Ralf, who raced in F3 until the recent past.
This is Mercedes' third junior signing after officially introducing karters Andrea Kimi Antonelli and Alex Powell back in April. With Esteban Ocon and George Russell, it makes for five drivers in their junior F1 programme for the upcoming season.
It is interesting to note that Mercedes is going after younger junior racers and not anyone already racing in the Formula 3 or Formula 2 categories, especially after facing difficulties in putting Ocon in an F1 car after he lost his Racing Point seat to Lance Stroll.

Kate Gosselin has made an unlikely new friend: A biker.
On a special episode of TLC's American Chopper, Thursday, motorcycle builders Senior, Junior and Mikey Teutul popped by the Gosselins' Pennsylvania home to help Jon custom-make a chopper. (The Teutul family also brought Kate a custom pink Vespa.)
As Jon chatted with Senior and Junior about his bike, Kate got to know Mikey. "When I got down there, she came out and sat down, and I sat next to her," said Mikey, who added that Kate "wasn't bothered" by the motorcycle crowd. "I thought she would be more intimidated. We threw blows a little bit. And in a matter of minutes, we were like old friends. I had the chance to spend most of the day with her; she even got on the bike with me."

Trevecca, ranked 17th in the NAIA, kept its strong start to the season rolling Friday afternoon with an 11-6 home victory over Bethel (Ind.). The win improved the Trojans to 8-2, while Bethel remained winless on the young season.

Trevecca wasted little time getting on the scoreboard, jumping out to a 2-0 lead after the first inning. Bethel answered in the third, scratching across two runs to even the game and briefly shift the momentum.

The Trojans responded right away. In the bottom of the third, Trevecca's lineup strung together a four-run rally to regain control. The home team then broke the game open in the sixth, plating five more runs to build a commanding 11-3 advantage.

Bethel refused to go quietly. The visitors mounted a late push in the ninth, adding three runs to make the final score more respectable, but the deficit proved too large to overcome.

Nick Shoup set the tone on the mound for Trevecca. The starter earned the win after working six solid innings and striking out seven batters, keeping Bethel's hitters off balance for most of his outing. Ben Johnson took over from there and pitched the final three innings to close out the victory.

At the plate, Marty Parks led the way with a perfect day, finishing four-for-four. His steady production helped fuel a balanced Trojans attack that also got key contributions from Dylan Lynch, Landry Walker, Adam Bland and Aaron Bree.

Daniel Halley was charged with the loss for Bethel, which continues to search for its first win of the season.

The two teams have little time to rest. They are set to meet again Saturday in a rescheduled doubleheader, giving Trevecca a chance to extend its momentum and Bethel another opportunity to break into the win column.

MBC’s “Section TV” offered viewers an emotional look at the farewell to “Infinite Challenge” on April 2, airing behind-the-scenes footage from the long-running variety show’s final shoot and wrap party.

The scenes captured the close bonds built over 13 years, as cast members and production staff struggled to contain their feelings after filming ended. Yoo Jae Suk comforted tearful staff members, while Jung Joon Ha openly wept. Before leaving the set, the group gathered for a commemorative photograph, marking the end of their time together on the show.

The farewell continued at a restaurant, where more than 100 cast and crew members assembled for a wrap party. MBC’s president attended the gathering, praised “Infinite Challenge” and presented a plaque recognizing the program. The occasion gave those who had worked on the series a chance to celebrate its run while saying their goodbyes.

Throughout the gathering, the members made time to thank staff individually and sign autographs. Those personal exchanges followed the emotional moments on set, keeping the focus on the people whose work had sustained the program over the years.

In interviews shown during the report, the cast reflected on the love viewers had given “Infinite Challenge” throughout its 13-year history. They also discussed the support they had received from one another, the memorable nicknames associated with their time on the show and the hard work behind its long run.

Yoo Jae Suk offered a straightforward answer about how he would spend the Thursdays previously reserved for filming: he planned to rest. His response highlighted a change in routine after years of returning to the program’s regular shooting schedule.

Producer Kim Tae Ho, meanwhile, expressed hope that “Infinite Challenge” could return in an improved form in the future. His comments looked beyond the farewell, even as the footage centered on the cast and crew bringing this chapter to a close.

Together, the final-shoot scenes, restaurant celebration and interviews presented a farewell shaped by gratitude—to the viewers who had supported the show and to the colleagues who had spent years making it together.

By using dozens of Twitter accounts, researchers at Texas A&M University are creating "honeypots," or fake accounts that are supposed to lure spammers, who are eager to spread malware or phish for information, to social networks. And their work is being partially supported by a research grant from an unlikely source -- one of Twitter's online competitors, Google. From the Technology Review:
The honeypot accounts, like http://twitter.com/tayBourne, automatically post updates drawn from a collection of 120,000 real tweets harvested from Twitter. The team has also deployed honeypots on MySpace and created software that uses dummy profiles on both networks to learn about spammer tactics. "We have a bot monitor who contacts our profiles," says [ Kyumin ] Lee. "It looks at what they put in their messages and also accesses their profile to see their demographic information and past updates."
So far, Lee says, "Our 61 honeypots tempted and collected 30,867 spammers on Twitter."
The fake accounts try not to mimic a real person and are allocated to a dark address space, and legitimate users are segregated from the spammers.
Lee said that most of the spammers pretend to be (surprise!) college-age females from California and (shock!) target men. Why is it so prevalent on social network sites? Social networks like Twitter and Facebook are extremely vulnerable to phishing because users tend to trust their social networks more, and due to the widespread use of URL shorteners.
Google funding research isn't new. Its Google Research Blog chronicles most of the projects it funds, including a book on text processing, human-computer social interaction and other computer science research. Ridding the world of spammers is obviously a necessity for anyone using a computer and definitely for Internet entrepreneurs, so Google's money is well-spent -- even if it also helps its competitors.
Next on Lee's research agenda on Google's dime: Facebook.
